Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One.

Saṃyuttanikāyo

The Connected Discourses

Khandhavaggo

The Section on the Aggregates

1. Khandhasaṃyuttaṃ

1. The Connected Discourses on the Aggregates

1. Nakulapituvaggo

1. The Chapter on Nakulapitā

1. Nakulapitusuttaṃ

1. The Discourse to Nakulapitā

1. Evaṃ [T 3.0001][V 2.0001][P 3.0001][M 2.0001] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire suṃsumāragire (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Atha kho nakulapitā gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho nakulapitā gahapati bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

1. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, a sanctuary for deer. Then the householder Nakulapitā approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said this to the Blessed One:

“Ahamasmi[V 2.0002], bhante, jiṇṇo vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto āturakāyo abhikkhaṇātaṅko. Aniccadassāvī kho panāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato manobhāvanīyānañca bhikkhūnaṃ. Ovadatu maṃ, bhante, bhagavā; anusāsatu maṃ, bhante, bhagavā; yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

“Venerable sir, I am old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and have reached the final stage. I am afflicted in body and constantly ailing. And, venerable sir, I am not able to see the Blessed One and the mind-developing monks constantly. May the Blessed One, venerable sir, advise me; may the Blessed One, venerable sir, instruct me, for what will be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.”

“Evametaṃ, gahapati, evametaṃ, gahapati! Āturo hāyaṃ, gahapati, kāyo aṇḍabhūto pariyonaddho. Yo [T 3.0002] hi, gahapati, imaṃ kāyaṃ pariharanto muhuttampi ārogyaṃ paṭijāneyya, kimaññatra bālyā? Tasmātiha te, [M 2.0002] gahapati, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘āturakāyassa me sato cittaṃ anāturaṃ bhavissatī’ti. Evañhi te, gahapati, sikkhitabba”nti.

“So it is, householder, so it is! This body, householder, is afflicted, frail, and enveloped. For who, householder, while carrying this body around, would claim even a moment of health, except out of foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘Though my body be afflicted, my mind will be unafflicted.’ Thus, householder, should you train yourself.”

Atha kho nakulapitā gahapati bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā [P 3.0002] anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho nakulapitaraṃ gahapatiṃ āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca – “vippasannāni kho te, gahapati, indriyāni; parisuddho mukhavaṇṇo pariyodāto. Alattha no ajja bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṃ kathaṃ savanāyā”ti?

Then the householder Nakulapitā, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. To the householder Nakulapitā sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this: “Householder, your faculties are serene; your facial complexion is pure and bright. Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk today in the presence of the Blessed One?”

“Kathañhi no siyā, bhante! Idānāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya amatena abhisitto”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, gahapati, bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya amatena abhisitto”ti? “Idhāhaṃ, bhante, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno khvāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ahamasmi, bhante, jiṇṇo vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto āturakāyo abhikkhaṇātaṅko. Aniccadassāvī kho panāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato manobhāvanīyānañca bhikkhūnaṃ. Ovadatu maṃ, bhante, bhagavā; anusāsatu maṃ, bhante, bhagavā; yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’”ti.

“How could it not be so, venerable sir! Just now, venerable sir, I have been sprinkled by the Blessed One with the deathless water of the Dhamma discourse.” “But how, householder, were you sprinkled by the Blessed One with the deathless water of the Dhamma discourse?” “Here, venerable sir, I approached the Blessed One; having approached, I paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable sir, I said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, I am old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and have reached the final stage. I am afflicted in body and constantly ailing. And, venerable sir, I am not able to see the Blessed One and the mind-developing monks constantly. May the Blessed One, venerable sir, advise me; may the Blessed One, venerable sir, instruct me, for what will be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.’”

“Evaṃ vutte[T 3.0003], maṃ, bhante, bhagavā etadavoca – ‘evametaṃ, gahapati, evametaṃ, gahapati! Āturo hāyaṃ, gahapati, kāyo aṇḍabhūto pariyonaddho. Yo hi, gahapati, imaṃ kāyaṃ pariharanto [V 2.0003] muhuttampi ārogyaṃ paṭijāneyya, kimaññatra bālyā? Tasmātiha te gahapati, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – āturakāyassa me sato cittaṃ anāturaṃ bhavissatīti. Evañhi te, gahapati, sikkhitabba’nti. Evaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya amatena abhisitto”ti.

“When this was said, venerable sir, the Blessed One said this to me: ‘So it is, householder, so it is! This body, householder, is afflicted, frail, and enveloped. For who, householder, while carrying this body around, would claim even a moment of health, except out of foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train thus: “Though my body is afflicted, my mind will be unafflicted.” Thus, householder, should you train yourself.’ Thus indeed, venerable sir, was I sprinkled by the Blessed One with the deathless water of the Dhamma discourse.”

“Na hi pana taṃ, gahapati, paṭibhāsi bhagavantaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ (sī.) uttariṃ paṭipucchituṃ – ‘kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, āturakāyo ceva hoti āturacitto ca, kittāvatā ca pana āturakāyo hi kho hoti no ca āturacitto’”ti[M 2.0003]? “Dūratopi [P 3.0003] kho mayaṃ, bhante, āgaccheyyāma āyasmato sāriputtassa santike etassa bhāsitassa atthamaññātuṃ. Sādhu vatāyasmantaṃyeva sāriputtaṃ paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho”ti.

“But, householder, did it not occur to you to ask the Blessed One further: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is one afflicted in body and also afflicted in mind? And to what extent is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind?’” “Indeed, venerable sir, we would come even from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this utterance. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this utterance were to become clear to the Venerable Sāriputta himself.”

“Tena hi, gahapati, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho nakulapitā gahapati āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosi. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

“In that case, householder, listen and attend carefully. I shall speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Nakulapitā responded to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Kathañca, gahapati, āturakāyo ceva hoti, āturacitto ca? Idha, gahapati, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ [T 3.0004] vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpa’nti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpa’nti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

“And how, householder, is one both afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? Here, householder, an uninstructed ordinary person—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in the noble Dhamma; who has not seen good people, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of good people—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He is one who abides obsessed with the thought: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ For him who abides obsessed with the thought ‘I am form, form is mine,’ that form changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise in him.

“Vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā vedanaṃ, vedanāya vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ vedanā, mama vedanā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ vedanā, mama vedanā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, sā vedanā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa vedanāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

“He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He is one who abides obsessed with the thought: ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine.’ For him who abides obsessed with the thought ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine,’ that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise in him.

“Saññaṃ attato samanupassati, saññāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā saññaṃ, saññāya vā [V 2.0004] attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ saññā, mama saññā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ saññā, mama saññā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, sā saññā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa saññāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

“He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He abides obsessed with the thought: ‘I am perception, perception is mine.’ For one who abides obsessed with the thought ‘I am perception, perception is mine,’ that perception changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.

“Saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, saṅkhāravantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā saṅkhāre, saṅkhāresu vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ saṅkhārā, mama saṅkhārā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ saṅkhārā, mama saṅkhārā’ti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, te saṅkhārā vipariṇamanti [T 3.0005] aññathā honti. Tassa saṅkhāravipariṇāmaññathābhāvā [P 3.0004] uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

He regards volitional formations as self, or the self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in the self, or the self as in volitional formations. He abides obsessed with the thought: ‘I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.’ For one who abides so obsessed, those volitional formations change and become otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of the volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.

“Viññāṇaṃ [M 2.0004] attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ viññāṇaṃ, mama viññāṇa’nti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ viññāṇaṃ, mama viññāṇa’nti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, āturakāyo ceva hoti āturacitto ca.

He regards consciousness as self, or the self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in the self, or the self as in consciousness. He abides obsessed with the thought: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.’ For one who abides so obsessed, that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. Thus indeed, householder, one is afflicted in body and also afflicted in mind.

“Kathañca, gahapati, āturakāyo hi kho hoti no ca āturacitto? Idha, gahapati, sutavā ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpa’nti na pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpa’nti apariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

And how, householder, is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple—a seer of the noble ones, skilled in the noble Dhamma, well-trained in the noble Dhamma; a seer of good persons, skilled in the Dhamma of good persons, well-trained in the Dhamma of good persons—does not regard form as self, or the self as possessing form, or form as in the self, or the self as in form. He does not abide obsessed with the thought: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ For one who does not abide so obsessed, that form changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the changing and becoming otherwise of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.

“Na vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, na vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā vedanaṃ, na vedanāya vā attānaṃ[T 3.0006]. ‘Ahaṃ vedanā, mama vedanā’ti na pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ vedanā, mama vedanā’ti apariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, sā vedanā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa vedanāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

He does not regard feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He does not abide obsessed with the thought: ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine.’ For one who does not abide obsessed with this thought, that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of that feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.

“Na [V 2.0005] saññaṃ attato samanupassati, na saññāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā saññaṃ, na saññāya vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ saññā, mama saññā’ti na pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ saññā, mama saññā’ti apariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, sā saññā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa saññāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

He does not regard perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He does not abide obsessed with the thought: ‘I am perception, perception is mine.’ For one who does not abide obsessed with this thought, that perception changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of that perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.

``Na [P 3.0005] saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, na saṅkhāravantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā saṅkhāre, na saṅkhāresu vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ saṅkhārā, mama saṅkhārā’ti na pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ saṅkhārā, mama saṅkhārā’ti apariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, te saṅkhārā vipariṇamanti aññathā honti. Tassa saṅkhāravipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

He does not regard volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations. He does not abide obsessed with the thought: ‘I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.’ For one who does not abide obsessed with this thought, those volitional formations change and become otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of those volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.

“Na [M 2.0005] viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā viññāṇaṃ, na viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. ‘Ahaṃ viññāṇaṃ, mama viññāṇa’nti na pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hoti. Tassa ‘ahaṃ viññāṇaṃ, mama viññāṇa’nti apariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino, taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti[T 3.0007]. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, āturakāyo hoti no ca āturacitto”ti.

He does not regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. He does not abide obsessed with the thought: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.’ For one who does not abide obsessed with this thought, that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise. Thus, householder, one is afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind.”

Idamavoca āyasmā sāriputto. Attamano nakulapitā gahapati āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

The Venerable Sāriputta said this. The householder Nakulapitā, being pleased, greatly delighted in what was said by the Venerable Sāriputta. The first.

2. Devadahasuttaṃ

2. The Devadaha Sutta

2. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu sakyesu (ka.) viharati devadahaṃ nāma sakyānaṃ nigamo. Atha kho sambahulā pacchābhūmagamikā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “icchāma mayaṃ, bhante, pacchābhūmaṃ janapadaṃ gantuṃ, pacchābhūme janapade nivāsaṃ kappetu”nti.

2. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in a market town of the Sakyans named Devadaha. Then a number of monks who wished to go to the Pacchābhūma country approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, we wish to go to the Pacchābhūma country and to take up residence in the Pacchābhūma country.”

“Apalokito [V 2.0006] pana vo, bhikkhave, sāriputto”ti? “Na kho no, bhante, apalokito āyasmā sāriputto”ti. “Apaloketha, bhikkhave, sāriputtaṃ. Sāriputto, bhikkhave, paṇḍito, bhikkhūnaṃ anuggāhako sabrahmacārīna”nti. “Evaṃ [P 3.0006] bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ.

2. “But, monks, have you taken leave of Sāriputta?” “Indeed, Venerable Sir, we have not taken leave of the Venerable Sāriputta.” “Monks, take leave of Sāriputta. Monks, Sāriputta is wise, a supporter of his companions in the holy life.” “Even so, Venerable Sir,” those monks replied in assent to the Blessed One.

Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato avidūre aññatarasmiṃ eḷagalāgumbe nisinno hoti. Atha kho te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā sāriputtena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ [T 3.0008] sāraṇīyaṃ sārāṇīyaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavocuṃ – “icchāma mayaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, pacchābhūmaṃ janapadaṃ gantuṃ, pacchābhūme janapade nivāsaṃ kappetuṃ. Apalokito no satthā”ti.

Now at that time the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain Eḷagalā thicket. Then those monks, having greatly delighted in and rejoiced at what was said by the Blessed One, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, they exchanged joyful greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having concluded the talk that was joyful and memorable, they sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, those monks said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the Pacchābhūma country and to take up residence in the Pacchābhūma country. We have taken leave of the Teacher.'

“Santi [M 2.0006] hāvuso, nānāverajjagataṃ bhikkhuṃ pañhaṃ pucchitāro – khattiyapaṇḍitāpi brāhmaṇapaṇḍitāpi gahapatipaṇḍitāpi samaṇapaṇḍitāpi. Paṇḍitā hāvuso, manussā vīmaṃsakā – ‘kiṃvādī panāyasmantānaṃ kiṃvādāyasmantānaṃ (pī. ka.) satthā kimakkhāyīti, kacci vo āyasmantānaṃ dhammā sussutā suggahitā sumanasikatā sūpadhāritā suppaṭividdhā paññāya, yathā byākaramānā āyasmanto vuttavādino ceva bhagavato assatha, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyātha, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyātha, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo vādānupāto (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pāṭhantaraṃ) gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā’”ti?

“Friends, there are those who would question a monk who goes to various regions—wise nobles, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics. People are wise, friends, and inquisitive: ‘What does your Teacher advocate? What does he proclaim?’ Have the teachings been well-heard, well-grasped, well-attended to, well-borne in mind, and well-penetrated by wisdom by you, venerable sirs, so that when explaining, you would be speaking in accordance with what was spoken by the Blessed One, not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no reasoned assertion or counter-assertion would give cause for reproach?”

“Dūratopi kho mayaṃ, āvuso, āgaccheyyāma āyasmato sāriputtassa santike etassa bhāsitassa atthamaññātuṃ. Sādhu vatāyasmantaṃyeva sāriputtaṃ paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho”ti. “Tena hāvuso, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

“Friend, we would come even from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good indeed if the meaning of this statement would become clear to the Venerable Sāriputta himself.” “In that case, friends, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks assented to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Santi [P 3.0007] hāvuso, nānāverajjagataṃ bhikkhuṃ pañhaṃ pucchitāro – khattiyapaṇḍitāpi [V 2.0007] …pe… samaṇapaṇḍitāpi. Paṇḍitā hāvuso, manussā vīmaṃsakā [T 3.0009] – ‘kiṃvādī panāyasmantānaṃ satthā kimakkhāyī’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, āvuso, evaṃ byākareyyātha – ‘chandarāgavinayakkhāyī kho no, āvuso, satthā’”ti.

“Friends, there are those who would question a monk who goes to various regions—wise nobles... and wise ascetics. People are wise, friends, and inquisitive: ‘What does your Teacher advocate? What does he proclaim?’ When asked thus, friends, you should answer in this way: ‘Our Teacher, friends, proclaims the removal of desire and lust.’”

“Evaṃ byākatepi kho, āvuso, assuyeva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchitāro – khattiyapaṇḍitāpi…pe… samaṇapaṇḍitāpi. Paṇḍitā hāvuso, manussā vīmaṃsakā – ‘kismiṃ panāyasmantānaṃ chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, āvuso, evaṃ byākareyyātha – ‘rūpe kho, āvuso, chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’”ti.

“Indeed, friends, even when it is explained thus, there will certainly be those who ask further questions—wise nobles... and wise ascetics. For, friends, wise people are inquisitive; they may ask: ‘In what, then, does the venerable ones’ Teacher teach the removal of desire and lust?’ When asked thus, friends, you should answer in this way: ‘Friends, our Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust in form, in feeling, in perception, in formations, and in consciousness.’”

“Evaṃ byākatepi kho, āvuso, assuyeva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchitāro – khattiyapaṇḍitāpi…pe… samaṇapaṇḍitāpi. Paṇḍitā hāvuso, manussā vīmaṃsakā – ‘kiṃ panāyasmantānaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā rūpe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, āvuso, evaṃ byākareyyātha – ‘rūpe kho, āvuso[M 2.0007], avigatarāgassa avītarāgassa (syā. kaṃ.) avigatachandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu avigatarāgassa…pe… avigatataṇhassa tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā [T 3.0010] uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Viññāṇe avigatarāgassa avigatachandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Idaṃ kho no, āvuso, ādīnavaṃ disvā rūpe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’”ti.

“Indeed, friends, even when it is explained thus, there will certainly be those who ask further questions—wise nobles... and wise ascetics. For, friends, wise people are inquisitive; they may ask: ‘Seeing what drawback, then, does the venerable ones’ Teacher teach the removal of desire and lust in form, in feeling, in perception, in formations, and in consciousness?’ When asked thus, friends, you should answer in this way: ‘Friends, for one in whom lust, desire, affection, thirst, feverishness, and craving for form have not departed, due to the alteration and becoming otherwise of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. For one in whom lust... and craving for feeling, perception, and formations have not departed, due to the alteration and becoming otherwise of those formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. For one in whom lust, desire, affection, thirst, feverishness, and craving for consciousness have not departed, due to the alteration and becoming otherwise of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Indeed, friends, it is seeing this drawback that our Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust in form, in feeling, in perception, in formations, and in consciousness.’”

“Evaṃ [P 3.0008] byākatepi kho, āvuso, assuyeva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchitāro – khattiyapaṇḍitāpi brāhmaṇapaṇḍitāpi gahapatipaṇḍitāpi samaṇapaṇḍitāpi. Paṇḍitā hāvuso, manussā vīmaṃsakā – ‘kiṃ panāyasmantānaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ disvā rūpe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe[V 2.0008], āvuso, evaṃ byākareyyātha – ‘rūpe kho, āvuso, vigatarāgassa vigatachandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu vigatarāgassa vigatachandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Viññāṇe vigatarāgassa vigatachandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti [T 3.0011] sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Idaṃ kho no, āvuso, ānisaṃsaṃ disvā rūpe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe chandarāgavinayakkhāyī satthā’”ti.

“Even when this is explained, friends, there will still be further questioners—wise nobles, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics. For people, friends, are wise and inquisitive, and they may ask: ‘What benefit, seeing which, does the Teacher of the venerable ones teach the removal of desire and lust for form, for feeling, for perception, for formations, and for consciousness?’ When asked thus, friends, you should answer thus: ‘Friends, for one whose lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for form have departed, due to the alteration and change of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. For one whose lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for feeling… for perception… for formations have departed, due to the alteration and change of those formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. For one whose lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for consciousness have departed, due to the alteration and change of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. It is this benefit, friends, seeing which our Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for form, for feeling, for perception, for formations, and for consciousness.’”

“Akusale cāvuso, dhamme upasampajja viharato diṭṭhe ceva dhamme sukho vihāro abhavissa avighāto anupāyāso apariḷāho, kāyassa ca bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugati pāṭikaṅkhā, nayidaṃ bhagavā akusalānaṃ [M 2.0008] dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vaṇṇeyya. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, akusale dhamme upasampajja viharato diṭṭhe ceva dhamme dukkho vihāro savighāto saupāyāso sapariḷāho, kāyassa ca bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā, tasmā bhagavā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vaṇṇeti.

“Friends, if for one dwelling, having become endowed with unwholesome states, there were in this very life a pleasant abiding—without vexation, without distress, without torment—and if, after death, with the breaking up of the body, a good destination could be expected, the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But because, friends, for one dwelling, having become endowed with unwholesome states, there is in this very life a painful abiding—with vexation, with distress, with torment—and after death, with the breaking up of the body, a bad destination can be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.”

“Kusale cāvuso, dhamme upasampajja viharato diṭṭhe ceva dhamme dukkho vihāro abhavissa savighāto saupāyāso [P 3.0009] sapariḷāho, kāyassa ca bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā, nayidaṃ bhagavā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadaṃ vaṇṇeyya. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, kusale dhamme upasampajja viharato diṭṭhe ceva dhamme sukho vihāro avighāto anupāyāso apariḷāho, kāyassa ca bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugati pāṭikaṅkhā, tasmā bhagavā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadaṃ vaṇṇetī”ti.

“Friends, if for one dwelling, having become endowed with wholesome states, there were in this very life a painful abiding—with vexation, with distress, with torment—and if, after death, with the breaking up of the body, a bad destination could be expected, the Blessed One would not praise this endowment with wholesome states. But because, friends, for one dwelling, having become endowed with wholesome states, there is in this very life a pleasant abiding—without vexation, without distress, without torment—and after death, with the breaking up of the body, a good destination can be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the endowment with wholesome states.”

Idamavocāyasmā sāriputto. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti. Dutiyaṃ.

The Venerable Sāriputta said this. Those monks, delighted, rejoiced in what was said by the Venerable Sāriputta. The Second.

3. Hāliddikānisuttaṃ

3. The Discourse to Hāliddikāni

3. Evaṃ [T 3.0012][V 2.0009] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno avantīsu viharati kuraraghare kulaghare (ka.) papāte pabbate. Atha kho hāliddikāni hāliddakāni (sī.), haliddikāni (syā.) gahapati yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho hāliddikāni gahapati āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “vuttamidaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā aṭṭhakavaggiye māgaṇḍiyapañhe –

3. Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantis at Kuraraghara on a precipitous mountain. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhakavagga, in the Māgaṇḍiya Question:

“Okaṃ pahāya aniketasārī,

Gāme akubbaṃ akrubbaṃ (ka.) muni santhavāni sandhavāni (ka.);

Kāmehi ritto apurakkharāno apurekkharāno (sī. suttanipātepi) moggallāne 5-135 suttampi oloketabbaṃ,

Kathaṃ na viggayha janena kayirā”ti.

“Having abandoned the abode, not resorting to a home, the sage, forming no intimacies in the village, devoid of sensual pleasures, not accumulating for the future, would not engage in disputes with people.”

“Imassa nu kho, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa kathaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti?

“Venerable sir, how is the meaning of this statement, spoken in brief by the Blessed One, to be understood in detail?”

“Rūpadhātu [M 2.0009] kho, gahapati, viññāṇassa oko. Rūpadhāturāgavinibandhañca … vinibaddhañja (pī. sī. aṭṭha.) pana viññāṇaṃ ‘okasārī’ti vuccati. Vedanādhātu kho, gahapati, viññāṇassa oko. Vedanādhāturāgavinibandhañca pana viññāṇaṃ ‘okasārī’ti vuccati. Saññādhātu [P 3.0010] kho, gahapati, viññāṇassa oko. Saññādhāturāgavinibandhañca pana viññāṇaṃ ‘okasārī’ti vuccati. Saṅkhāradhātu kho, gahapati, viññāṇassa oko. Saṅkhāradhāturāgavinibandhañca pana viññāṇaṃ ‘okasārī’ti vuccati. Evaṃ [T 3.0013] kho, gahapati, okasārī hoti.

“The form element, householder, is the abode of consciousness. And consciousness that is bound by lust for the form element is called ‘one who resorts to the abode.’ The feeling element, householder, is the abode of consciousness. And consciousness that is bound by lust for the feeling element is called ‘one who resorts to the abode.’ The perception element, householder, is the abode of consciousness. And consciousness that is bound by lust for the perception element is called ‘one who resorts to the abode.’ The formations element, householder, is the abode of consciousness. And consciousness that is bound by lust for the formations element is called ‘one who resorts to the abode.’ Thus, householder, one becomes one who resorts to the abode.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, anokasārī hoti? Rūpadhātuyā kho, gahapati, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī nandi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) yā taṇhā ye upayupādānā upāyupādānā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā te tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā anabhāvakatā (sī. pī.), anabhāvaṃgatā (syā. kaṃ.) āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tasmā tathāgato ‘anokasārī’ti vuccati. Vedanādhātuyā kho, gahapati… saññādhātuyā kho, gahapati… saṅkhāradhātuyā kho, gahapati… viññāṇadhātuyā kho, gahapati, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā [V 2.0010] taṇhā ye upayupādānā cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā te tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tasmā tathāgato ‘anokasārī’ti vuccati. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, anokasārī hoti.

“And how, householder, does one not resort to an abode? As for the form element, householder, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever attachments and clingings, determinations, adherences, and underlying tendencies of the mind—these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and are by nature unable to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who does not resort to an abode.’ As for the feeling element, householder… as for the perception element, householder… as for the formations element, householder… as for the consciousness element, householder, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever attachments and clingings, determinations, adherences, and underlying tendencies of the mind—these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and are by nature unable to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who does not resort to an abode.’ Thus, householder, one does not resort to an abode.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, niketasārī hoti? Rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, ‘niketasārī’ti vuccati. Saddanimitta…pe… gandhanimitta… rasanimitta… phoṭṭhabbanimitta… dhammanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, ‘niketasārī’ti vuccati. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, niketasārī hoti.

“And how, householder, is one a home-seeker? Householder, one who is bound by attachment to the home that is the sign of form is called a ‘home-seeker.’ One who is bound by attachment to the home that is the sign of sound… smell… taste… touch… a mental object is called a ‘home-seeker.’ In this way, householder, one is a home-seeker.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, aniketasārī hoti? Rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tasmā tathāgato ‘aniketasārī’ti vuccati. Saddanimitta… gandhanimitta… rasanimitta… phoṭṭhabbanimitta… dhammanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā [P 3.0011] āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tasmā [M 2.0010] tathāgato ‘aniketasārī’ti [T 3.0014] vuccati. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, aniketasārī hoti.

“And how, householder, is one not a home-seeker? Householder, for the Tathāgata, the bonds of attachment to the home that is the sign of form have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who is not a home-seeker.’ The bonds of attachment to the home that is the sign of sound… smell… taste… touch… a mental object, householder, for the Tathāgata have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who is not a home-seeker.’ In this way, householder, one is not a home-seeker.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, gāme santhavajāto sandhavajāto (ka.) hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekacco gihīhi gihi (ka.) saṃsaṭṭho viharati sahanandī sahasokī, sukhitesu sukhito, dukkhitesu dukkhito, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā tesu yogaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, gāme santhavajāto hoti.

“And how, householder, does one become intimate in a village? Here, householder, a certain person dwells associated with householders, rejoicing with them and sorrowing with them; happy when they are happy, sorrowful when they are sorrowful; and when their duties and tasks arise, personally undertakes the effort in them. In this way, householder, one becomes intimate in a village.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, gāme na santhavajāto hoti? Idha, gahapati, bhikkhu gihīhi gihi (ka.) asaṃsaṭṭho viharati na sahanandī na sahasokī na sukhitesu sukhito na dukkhitesu dukkhito, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu na attanā tesu yogaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, gāme na santhavajāto hoti.

“And how, householder, does one not become intimate in a village? Here, householder, a monk dwells unassociated with householders, not rejoicing with them nor sorrowing with them; not happy when they are happy, not sorrowful when they are sorrowful; and when their duties and tasks arise, does not personally undertake the effort in them. In this way, householder, one does not become intimate in a village.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, kāmehi aritto hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekacco kāmesu avigatarāgo [V 2.0011] hoti avigatachando avigatapemo avigatapipāso avigatapariḷāho avigatataṇho. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, kāmehi aritto hoti.

“And how, householder, is one not free from sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain person’s passion for sensual pleasures has not departed, their desire has not departed, their affection has not departed, their thirst has not departed, their fever has not departed, and their craving has not departed. Thus, householder, one is not free from sensual pleasures.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, kāmehi ritto hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekacco kāmesu vigatarāgo hoti vigatachando vigatapemo vigatapipāso vigatapariḷāho vigatataṇho[T 3.0015]. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, kāmehi ritto hoti.

“And how, householder, is one free from sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain person’s passion for sensual pleasures has departed, their desire has departed, their affection has departed, their thirst has departed, their fever has departed, and their craving has departed. Thus, householder, one is free from sensual pleasures.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, purakkharāno hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekaccassa evaṃ hoti – ‘evaṃrūpo siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃvedano siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsañño siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsaṅkhāro siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃviññāṇo siyaṃ anāgatamaddhāna’nti. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, purakkharāno hoti.

“And how, householder, is one who projects forward? Here, householder, it occurs to a certain person thus: ‘May I have such a form in the future! May I have such a feeling in the future! May I have such a perception in the future! May I have such volitional formations in the future! May I have such a consciousness in the future!’ Thus, householder, one is a person who projects forward.”

“Kathañca, gahapati, apurakkharāno hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekaccassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘evaṃrūpo siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃvedano siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsañño siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsaṅkhāro siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃviññāṇo [P 3.0012] siyaṃ anāgatamaddhāna’nti. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, apurakkharāno hoti.

“And how, householder, is one who does not project forward? Here, householder, it does not occur to a certain person thus: ‘May I have such a form in the future! May I have such a feeling in the future! May I have such a perception in the future! May I have such volitional formations in the future! May I have such a consciousness in the future!’ Thus, householder, one is a person who does not project forward.”

“Kathañca[M 2.0011], gahapati, kathaṃ viggayha janena kattā hoti? Idha, gahapati, ekacco evarūpiṃ kathaṃ kattā hoti – ‘na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi; ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi. Kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi? Micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi; ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno. Pure vacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca; pacchā vacanīyaṃ pure avaca. Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ. Āropito te vādo; cara vādappamokkhāya. Niggahitosi; nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī’ti. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, kathaṃ viggayha janena kattā hoti.

“And how, householder, does one become a speaker of contentious talk with people? Here, householder, someone becomes a speaker of such talk as this: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What should be said first, you said last; what should be said last, you said first. My statement is coherent; yours is incoherent. What you have long practiced is overturned. A charge has been laid against you; go and work for your release from this charge. You are defeated; disentangle yourself if you can.’ This, householder, is how one becomes a speaker of contentious talk with people.”

“Kathañca[T 3.0016], gahapati, kathaṃ na viggayha janena kattā hoti? Idha, gahapati, bhikkhu na evarūpiṃ kathaṃ kattā hoti – ‘na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi…pe… nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī’ti. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, kathaṃ na viggayha janena kattā hoti.

“And how, householder, does one not become a speaker of contentious talk with people? Here, householder, a monk does not become a speaker of such talk as this: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline… disentangle yourself if you can.’ This, householder, is how one does not become a speaker of contentious talk with people.”

“Iti [V 2.0012] kho, gahapati, yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā aṭṭhakavaggiye māgaṇḍiyapañhe –

“Thus, householder, regarding what was spoken by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhakavagga, in the Māgaṇḍiya Question:

“Okaṃ pahāya aniketasārī,

Gāme akubbaṃ munisanthavāni;

Kāmehi ritto apurakkharāno,

Kathaṃ na viggayha janena kayirā”ti.

‘Having abandoned the abode, not seeking a home, the sage makes no intimacies in the village; devoid of sensual pleasures, projecting nothing forward, how could he engage in contentious talk with people?’”

“Imassa kho, gahapati, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Householder, the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One should be seen in detail in this way.”

4. Dutiyahāliddikānisuttaṃ

4. The Second Discourse to Hāliddikāni

4. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno avantīsu viharati kuraraghare papāte pabbate. Atha [P 3.0013] kho hāliddikāni gahapati yenāyasmā mahākaccāno…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho hāliddikāni [T 3.0017] gahapati āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “vuttamidaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā sakkapañhe – ‘ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā, te accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemino accantabrahmacārino accantapariyosānā seṭṭhā devamanussāna’”nti.

4. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs at Kuraraghara on the Papāta mountain. Then the householder Hāliddikāni went to the Venerable Mahākaccāna… Seated to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the Questions of Sakka: ‘Those ascetics and brahmins who are liberated through the destruction of craving—they are the ultimate goal, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate consummation, the best among gods and humans.’”

“Imassa nu kho, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa kathaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti?

“Venerable sir, how should the detailed meaning of this utterance, spoken in brief by the Blessed One, be understood?”

“Rūpadhātuyā [M 2.0012] kho, gahapati, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā ye upayupādānā cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā, tesaṃ khayā virāgā nirodhā cāgā paṭinissaggā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati.

Householder, in regard to the form element, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, engagement and clinging, and mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are—with their destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment, the mind is said to be well liberated.

“Vedanādhātuyā kho, gahapati… saññādhātuyā kho, gahapati… saṅkhāradhātuyā kho, gahapati… viññāṇadhātuyā [V 2.0013] kho, gahapati, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā ye upayupādānā cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā, tesaṃ khayā virāgā nirodhā cāgā paṭinissaggā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati.

In regard to the element of feeling, householder… in regard to the element of perception, householder… in regard to the element of formations, householder… in regard to the element of consciousness, householder, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, engagement and clinging, and mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are—with their destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment, the mind is said to be well liberated.

“Iti kho, gahapati, yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā sakkapañhe – ‘ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā te accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemino accantabrahmacārino accantapariyosānā seṭṭhā devamanussāna’”nti.

Thus, householder, as it was said by the Blessed One in the Questions of Sakka: 'Those ascetics and brahmins who are liberated through the destruction of craving are of ultimate accomplishment, ultimate security from bondage, ultimate holy life, ultimate consummation, the best among gods and humans.'

“Imassa kho, gahapati, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

Householder, the meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One should be understood in detail in this way. The Fourth.

5. Samādhisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Concentration

5. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane [T 3.0018] anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha; samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti? Rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, vedanāya samudayañca atthaṅgamañca[P 3.0014], saññāya samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, saṅkhārānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca”.

5. Thus I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, develop concentration. A concentrated bhikkhu, bhikkhus, understands things as they really are. And what does he understand as it really is? The origin and passing away of form, the origin and passing away of feeling, the origin and passing away of perception, the origin and passing away of formations, the origin and passing away of consciousness.”

“Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpassa samudayo, ko vedanāya samudayo, ko saññāya samudayo, ko saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo, ko viññāṇassa samudayo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati.

And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of form, what is the origin of feeling, what is the origin of perception, what is the origin of formations, what is the origin of consciousness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights, welcomes, and abides attached.

“Kiñca abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati? Rūpaṃ abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa rūpaṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī. Yā rūpe nandī tadupādānaṃ. Tassupādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā [V 2.0014] jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

And what does one delight in, welcome, and abide attached to? One delights in, welcomes, and abides attached to form. For one who delights in, welcomes, and abides attached to form, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in form, that is clinging. With that clinging as condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

“Vedanaṃ [M 2.0013] abhinandati…pe… saññaṃ abhinandati… saṅkhāre abhinandati… viññāṇaṃ abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa viññāṇaṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī. Yā viññāṇe nandī tadupādānaṃ. Tassupādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā…pe… [T 3.0019] evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

One delights in feeling… one delights in perception… one delights in formations… one delights in, welcomes, and abides attached to consciousness. For one who delights in, welcomes, and abides attached to consciousness, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in consciousness, that is clinging. With that clinging as condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition… Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

“Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, rūpassa samudayo; ayaṃ vedanāya samudayo; ayaṃ saññāya samudayo; ayaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo; ayaṃ viññāṇassa samudayo.

Bhikkhus, this is the origin of form; this is the origin of feeling; this is the origin of perception; this is the origin of formations; this is the origin of consciousness.

“Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpassa atthaṅgamo, ko vedanāya… ko saññāya… ko saṅkhārānaṃ… ko viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo?

And what, bhikkhus, is the passing away of form? What is the passing away of feeling? What is the passing away of perception? What is the passing away of formations? What is the passing away of consciousness?

Idha, bhikkhave, nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati.

Here, bhikkhus, one does not delight, does not welcome, and does not abide attached.

“Kiñca nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati? Rūpaṃ nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa rūpaṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato yā rūpe nandī sā nirujjhati. Tassa nandīnirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

And what does one not delight in, not welcome, and not abide attached to? One does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it. For one who does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it, the delight in form that he has ceases. With the cessation of that delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

“Vedanaṃ nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa vedanaṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosā [P 3.0015] tiṭṭhato yā vedanāya nandī sā nirujjhati. Tassa nandīnirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

One does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it. For one who does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it, the delight in feeling that he has ceases. With the cessation of that delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

“Saññaṃ nābhinandati…pe… saṅkhāre nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa [V 2.0015] saṅkhāre anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato yā saṅkhāresu nandī sā nirujjhati. Tassa nandīnirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

One does not delight in perception… One does not delight in formations, does not welcome them, and does not abide attached to them. For one who does not delight in formations, does not welcome them, and does not abide attached to them, the delight in formations that he has ceases. With the cessation of that delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

“Viññāṇaṃ nābhinandati nābhivadati [T 3.0020] nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa viññāṇaṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato yā viññāṇe nandī sā nirujjhati. Tassa nandīnirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

One does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it. For one who does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it, the delight in consciousness that he has ceases. With the cessation of that delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

“Ayaṃ[M 2.0014], bhikkhave, rūpassa atthaṅgamo, ayaṃ vedanāya atthaṅgamo, ayaṃ saññāya atthaṅgamo, ayaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, ayaṃ viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

Bhikkhus, this is the passing away of form, this is the passing away of feeling, this is the passing away of perception, this is the passing away of formations, this is the passing away of consciousness.” The Fifth.

6. Paṭisallāṇasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Seclusion

6. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Paṭisallāṇe, bhikkhave, yogamāpajjatha. Paṭisallīṇo, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti? Rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, vedanāya samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, saññāya samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, saṅkhārānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca, viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca”…pe… (yathā paṭhamasutte tathā vitthāretabbo.) Chaṭṭhaṃ.

6. At Savatthi. 'O monks, engage in the practice of meditation in seclusion. O monks, a monk who is in seclusion knows distinctly as it really is. And what does he know distinctly as it really is? The arising and cessation of form, the arising and cessation of feeling, the arising and cessation of perception, the arising and cessation of volitional formations, the arising and cessation of consciousness...' (To be elaborated as in the first discourse.) The Sixth.

7. Upādāparitassanāsuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Agitation Through Clinging

7. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Upādāparitassanañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi anupādāaparitassanañca. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ[P 3.0016], bhante”ti, kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

7. At Savatthi. 'O monks, I will teach you agitation through clinging and non-agitation without clinging. Listen to it, attend closely; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, upādāparitassanā hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa [V 2.0016] akovido sappurisadhamme [T 3.0021] avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Tassa taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā rūpavipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso pariyādānā uttāsavā ca hoti vighātavā ca apekkhavā ca upādāya ca paritassati.

'And how, O monks, is there agitation through clinging? Here, O monks, an uninstructed worldling—who does not see the noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who does not see true men, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true men—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. That form of his changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of form, his consciousness follows in accordance with the alteration of form. Agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born of his consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of form beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is beset, he becomes alarmed, distressed, and anxious, and through clinging he is agitated.

“Vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā vedanaṃ, vedanāya vā attānaṃ. Tassa sā vedanā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa vedanāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā vedanāvipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa vedanāvipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso pariyādānā uttāsavā ca hoti vighātavā ca apekkhavā ca upādāya ca paritassati.

He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. That feeling of his changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of feeling, his consciousness follows in accordance with the alteration of feeling. Agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born of his consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of feeling beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is beset, he becomes alarmed, distressed, and anxious, and through clinging he is agitated.

“Saññaṃ [M 2.0015] attato samanupassati…pe… saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, saṅkhāravantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā saṅkhāre, saṅkhāresu vā attānaṃ. Tassa te saṅkhārā vipariṇamanti aññathā honti. Tassa saṅkhāravipariṇāmaññathābhāvā saṅkhāravipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa saṅkhāravipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso pariyādānā uttāsavā ca hoti vighātavā ca apekkhavā ca upādāya ca paritassati.

He regards perception as self... He regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations. Those volitional formations of his change and become otherwise. With the change and alteration of the volitional formations, his consciousness follows in accordance with the alteration of the volitional formations. Agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born of his consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of the volitional formations beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is beset, he becomes alarmed, distressed, and anxious, and through clinging he is agitated.

“Viññāṇaṃ attato [T 3.0022] samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Tassa taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā [P 3.0017] viññāṇavipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso pariyādānā uttāsavā ca hoti vighātavā ca apekkhavā ca upādāya ca paritassati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, upādāparitassanā hoti.

He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of consciousness, his consciousness follows in accordance with the alteration of consciousness. Agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born of his consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of consciousness beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is beset, he becomes alarmed, distressed, and anxious, and through clinging he is agitated. Thus, O monks, does agitation through clinging occur.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, anupādāaparitassanā hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ [V 2.0017] vā attānaṃ; na attani vā rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Tassa taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā na rūpavipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa na rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso apariyādānā na cevuttāsavā na ceva uttāsavā (pī. ka.) hoti na ca vighātavā na ca apekkhavā, anupādāya ca na paritassati.

'And how, O monks, is there non-agitation without clinging? Here, O monks, a learned noble disciple—who is accustomed to seeing the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who is accustomed to seeing good persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of good persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of good persons—does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. That form of his changes and becomes otherwise. Because of the change and alteration of form, his consciousness does not follow in accordance with the alteration of form. For him, agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born from consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of form do not beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is not beset, he is not alarmed, nor distressed, nor concerned; and without clinging, he is not agitated.

“Na vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, na vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā vedanaṃ, na vedanāya vā attānaṃ. Tassa sā vedanā vipariṇamati aññathā hoti[T 3.0023]. Tassa vedanāvipariṇāmaññathābhāvā na vedanāvipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa na vedanāvipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti[M 2.0016]. Cetaso apariyādānā na cevuttāsavā hoti na ca vighātavā na ca apekkhavā, anupādāya ca na paritassati.

He does not regard feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. That feeling of his changes and becomes otherwise. Because of the change and alteration of feeling, his consciousness does not follow in accordance with the alteration of feeling. For him, agitations and the arising of unwholesome states born from consciousness following in accordance with the alteration of feeling do not beset his mind and remain. Because his mind is not beset, he is not alarmed, nor distressed, nor concerned; and without clinging, he is not agitated.

“Na saññaṃ…pe… na saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, na saṅkhāravantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā saṅkhāre, na saṅkhāresu vā attānaṃ. Tassa te saṅkhārā vipariṇamanti aññathā honti. Tassa saṅkhāravipariṇāmaññathābhāvā na saṅkhāravipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa na saṅkhāravipariṇāmānuparivattijā [P 3.0018] paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso apariyādānā na cevuttāsavā hoti na ca vighātavā na ca apekkhavā, anupādāya ca na paritassati.

He does not regard perception... He does not regard formations as self, or self as possessing formations, or formations as in self, or self as in formations. Those formations of his change and become otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of the formations, consciousness does not follow in sequence with the change of the formations. For him, longings and the arising of unwholesome states born of following in sequence with the change of the formations do not overcome his mind and remain. Because his mind is not overcome, he is not alarmed, nor distressed, nor anxious; and without clinging, he does not crave.

“Na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ…pe… tassa taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā na viññāṇavipariṇāmānuparivatti viññāṇaṃ hoti. Tassa na viññāṇavipariṇāmānuparivattijā paritassanā dhammasamuppādā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso apariyādānā na cevuttāsavā hoti na ca vighātavā na ca apekkhavā, anupādāya ca na paritassati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, anupādā aparitassanaṃ hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

He does not regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness... That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and becoming otherwise of consciousness, consciousness does not follow in sequence with the change of consciousness. For him, longings and the arising of unwholesome states born of following in sequence with the change of consciousness do not overcome his mind and remain. Because his mind is not overcome, he is not alarmed, nor distressed, nor anxious; and without clinging, he does not crave. Thus indeed, Bhikkhus, there is non-agitation without clinging.” Seventh.

8. Dutiyaupādāparitassanāsuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on Clinging and Agitation

8. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0024][V 2.0018]. “Upādāparitassanañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi anupādāaparitassanañca. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… kathañca, bhikkhave, upādāparitassanā hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Tassa taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Vedanaṃ etaṃ mama…pe… saññaṃ etaṃ mama… saṅkhāre etaṃ mama… viññāṇaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Tassa taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, upādāparitassanā hoti.

8. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you agitation through clinging and non-agitation through non-clinging. Listen to that… And how, bhikkhus, does agitation through clinging occur? Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling regards form thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ That form of his alters and becomes otherwise. From the alteration and change of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. He regards feeling thus: ‘This is mine’… perception thus: ‘This is mine’… formations thus: ‘This is mine’… He regards consciousness thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ That consciousness of his alters and becomes otherwise. From the alteration and change of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that agitation through clinging occurs.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, anupādāaparitassanā hoti? Idha[P 3.0019], bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. Tassa taṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa [M 2.0017] rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Vedanaṃ netaṃ mama… saññaṃ netaṃ mama… saṅkhāre netaṃ mama… viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. Tassa taṃ viññāṇaṃ vipariṇamati aññathā hoti. Tassa viññāṇavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā[T 3.0025]. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, anupādāaparitassanā hotī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“And how, bhikkhus, does non-agitation through non-clinging occur? Here, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple regards form thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ That form of his alters and becomes otherwise. From the alteration and change of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. He regards feeling thus: ‘This is not mine’… perception thus: ‘This is not mine’… formations thus: ‘This is not mine’… He regards consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ That consciousness of his alters and becomes otherwise. From the alteration and change of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that non-agitation through non-clinging occurs.” Eighth.

9. Kālattayaaniccasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Impermanence in the Three Times

9. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ rūpasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ rūpaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa rūpassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti. Vedanā aniccā…pe… [V 2.0019] saññā aniccā… saṅkhārā aniccā atītānāgatā; ko pana vādo paccuppannānaṃ! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītesu saṅkhāresu anapekkho hoti; anāgate saṅkhāre nābhinandati; paccuppannānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti. Viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ viññāṇasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ viññāṇaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa viññāṇassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hotī”ti. Navamaṃ.

9. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form that is past and future is impermanent; what is there to say of present form! Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past form, does not delight in future form, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present form. Feeling is impermanent… Perception is impermanent… Formations that are past and future are impermanent; what is there to say of present formations! Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past formations, does not delight in future formations, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present formations. Consciousness that is past and future is impermanent; what is there to say of present consciousness! Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present consciousness.” Ninth.

10. Kālattayadukkhasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Suffering in the Three Times

10. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo [P 3.0020] paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ rūpasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ rūpaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa rūpassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti. Vedanā dukkhā… saññā dukkhā… saṅkhārā dukkhā… viññāṇaṃ [T 3.0026] dukkhaṃ atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ viññāṇasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ viññāṇaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa viññāṇassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hotī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

10. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form that is past and future is suffering; what is there to say of present form! Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past form, does not delight in future form, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present form. Feeling is suffering… perception is suffering… formations are suffering… Consciousness that is past and future is suffering; what is there to say of present consciousness! Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present consciousness.” Tenth.

11. Kālattayaanattasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on Not-Self in the Three Times

11. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0018]. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ rūpasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ rūpaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa rūpassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno [V 2.0020] hoti. Vedanā anattā… saññā anattā… saṅkhārā anattā… viññāṇaṃ anattā atītānāgataṃ; ko pana vādo paccuppannassa! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako atītasmiṃ viññāṇasmiṃ anapekkho hoti; anāgataṃ viññāṇaṃ nābhinandati; paccuppannassa viññāṇassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hotī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

11. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form that is past and future is not-self; what then is to be said of present form? Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past form, does not delight in future form, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present form. Feeling is not-self… perception is not-self… formations are not-self… consciousness that is past and future is not-self; what then is to be said of present consciousness? Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple is unconcerned with past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of present consciousness.” Eleventh.

Nakulapituvaggo paṭhamo.

The First Nakulapitu Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that is:

Nakulapitā devadahā, dvepi hāliddikāni ca;

Samādhipaṭisallāṇā, upādāparitassanā [P 3.0021] duve;

Atītānāgatapaccuppannā, vaggo tena pavuccati.

Nakulapitā and Devadaha, and the two Hāliddikāni suttas; Samādhi and Paṭisallāṇa, the two Upādāparitassanā suttas; The three on the Past, Future, and Present—for that reason it is called a chapter.

2. Aniccavaggo

2. The Chapter on Impermanence

1. Aniccasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Impermanence

12. Evaṃ [T 3.0027] me sutaṃ – sāvatthiyaṃ. Tatra kho…pe… “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā, saññā aniccā, saṅkhārā aniccā, viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati, saññāyapi nibbindati, saṅkhāresupi nibbindati, viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati[V 2.0021]; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

12. Thus have I heard. At Sāvatthī. There… “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’” First.

2. Dukkhasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Suffering

13. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ, vedanā dukkhā, saññā dukkhā, saṅkhārā dukkhā, viññāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

13. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is suffering, feeling is suffering, perception is suffering, formations are suffering, consciousness is suffering. Seeing thus… (and so forth) …he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’” Second.

3. Anattasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Not-Self

14. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0019]. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā, vedanā anattā, saññā anattā, saṅkhārā anattā, viññāṇaṃ anattā. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati, saññāyapi nibbindati, saṅkhāresupi nibbindati, viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti[T 3.0028], vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

14. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not-self; feeling is not-self; perception is not-self; formations are not-self; consciousness is not-self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Third.

4. Yadaniccasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on What Is Impermanent

15. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[P 3.0022]. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ; yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā; yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanā aniccā. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ; yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā; yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saññā aniccā…pe… saṅkhārā aniccā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ; yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā; yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya [V 2.0022] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

15. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling is impermanent… Perception is impermanent… Formations are impermanent… Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Fourth.

5. Yaṃdukkhasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on What Is Suffering

16. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā; yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanā dukkhā… saññā dukkhā… saṅkhārā dukkhā… viññāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā; yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

16. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is suffering. What is suffering is not-self; what is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling is suffering… perception is suffering… formations are suffering… consciousness is suffering. What is suffering is not-self; what is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Fifth.

6. Yadanattāsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on What Is Not-Self

17. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama[T 3.0029][P 3.0023], nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanā anattā… saññā anattā… saṅkhārā anattā… viññāṇaṃ anattā[M 2.0020]. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

17. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling is not-self… perception is not-self… formations are not-self… consciousness is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Sixth.

7. Sahetuaniccasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Impermanence with Cause

18. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo rūpassa uppādāya, sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūtaṃ, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ kuto niccaṃ bhavissati! Vedanā aniccā.
