The Saṅgha of monks has been dismissed by the Blessed One, venerable sir. There are monks here who are new, not long gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. For them, not seeing the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a reversal. Just as a young calf, not seeing its mother, there might be an alteration, there might be a reversal, so too there are monks here who are new, not long gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline; for them, not seeing the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a reversal. Just as young seeds, not obtaining water, there might be an alteration, there might be a reversal, so too there are monks here who are new, not long gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline; for them, not obtaining the sight of the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a reversal. Let the Blessed One delight in the Saṅgha of monks, venerable sir! Let the Blessed One address the Saṅgha of monks! Just as the Blessed One formerly supported the Saṅgha of monks, so too let him support the Saṅgha of monks now.'

Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho brahmā sahampati bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyi.

The Blessed One consented by his silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing the Blessed One's consent, paid homage to him, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and disappeared right there.

Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena nigrodhārāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi abhisaṅkhāresi (syā. kaṃ.), abhisaṅkhāyi (pī.), abhisaṅkharoti (ka.) yathā te bhikkhū (ekadvīhikāya sārajjamānarūpā yenāhaṃ yena bhagavā (?) tenupasaṅkameyyuṃ. Tepi bhikkhū [V 2.0086]) ( ) sī. syā. kaṃ. potthakesu natthi ekadvīhikāya sārajjamānarūpā yena bhagavā [P 3.0093] tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ [T 3.0113] nisinne kho te bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca –

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One arose from seclusion and went to the Nigrodhārāma. Having gone there, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that those monks, being apprehensive, would approach him one by one or two by two. And those monks, being apprehensive, approached the Blessed One one by one or two by two. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To those monks sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this:

“Antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ. Abhisāpoyaṃ, bhikkhave, lokasmiṃ piṇḍolo vicarasi pattapāṇīti. Tañca kho etaṃ, bhikkhave, kulaputtā upenti atthavasikā, atthavasaṃ paṭicca; neva rājābhinītā, na corābhinītā, na iṇaṭṭā, na bhayaṭṭā, na ājīvikāpakatā; api ca kho otiṇṇāmha jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethāti.

‘Monks, this is the lowest of livelihoods, that is, the life of an alms-gatherer. Monks, in the world, this is a curse: “You wander as an alms-gatherer, bowl in hand.” And yet, monks, sons of good family undertake this for the sake of a higher purpose, on account of that higher purpose; not because they are pursued by kings, not because they are pursued by thieves, not because they are in debt, not because they are in fear, not because they have lost their livelihood; but rather: “We are overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. We are overwhelmed by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.”’

“Evaṃ pabbajito cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kulaputto. So ca hoti abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo muṭṭhassati asampajāno asamāhito vibbhantacitto pākatindriyo. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave[M 2.0077], chavālātaṃ ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ, neva gāme kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, nāraññe kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi gihibhogā ca parihīno, sāmaññatthañca na paripūreti.

‘And so, monks, this son of good family has gone forth. But he is covetous, of intense passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt mental intentions, of lapsed mindfulness, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a bewildered mind, and with faculties unrestrained. Just as, monks, a firebrand from a charnel ground, burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle, serves no purpose as firewood in the village nor serves any purpose as firewood in the forest; so I declare this person to be of like simile: he is deprived of the enjoyments of a householder and does not fulfill the purpose of recluseship.’

“Tayome, bhikkhave, akusalavitakkā – kāmavitakko, byāpādavitakko, vihiṃsāvitakko. Ime ca bhikkhave, tayo akusalavitakkā kva aparisesā nirujjhanti? Catūsu vā satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittassa viharato animittaṃ vā samādhiṃ bhāvayato. Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, alameva animitto samādhi bhāvetuṃ. Animitto, bhikkhave, samādhi [T 3.0114] bhāvito bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso.

‘Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: the thought of sensuality, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty. And where, monks, do these three unwholesome thoughts cease without remainder? For one who dwells with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, or for one who develops the signless concentration. Monks, it is truly fitting to develop this signless concentration. The signless concentration, monks, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.’

“Dvemā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyo – bhavadiṭṭhi ca vibhavadiṭṭhi [P 3.0094] ca. Tatra kho, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘atthi nu kho taṃ kiñci lokasmiṃ yamahaṃ upādiyamāno na vajjavā assa’nti? So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘natthi nu kho taṃ kiñci lokasmiṃ yamahaṃ upādiyamāno na vajjavā assaṃ. Ahañhi rūpaññeva upādiyamāno upādiyeyyaṃ vedanaññeva… saññaññeva… saṅkhāreyeva viññāṇaññeva upādiyamāno upādiyeyyaṃ. Tassa me assa ayaṃ (ka.) upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā [V 2.0087] sambhaveyyuṃ. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo assā’”ti.

“Monks, there are these two views: the view of being and the view of non-being. Therein, monks, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Is there anything at all in the world that, by clinging to which, I would not be blameworthy?’ He understands thus: ‘There is nothing at all in the world that, by clinging to which, I would not be blameworthy. For if I were to cling, I would cling only to form; or only to feeling… or only to perception… or only to formations… or only to consciousness. For me, with clinging as a condition, there would be becoming; with becoming as a condition, birth; with birth as a condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would come to be. Thus would be the arising of this entire mass of suffering.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ…pe… tasmātiha, bhikkhave, evaṃ passaṃ… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“What do you think, monks? Is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, indeed, venerable sir.” “Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… Therefore, monks, seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

9. Pālileyyasuttaṃ

9. The Pālileyya Sutta

81. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Atha [T 3.0115] kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kosambiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Kosambiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sāmaṃ senāsanaṃ [P 3.0095] saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā [M 2.0078] upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ eko adutiyo cārikaṃ pakkāmi.

81. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Kosambī for alms. After going for alms in Kosambī and returning from his alms round, after his meal, he put his lodging in order himself, took his bowl and outer robe, and without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, set out alone, without a companion, on a wandering tour.

Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu acirapakkantassa bhagavato yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “esāvuso, ānanda, bhagavā sāmaṃ senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ eko adutiyo cārikaṃ pakkanto”ti. “Yasmiṃ, āvuso, samaye bhagavā sāmaṃ senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ eko adutiyo cārikaṃ [V 2.0088] pakkamati, ekova bhagavā tasmiṃ samaye viharitukāmo hoti; na bhagavā tasmiṃ samaye kenaci anubandhitabbo hotī”ti.

Then a certain bhikkhu, not long after the Blessed One had departed, approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has put his lodging in order himself, taken his bowl and outer robe, and without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, has set out alone, without a companion, on a wandering tour.” “Friend, at a time when the Blessed One puts his lodging in order himself, takes his bowl and outer robe, and without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, sets out alone, without a companion, on a wandering tour, the Blessed One wishes to dwell alone. At such a time, the Blessed One should not be followed by anyone.”

Atha kho bhagavā anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena pālileyyakaṃ pārileyyakaṃ (sī. pī.) tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā pālileyyake viharati bhaddasālamūle. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavocuṃ – “cirassutā kho [T 3.0116] no, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammī kathā; icchāma mayaṃ, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṃ kathaṃ sotu”nti.

Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One was dwelling at the root of a magnificent sal tree. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their courteous and friendly talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we heard a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One. We wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One.”

Atha kho āyasmā ānando tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ yena pālileyyakaṃ bhaddasālamūlaṃ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho te bhikkhū bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṃsesi. Tena [P 3.0096] kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “kathaṃ nu kho jānato kathaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotī”ti? Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – “vicayaso desito, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo; vicayaso desitā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā; vicayaso desitā cattāro sammappadhānā; vicayaso [M 2.0079] desitā cattāro iddhipādā; vicayaso desitāni pañcindriyāni; vicayaso desitāni pañca balāni; vicayaso desitā sattabojjhaṅgā; vicayaso desito ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Evaṃ vicayaso desito, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ vicayaso desite kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme atha ca panidhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘kathaṃ nu kho jānato kathaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotī’”ti?

Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with those bhikkhus, approached the Blessed One at the root of the Bhaddasāla tree in Pālileyyaka. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. When those bhikkhus were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened them with a talk on the Dhamma. Now at that time, this reflection arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: ‘For one who knows in what way, and sees in what way, does the immediate destruction of the taints occur?’ Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in that bhikkhu's mind, addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me analytically; the four foundations of mindfulness have been taught analytically; the four right strivings have been taught analytically; the four bases of spiritual power have been taught analytically; the five faculties have been taught analytically; the five powers have been taught analytically; the seven factors of enlightenment have been taught analytically; the Noble Eightfold Path has been taught analytically. Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me analytically. And yet, while the Dhamma has been thus taught by me analytically, this reflection has arisen in the mind of a certain bhikkhu here: “For one who knows in what way, and sees in what way, does the immediate destruction of the taints occur?”’

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, jānato kathaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti? Idha bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa [T 3.0117] akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro [V 2.0089] kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Sāpi vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Sopi phasso anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā[P 3.0097]. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, for one who knows, how for one who sees, is there the immediate destruction of the taints? Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has not seen true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—repeatedly regards form as self. Whatever, bhikkhus, that repeated regarding is, that is a formation. And what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? For an uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That craving too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That feeling too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That contact too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That ignorance too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Thus indeed, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.”

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati; api ca kho rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā… sāpi vedanā… sopi phasso… sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

“He does not, indeed, repeatedly regard form as self; but rather, he repeatedly regards the self as possessing form. Whatever, bhikkhus, that repeated regarding is, that is a formation. And what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? For an uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That craving too, that feeling too, that contact too, and that ignorance too are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Thus indeed, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.”

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ [T 3.0118] samanupassati; api ca kho attani rūpaṃ samanupassati. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave[M 2.0080], samanupassanā saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā… sāpi vedanā… sopi phasso… sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

“He does not, indeed, repeatedly regard form as self, nor the self as possessing form; but rather, he repeatedly regards form as in the self. Whatever, bhikkhus, that repeated regarding is, that is a formation. And what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? For an uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That craving too, that feeling too, that contact too, and that ignorance too are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Thus indeed, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.”

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, na attani rūpaṃ samanupassati; api ca kho rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayite phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa [V 2.0090] uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā [P 3.0098]… sāpi vedanā… sopi phasso… sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato…pe… āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

“He does not, indeed, repeatedly regard form as self, nor the self as possessing form, nor form in the self; but rather, he repeatedly regards the self as in form. Whatever, bhikkhus, that repeated regarding is, that is a formation. And what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? For an uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That craving too, that feeling too, that contact too, and that ignorance too are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Thus indeed, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.”

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ, na attani rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassati; api ca kho [T 3.0119] vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, api ca kho vedanāvantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, api ca kho attani vedanaṃ samanupassati, api ca kho vedanāya attānaṃ samanupassati; api ca kho saññaṃ… api ca kho saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, api ca kho saṅkhāravantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, api ca kho attani saṅkhāre samanupassati, api ca kho saṅkhāresu attānaṃ samanupassati; api ca kho viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, api ca kho viññāṇavantaṃ attānaṃ, api ca kho attani viññāṇaṃ, api ca kho viññāṇasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno…pe… kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayite phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā… sāpi vedanā… sopi phasso [M 2.0081]… sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

“He does not, indeed, repeatedly regard form as self, nor the self as possessing form, nor form in the self, nor the self in form. Or he repeatedly regards feeling as self; or he repeatedly regards the self as possessing feeling; or he repeatedly regards feeling in the self; or he repeatedly regards the self in feeling. Or he repeatedly regards perception… Or he repeatedly regards formations as self; or he repeatedly regards the self as possessing formations; or he repeatedly regards formations in the self; or he repeatedly regards the self in formations. Or he repeatedly regards consciousness as self; or he repeatedly regards the self as possessing consciousness; or he repeatedly regards consciousness in the self; or he repeatedly regards the self in consciousness. Whatever, bhikkhus, that repeated regarding is, that is a formation. And what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? For an uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. That craving too, that feeling too, that contact too, and that ignorance too are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Thus indeed, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.”

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na vedanaṃ attato samanupassati, na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati; api ca kho evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti. Yā kho pana [T 3.0120] sā, bhikkhave, sassatadiṭṭhi saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

He does not, indeed, regard form as self, nor does he regard feeling as self, nor perception… nor formations… nor consciousness as self. Yet he holds this view: ‘That which is the self is the world; after death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ Bhikkhus, that eternalist view is a formation. And that formation, what is its source… and so on… In this way also, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs without interval.

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na vedanaṃ [P 3.0099]… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati; nāpi evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – ‘so attā [V 2.0091] so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti. Api ca kho evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – ‘no cassaṃ no ca me siyā nābhavissaṃ na me bhavissatī’ti. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, ucchedadiṭṭhi saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

He does not regard form as self, nor feeling... nor perception... nor formations... nor consciousness as self; nor does he hold this view: ‘That which is the self is the world; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ But he does hold this view: ‘I would not be, and it would not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine.’ Bhikkhus, that annihilationist view is a formation. And that formation—what is its source, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? Bhikkhus, for the uninstructed worldling, who is touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that craving. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation too is impermanent... and so on... Thus, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs without interval.

“Na heva kho rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… na viññāṇasmiṃ attato samanupassati, nāpi evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti; nāpi evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – ‘no cassaṃ no ca me siyā nābhavissaṃ na me bhavissatī’ti; api ca kho kaṅkhī hoti [T 3.0121] vicikicchī aniṭṭhaṅgato saddhamme. Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, kaṅkhitā vicikicchitā aniṭṭhaṅgatatā saddhamme saṅkhāro so. So pana saṅkhāro kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo? Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā; tatojo so saṅkhāro. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato [M 2.0082] paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi taṇhā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Sāpi vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Sopi phasso anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Sāpi avijjā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotī”ti. Navamaṃ.

He does not regard form as self, nor feeling… nor perception… nor formations… nor consciousness as self… nor does he regard self in consciousness. Nor does he hold this view: ‘That which is the self is the world; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ Nor does he hold this view: ‘I would not be, and it would not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine.’ But rather, he is doubtful, perplexed, and has not come to a conclusion regarding the good Dhamma. Bhikkhus, whatever doubt, perplexity, and lack of conclusion there is regarding the good Dhamma, that is a formation. And that formation, what is its source, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? Bhikkhus, for an uninstructed worldling, touched by a feeling born of contact associated with ignorance, craving arises; that formation is born from that. Thus, bhikkhus, that formation, too, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. That craving, too, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. That feeling, too, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. That contact, too, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. That ignorance, too, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. Bhikkhus, for one who knows thus, for one who sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs without interval.” The Ninth.

10. Puṇṇamasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Full Moon

82. Ekaṃ [P 3.0100] samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā tadahuposathe pannarase puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ajjhokāse nisinno hoti.

82. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, in the palace of Migāra’s mother, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Now at that time, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon, the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ [V 2.0092] paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “puccheyyāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ kiñcideva kañcideva (?) desaṃ, sace me bhagavā okāsaṃ karoti pañhassa veyyākaraṇāyā”ti? “Tena hi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sake āsane nisīditvā puccha yadākaṅkhasī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā sake āsane nisīditvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [T 3.0122] – “ime nu kho, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho”ti.

Then a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, raised his hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said to him: 'Venerable sir, I would ask the Blessed One about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity for an explanation of the question.' 'In that case, bhikkhu, sit down in your own seat and ask whatever you wish.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. Having sat down in his own seat, he said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, are these the five aggregates subject to clinging, that is to say: the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging?'

“Ime kho pana, bhikkhu, pañcupādānakkhandhā; seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

'These, bhikkhu, are the five aggregates subject to clinging, that is to say: the aggregate of form subject to clinging… and so on… the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.' 'Very good, venerable sir.' That bhikkhu, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Blessed One's words, asked him a further question:

“Ime kho pana, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā kiṃmūlakā”ti? “Ime kho, bhikkhu, pañcupādānakkhandhā chandamūlakā”ti…pe… taññeva nu kho, bhante, upādānaṃ te pañcupādānakkhandhā udāhu aññatra pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi upādānanti? “Na kho, bhikkhu, taññeva upādānaṃ te pañcupādānakkhandhā [P 3.0101] nāpi aññatra pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi upādānaṃ, api ca yo tattha chandarāgo taṃ tattha upādāna”nti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

'Venerable sir, what is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'Bhikkhu, these five aggregates subject to clinging have desire as their root.' … 'Venerable sir, is clinging the same as those five aggregates subject to clinging, or is clinging something other than the five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'Bhikkhu, clinging is not the same as those five aggregates subject to clinging, nor is clinging something other than the five aggregates subject to clinging. Rather, the desire and lust that is there in relation to them, that is the clinging there.' 'Very good, venerable sir.' That bhikkhu… and so on… asked a further question:

“Siyā [M 2.0083] pana, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavemattatā”ti? “Siyā, bhikkhū”ti bhagavā avoca – “idha, bhikkhu, ekaccassa evaṃ hoti – ‘evaṃrūpo siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃvedano siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsañño siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, evaṃsaṅkhāro siyaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ[T 3.0123], evaṃviññāṇo siyaṃ anāgatamaddhāna’nti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, siyā pañcupādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavemattatā”ti? “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

“Venerable sir, could there be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging?” “There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to someone thus: ‘In a future time, may I have such form! In a future time, may I have such feeling! In a future time, may I have such perception! In a future time, may I have such formations! In a future time, may I have such consciousness!’ It is in this way, bhikkhu, that there can be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging.” “Very good, venerable sir.” That bhikkhu… and so on… asked a further question:

“Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, khandhānaṃ khandhādhivacana”nti? “Yaṃ kiñci, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, ayaṃ vuccati rūpakkhandho. Yā kāci vedanā… yā kāci saññā [V 2.0093]… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, ayaṃ vuccati viññāṇakkhandho. Ettāvatā kho, bhikkhu, khandhānaṃ khandhādhivacana”nti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… apucchi –

“Venerable sir, to what extent is the term ‘aggregate’ applied to the aggregates?” “Whatever form there is, monk, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of form. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever volitional formations… whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness. To this extent, monk, the term ‘aggregate’ is applied to the aggregates.” “Very good, venerable sir.” Then that monk… asked further:

“Ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāya; ko hetu ko paccayo vedanākkhandhassa paññāpanāya; ko hetu ko paccayo saññākkhandhassa paññāpanāya; ko hetu ko paccayo saṅkhārakkhandhassa paññāpanāya; ko hetu ko paccayo viññāṇakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”ti? “Cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetu, cattāro mahābhūtā paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāya. Phasso hetu phasso paccayo vedanākkhandhassa paññāpanāya. Phasso hetu phasso paccayo saññākkhandhassa paññāpanāya. Phasso [P 3.0102] hetu[T 3.0124], phasso paccayo saṅkhārakkhandhassa paññāpanāya. Nāmarūpaṃ hetu, nāmarūpaṃ paccayo viññāṇakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… apucchi –

“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the form aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the aggregate of volitional formations? What is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate?” “Monk, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the designation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the aggregate of volitional formations. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate.” “Very good, venerable sir.” Then that monk… asked further:

“Kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, sakkāyadiṭṭhi hotī”ti? “Idha, bhikkhu, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ; vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ… attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ [M 2.0084] vā attānaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, sakkāyadiṭṭhi hotī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… apucchi –

“Venerable sir, how does identity view come to be?” “Here, monk, an uninstructed worldling—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma, and untrained in the noble Dhamma; who has not seen true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and untrained in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They regard feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. This, monk, is how identity view comes to be.” “Very good, venerable sir.” Then that monk… asked further:

“Kathaṃ pana, bhante, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī”ti? “Idha, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ; na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na [V 2.0094] attani vā viññāṇaṃ, na viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī”ti. “Sādhu[T 3.0125], bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu…pe… apucchi –

“But how, venerable sir, does identity view not come to be?” “Here, monk, a learned noble disciple, who sees the noble ones, is skilled in the noble Dhamma, and is well-trained in the noble Dhamma; who sees true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They do not regard feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. In this way, monk, identity view does not come to be.” “Very good, venerable sir.” Then that monk… asked further:

“Ko nu kho, bhante, rūpassa assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇaṃ; ko vedanāya… ko saññāya… ko saṅkhārānaṃ… ko viññāṇassa assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti? “Yaṃ kho, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ rūpassa assādo. Yaṃ rūpaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ – ayaṃ rūpassa ādīnavo. Yo rūpasmiṃ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ rūpassa nissaraṇaṃ. Yaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca… yaṃ saññaṃ [P 3.0103] paṭicca… ye saṅkhāre paṭicca… yaṃ viññāṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ viññāṇassa assādo. Yaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ – ayaṃ viññāṇassa ādīnavo. Yo viññāṇasmiṃ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ viññāṇassa nissaraṇa”nti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

“Venerable sir, what is the gratification of form, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the gratification of feeling… of perception… of volitional formations… of consciousness, what is the danger, and what is the escape?” “Monk, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form—that is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger of form. The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust for form—that is the escape from form. Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on feeling… in dependence on perception… in dependence on volitional formations… in dependence on consciousness—that is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger of consciousness. The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—that is the escape from consciousness.” “Very good, venerable sir.” That monk, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question.

“Kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti? “Yaṃ kiñci, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ – ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Yā [M 2.0085] kāci vedanā… yā [T 3.0126] kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ – ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti.

“Venerable sir, for one who knows thus and for one who sees thus, how is it that in this conscious body and in all external signs, the underlying tendencies of I-making, my-making, and conceit do not arise?” “Whatever form there is, monk, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form one sees as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever volitional formations… whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness one sees as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ It is thus, monk, for one who knows thus and for one who sees thus, that in this conscious body and in all external signs, the underlying tendencies of I-making, my-making, and conceit do not arise.”

Tena [V 2.0095] kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā, vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā; anattakatāni kammāni kathamattānaṃ katamattānaṃ (pī.), kammattānaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) phusissantī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi –

At that time, this thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: 'So it seems, friends, form is not-self, feeling… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self. How then can deeds done by what is not-self affect a self?' Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in that bhikkhu's mind, addressed the bhikkhus:

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya. Iti kira, bho, rūpaṃ anattā, vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā. Anattakatāni kammāni [P 3.0104] kathamattānaṃ phusissantīti? Paṭipucchāvinītā kho me tumhe, bhikkhave, tatra tatra tesu tesu dhammesu.

“Bhikkhus, it is possible that some foolish person here, being unwise and fallen into ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think to overreach the Teacher’s instruction, thinking: ‘So it seems, friends, form is not-self, feeling… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self. How then can deeds done by what is not-self affect a self?’ But you, bhikkhus, have been trained by me through questioning in these various matters.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti[T 3.0127]? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore… seeing thus… one understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

“Dve khandhā taññeva siyaṃ, adhivacanañca hetunā;

Sakkāyena duve vuttā, assādaviññāṇakena ca;

Ete dasavidhā vuttā, hoti bhikkhu pucchāyā”ti. dasamaṃ;

“Two on the aggregates, and likewise ‘It might be’; ‘Designation’ and ‘Cause’; Two are taught on ‘Identity View’, and on ‘Gratification and Consciousness’; With ‘The Bhikkhu’s Question’, it is thus. These ten kinds are taught. Tenth.”

Khajjanīyavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Khajjanīya Vagga, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for that is:

Assādo [V 2.0096][M 2.0086] dve samudayā, arahantehi apare dve;

Sīho khajjanī piṇḍolyaṃ, pālileyyena puṇṇamāti.

Gratification, two on Arising, and two others on the Arahants; The Lion, Devoured, Piṇḍolya, along with Pālileyya, and Puṇṇama.

9. Theravaggo

9. The Chapter on the Elders

1. Ānandasuttaṃ

1. The Sutta on Ānanda

83. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0128][P 3.0105]. Tatra kho āyasmā ānando bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, bhikkhave”ti. “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato ānandassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā ānando etadavoca –

83. At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:

“Puṇṇo nāma, āvuso, āyasmā mantāṇiputto mantāniputto (ka. sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) amhākaṃ navakānaṃ sataṃ bahūpakāro hoti. So amhe iminā ovādena ovadati – ‘upādāya, āvuso ānanda, asmīti hoti, no anupādāya. Kiñca upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya? Rūpaṃ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya’”.

“Friends, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is of great help to us who are junior bhikkhus. He advises us with this instruction: ‘Through clinging, friend Ānanda, the thought “I am” arises, not without clinging. And by clinging to what does the thought “I am” arise, not without clinging? By clinging to form, the thought “I am” arises, not without clinging. By clinging to feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, the thought “I am” arises, not without clinging.’”

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso ānanda, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko ādāse vā parisuddhe pariyodāte acche vā udakapatte sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno upādāya passeyya, no anupādāya; evameva kho, āvuso ānanda, rūpaṃ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.

“Just as, friend Ānanda, a woman or a man—young, youthful, and fond of adornment—looking at their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a clear bowl of water, would see it by depending on it, not without depending on it; in the very same way, friend Ānanda, by depending on form, the thought ‘I am’ arises, not without depending on it. By depending on feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, the thought ‘I am’ arises, not without depending on it.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso ānanda, ‘rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’”ti? ‘Aniccaṃ, āvuso’. Vedanā… saññā [V 2.0097]… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’ti? ‘Aniccaṃ, āvuso’. Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti [T 3.0129] pajānātīti. Puṇṇo nāma āvuso āyasmā mantāṇiputto amhākaṃ navakānaṃ [P 3.0106] sataṃ bahūpakāro hoti. So amhe iminā ovādena [M 2.0087] ovadati. Idañca pana me āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā dhammo abhisamitoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“What do you think, friend Ānanda, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, friend.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, friend.” “Therefore… seeing thus… one understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’ Friends, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is of great help to us who are junior bhikkhus. He advises us with this instruction. And having heard this Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, the Dhamma has been realized by me.” First.

2. Tissasuttaṃ

2. The Sutta on Tissa

84. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā tisso bhagavato pitucchāputto sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ evamāroceti – “api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo; disāpi me na pakkhāyanti; dhammāpi maṃ na paṭibhanti; thinamiddhañca thīnamiddhañca (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) me cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati; anabhirato ca brahmacariyaṃ carāmi; hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā”ti.

84. At Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One's paternal uncle's son, announced to a number of bhikkhus: “Friends, my body feels as if it were drugged; the directions are not clear to me; the teachings do not occur to me; sloth and torpor overwhelm my mind and remain; I practice the holy life without delight; and I have doubt about the teachings.”

Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “āyasmā, bhante, tisso bhagavato pitucchāputto sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ evamāroceti – ‘api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo; disāpi me na pakkhāyanti; dhammāpi maṃ na paṭibhanti; thinamiddhañca me cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati; anabhirato ca brahmacariyaṃ carāmi; hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā’”ti.

Then a number of bhikkhus went to the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One's paternal uncle's son, informs a number of bhikkhus thus: “Friends, my body feels as if it were drugged; the directions are not clear to me; the teachings do not occur to me; sloth and torpor overwhelm my mind and remain; I practice the holy life without delight; and I have doubt about the teachings.”'

Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena tissaṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantehī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā tisso tenupasaṅkami[T 3.0130]; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ tissaṃ etadavoca – “satthā taṃ, āvuso tissa, āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā tisso tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ tissaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, tissa, sambahulānaṃ [V 2.0098][P 3.0107] bhikkhūnaṃ evamārocesi – ‘api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo…pe… hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā’”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, tissa, rūpe avigatarāgassa avigatacchandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa, tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk: 'Come, monk, by my word call the monk Tissa.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' that monk replied to the Blessed One. Having assented, he went to the Venerable Tissa and said, 'The Teacher calls you, friend Tissa.' 'Yes, friend,' the Venerable Tissa replied to that monk. Then he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said this to the Venerable Tissa, who was seated to one side: 'Is it true, Tissa, that you informed a number of monks thus: "Friends, my body is as if sluggish... and doubt arises in me regarding the teachings"?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'What do you think, Tissa? For one who has not abandoned passion, desire, affection, thirst, burning, and craving for form, with the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise?' 'Yes, venerable sir.'

“Sādhu [M 2.0088] sādhu, tissa! Evañhetaṃ, tissa, hoti. Yathā taṃ rūpe avigatarāgassa… vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu avigatarāgassa…pe… tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Good, good, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa, for one who has not abandoned passion for form… for feeling… for perception… for formations… with the change and alteration of those formations, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise?” “Even so, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, tissa! Evañhetaṃ, tissa, hoti. Yathā taṃ viññāṇe avigatarāgassa avigatacchandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa, tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Good, good, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa. For one who has not abandoned passion, desire, affection, thirst, burning, and craving for consciousness, with the change and alteration of that consciousness, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise?” “Even so, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, tissa! Evañhetaṃ, tissa, hoti. Yathā taṃ viññāṇe avigatarāgassa. Taṃ [T 3.0131] kiṃ maññasi, tissa, rūpe vigatarāgassa vigatacchandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa, tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Good, good, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa, for one who has not abandoned passion for consciousness. What do you think, Tissa? For one in whom passion, desire, affection, thirst, burning, and craving for form have departed, with the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, tissa! Evañhetaṃ, tissa, hoti. Yathā taṃ rūpe vigatarāgassa… vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu vigatarāgassa… viññāṇe vigatarāgassa vigatacchandassa vigatapemassa [P 3.0108] vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Good, good, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa, for one in whom passion for form has departed… for feeling… for perception… for formations… for one in whom passion, desire, affection, thirst, burning, and craving for consciousness have departed, with the change and alteration of that consciousness, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, tissa! Evañhetaṃ, tissa, hoti. Yathā taṃ viññāṇe vigatarāgassa. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, tissa, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā [V 2.0099]… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Good, good, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa, for one in whom passion for consciousness has departed. What do you think, Tissa, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Therefore… seeing thus… one understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

“Seyyathāpi, tissa, dve purisā – eko puriso amaggakusalo, eko puriso maggakusalo. Tamenaṃ so amaggakusalo puriso amuṃ maggakusalaṃ purisaṃ maggaṃ puccheyya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ehi, bho purisa, ayaṃ maggo. Tena muhuttaṃ gaccha. Tena muhuttaṃ gantvā dakkhissasi dvedhāpathaṃ, tattha vāmaṃ muñcitvā dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhāhi. Tena muhuttaṃ gaccha. Tena muhuttaṃ gantvā dakkhissasi tibbaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ. Tena muhuttaṃ gaccha. Tena muhuttaṃ gantvā dakkhissasi mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallalaṃ[T 3.0132]. Tena muhuttaṃ gaccha. Tena muhuttaṃ [M 2.0089] gantvā dakkhissasi sobbhaṃ papātaṃ. Tena muhuttaṃ gaccha. Tena muhuttaṃ gantvā dakkhissasi samaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ ramaṇīya’”nti.

“Just as, Tissa, there are two men—one unskilled in the path, one skilled in the path. Among them, the man unskilled in the path would ask the skilled man about the path. He would say: ‘Come, good man, this is the path. Go along it for a moment. Having gone along it for a moment, you will see a fork in the road. There, abandon the left and take the right. Go along it for a moment. Having gone along it for a moment, you will see a dense forest thicket. Go along it for a moment. Having gone along it for a moment, you will see a great, low-lying swamp. Go along it for a moment. Having gone along it for a moment, you will see a chasm with a precipice. Go along it for a moment. Having gone along it for a moment, you will see a level, delightful stretch of ground.’”

“Upamā kho myāyaṃ, tissa, katā atthassa viññāpanāya. Ayaṃ cevettha attho – ‘puriso amaggakusalo’ti kho, tissa, puthujjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Puriso maggakusalo’ti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. ‘Dvedhāpatho’ti kho, tissa, vicikicchāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ[P 3.0109]. ‘Vāmo maggo’ti kho, tissa, aṭṭhaṅgikassetaṃ micchāmaggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – micchādiṭṭhiyā…pe… micchāsamādhissa. ‘Dakkhiṇo maggo’ti kho, tissa, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhiyā…pe… sammāsamādhissa. ‘Tibbo vanasaṇḍo’ti kho, tissa, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallala’nti kho, tissa, kāmānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Sobbho papāto’ti kho, tissa, kodhūpāyāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Samo bhūmibhāgo ramaṇīyo’ti kho, tissa, nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhirama, tissa, abhirama, tissa! Ahamovādena ahamanuggahena ahamanusāsaniyā”ti ahamāmisadhammānuggahena mamovādena mamānusāsaniyāti (ka.).

“This simile, Tissa, was made by me to convey the meaning. And this is the meaning herein: ‘A man unskilled in the path’ is a designation for an ordinary person. ‘A man skilled in the path’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘The fork in the road’ is a designation for doubt. ‘The left path’ is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, that is to say—wrong view… wrong concentration. ‘The right path’ is a designation for the noble eightfold path, that is to say—right view… right concentration. ‘The dense forest thicket’ is a designation for ignorance. ‘The great, low-lying swamp’ is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘The chasm with a precipice’ is a designation for anger and despair. ‘The level, delightful stretch of ground’ is a designation for Nibbāna. Delight, Tissa, delight! I am here with admonition, with support, and with instruction.”

Idamavoca [V 2.0100] bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā tisso bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti. Dutiyaṃ.

The Blessed One said this. Pleased, the Venerable Tissa delighted in the Blessed One's words. The Second.

3. Yamakasuttaṃ

3. The Yamaka Sutta

85. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā sāriputto sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane [T 3.0133] anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena yamakassa nāma bhikkhuno evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā”ti.

85. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery. Now at that time, a bhikkhu named Yamaka had conceived this evil wrong view: “I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body, and does not exist after death.”

Assosuṃ kho sambahulā bhikkhū yamakassa kira nāma bhikkhuno evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā”ti. Atha kho te bhikkhū yenāyasmā yamako [M 2.0090] tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā yamakena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ yamakaṃ etadavocuṃ –

Indeed, many bhikkhus heard that a certain bhikkhu named Yamaka had conceived such an evil wrong view: 'I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.' Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Yamaka. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Yamaka. Having concluded the courteous and memorable talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Yamaka:

“Saccaṃ kira te, āvuso yamaka, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ [P 3.0110] bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti? “Evaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti.

“Is it true, friend Yamaka, as it is said, that such an evil wrong view has arisen in you: 'I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death'?” “Even so, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way: 'A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.'”

“Mā, āvuso yamaka, evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi. Na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhācikkhanaṃ. Na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti. Evampi kho āyasmā [T 3.0134] yamako tehi bhikkhūhi vuccamāno tatheva taṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa voharati – “tathāhaṃ [V 2.0101] bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā”ti.

“Friend Yamaka, do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus: 'A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.'” Even when spoken to in this way by those bhikkhus, the Venerable Yamaka, forcefully grasping and adhering to that same evil wrong view, declared: “I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.”

Yato kho te bhikkhū nāsakkhiṃsu āyasmantaṃ yamakaṃ etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetuṃ, atha kho te bhikkhū uṭṭhāyāsanā yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavocuṃ – “yamakassa nāma, āvuso sāriputta, bhikkhuno evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’ti. Sādhāyasmā sāriputto yena yamako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā sāriputto tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā yamako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā yamakena saddhiṃ sammodi…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ yamakaṃ etadavoca –

When those bhikkhus were unable to cause the Venerable Yamaka to abandon that evil wrong view, then those bhikkhus, having risen from their seats, approached the place where the Venerable Sāriputta was. Having approached, they said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, an evil wrong view of this sort has arisen in the bhikkhu named Yamaka: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breaking up of the body; he is not after death." It would be good if the Venerable Sāriputta would approach the bhikkhu Yamaka out of compassion.' The Venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached the place where the Venerable Yamaka was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Yamaka... Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Yamaka:

“Saccaṃ kira te, āvuso yamaka, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo [P 3.0111] bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti? “Evaṃ [M 2.0091] khvāhaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ [T 3.0135] desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā”ti.

“Is it true, friend Yamaka, as is said, that an evil wrong view of this sort has arisen in you: ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breaking up of the body, and does not exist after death’?” “Indeed, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breaking up of the body, and does not exist after death.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, āvuso”. “Vedanā niccā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, āvuso”. Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“What do you think of this, friend Yamaka, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, friend.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, friend.” “Therefore, in this teaching… seeing thus… he knows distinctly: ‘There is no other task to be done for this state.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, rūpaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso” [V 2.0102]… “vedanaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”… “saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “That is not so, friend.” … “Do you regard feeling as the Tathāgata?” “That is not so, friend.”… “Do you regard perception… volitional formations… consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “That is not so, friend.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, rūpasmiṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Aññatra rūpā tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Vedanāya… aññatra vedanāya…pe… saññāya… aññatra saññāya… saṅkhāresu… aññatra saṅkhārehi… viññāṇasmiṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Aññatra viññāṇā tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata in form?” “That is not so, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata apart from form?” “That is not so, friend.” “In feeling?… Apart from feeling?… In perception?… Apart from perception?… In volitional formations?… Apart from volitional formations?… Do you regard the Tathāgata in consciousness?” “That is not so, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata apart from consciousness?” “That is not so, friend.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, rūpaṃ… vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard form… feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “That is not so, friend.”

“Taṃ [T 3.0136][P 3.0112] kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, ayaṃ so arūpī… avedano… asaññī… asaṅkhāro… aviññāṇo tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Ettha ca te, āvuso yamaka, diṭṭheva dhamme saccato thetato tathato (syā. kaṃ.) tathāgate anupalabbhiyamāne tathāgate anupalabbhamāne (?), kallaṃ nu te taṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti?

“What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard it thus: ‘The Tathāgata is formless… without feeling… without perception… without formations… without consciousness’?” “No, friend.” “And since, friend Yamaka, a Tathāgata is not apprehended by you in this very life as true and real, is it fitting for you to make this declaration: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he is not after death’?”

“Ahu kho me taṃ, āvuso sāriputta, pubbe aviddasuno pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; idañca panāyasmato sāriputtassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā tañceva pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ pahīnaṃ, dhammo ca me abhisamito”ti.

“Indeed, friend Sāriputta, formerly, when I was ignorant, I held that pernicious view. But now, having heard this Dhamma teaching from the Venerable Sāriputta, that same pernicious view has been abandoned, and the Dhamma has been comprehended by me.”

“Sace [M 2.0092] taṃ, āvuso yamaka, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘yo so, āvuso yamaka, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā kiṃ hotī’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭho tvaṃ, āvuso yamaka, kinti byākareyyāsī”ti? “Sace maṃ, āvuso, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘yo so, āvuso yamaka, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā kiṃ hotī’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, āvuso, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ – ‘rūpaṃ kho, āvuso, aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ; yaṃ dukkhaṃ taṃ [V 2.0103] niruddhaṃ tadatthaṅgataṃ. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ; yaṃ dukkhaṃ taṃ niruddhaṃ tadatthaṅgata’nti. Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ[T 3.0137], āvuso, evaṃ byākareyya”nti.

“If they were to ask you, friend Yamaka: ‘Friend Yamaka, that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed—what becomes of him after the breakup of the body, after death?’ Being asked thus, friend Yamaka, how would you answer?” “If, friend, they were to ask me thus: ‘Friend Yamaka, that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed—what becomes of him after the breakup of the body, after death?’ Being asked thus, friend, I would answer thus: ‘Form, indeed, friends, is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering has ceased, it has vanished. Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering has ceased, it has vanished.’ Being asked thus, friend, I would answer thus.”

“Sādhu sādhu, āvuso yamaka! Tena hāvuso, yamaka, upamaṃ te karissāmi etasseva atthassa bhiyyosomattāya ñāṇāya. Seyyathāpi, āvuso yamaka, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo; so ca ārakkhasampanno. Tassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmo jīvitā voropetukāmo. Tassa evamassa [P 3.0113] – ‘ayaṃ kho gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo; so ca ārakkhasampanno; nāyaṃ na hāyaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) sukaro pasayha jīvitā voropetuṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ anupakhajja jīvitā voropeyya’nti. So taṃ gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘upaṭṭhaheyyaṃ taṃ, bhante’ti. Tamenaṃ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upaṭṭhāpeyya. So upaṭṭhaheyya pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī. Tassa so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā mittatopi naṃ saddaheyya daheyya (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.); suhajjatopi naṃ saddaheyya; tasmiñca vissāsaṃ āpajjeyya. Yadā kho, āvuso, tassa purisassa evamassa – ‘saṃvissattho kho myāyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā’ti, atha naṃ rahogataṃ viditvā tiṇhena satthena jīvitā voropeyya.

“Good, good, friend Yamaka! Therefore, friend Yamaka, I will give you a simile for the sake of a fuller understanding of this same meaning. Suppose, friend Yamaka, there is a householder or a householder’s son who is wealthy, with great riches and great possessions, and he is well-guarded. Then some man might appear who wishes him non-benefit, non-welfare, and lack of safety from the yoke, who seeks to deprive him of life. That man might think: ‘This householder or householder’s son is wealthy, with great riches and great possessions, and he is well-guarded. It is not easy to deprive him of life by force. What if I were to draw near to him and deprive him of life?’ So he would approach that householder or householder’s son and say: ‘I will attend on you, sir.’ Then that householder or householder’s son would have him attend. He would attend on him, rising before him, retiring after him, responsive to what is to be done, agreeable in conduct, pleasing in speech. Then that householder or householder’s son would trust him as a friend, would trust him as a good-hearted person, and would place confidence in him. When, friend Yamaka, that man thinks: ‘This householder or householder’s son is intimate with me,’ then, having known him to be in a secluded place, he would deprive him of life with a sharp weapon.

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvuso yamaka, yadā hi so puriso amuṃ gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ āha – ‘upaṭṭhaheyyaṃ taṃ, bhante’ti, tadāpi so vadhakova. Vadhakañca pana [T 3.0138] santaṃ na aññāsi – ‘vadhako me’ti. Yadāpi so upaṭṭhahati pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī, tadāpi so vadhakova. Vadhakañca pana santaṃ [M 2.0093] na aññāsi – ‘vadhako me’ti. Yadāpi naṃ rahogataṃ viditvā tiṇhena satthena jīvitā voropeti, tadāpi so vadhakova. Vadhakañca pana santaṃ na aññāsi – ‘vadhako me’”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti. “Evameva kho, āvuso, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato [P 3.0114] samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ”.

“What do you think, friend Yamaka? When that man approached that householder or householder’s son and said, ‘I will attend on you, sir,’ even then he was a murderer. But the other did not recognize him as a murderer, and did not know: ‘He is my murderer.’ When he attended on him—rising before him, retiring after him, responsive to what is to be done, agreeable in conduct, and pleasing in speech—even then he was a murderer. But the other did not recognize him as a murderer, and did not know: ‘He is my murderer.’ When, having known him to be in a secluded place, he deprived him of life with a sharp weapon, even then he was a murderer. But the other did not recognize him as a murderer, and did not know: ‘He is my murderer.’” “That is so, friend.” “In the same way, friend, the uninstructed worldling—who is not a seer of the noble ones, not skilled and disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who is not a seer of true persons, not skilled and disciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling… perception… formations… consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.”

“So [V 2.0104] aniccaṃ rūpaṃ ‘aniccaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Aniccaṃ vedanaṃ ‘aniccā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Aniccaṃ saññaṃ ‘aniccā saññā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Anicce saṅkhāre ‘aniccā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Aniccaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘aniccaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti.

“He does not understand impermanent form as it actually is: ‘Form is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent feeling as it actually is: ‘Feeling is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent perception as it actually is: ‘Perception is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent formations as they actually are: ‘Formations are impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent consciousness as it actually is: ‘Consciousness is impermanent.’”

“Dukkhaṃ rūpaṃ ‘dukkhaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ… dukkhaṃ saññaṃ… dukkhe saṅkhāre… dukkhaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘dukkhaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti.

“He does not understand suffering form as it actually is: ‘Form is suffering.’ He does not understand suffering feeling… suffering perception… suffering formations… suffering consciousness as it actually is: ‘Consciousness is suffering.’”

“Anattaṃ rūpaṃ ‘anattā rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Anattaṃ [T 3.0139] vedanaṃ… anattaṃ saññaṃ… anatte saṅkhāre… anattaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘anattaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti.

“He does not understand not-self form as it actually is: ‘Form is not-self.’ He does not understand not-self feeling… not-self perception… not-self formations… not-self consciousness as it actually is: ‘Consciousness is not-self.’”

“Saṅkhataṃ rūpaṃ ‘saṅkhataṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Saṅkhataṃ vedanaṃ… saṅkhataṃ saññaṃ… saṅkhate saṅkhāre… saṅkhataṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘saṅkhataṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti.

“He does not understand conditioned form as it actually is: ‘Form is conditioned.’ He does not understand conditioned feeling… conditioned perception… conditioned formations… conditioned consciousness as it actually is: ‘Consciousness is conditioned.’”

“Vadhakaṃ rūpaṃ ‘vadhakaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vadhakaṃ vedanaṃ ‘vadhakā vedanā’ti… vadhakaṃ saññaṃ ‘vadhakā saññā’ti… vadhake saṅkhāre ‘vadhakā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vadhakaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘vadhakaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti.

He does not know distinctly, as it really is, form the killer as ‘form is a killer.’ He does not know distinctly, as it really is, feeling the killer as ‘feeling is a killer’… perception the killer as ‘perception is a killer’… formations the killers as ‘formations are killers.’ He does not know distinctly, as it really is, consciousness the killer as ‘consciousness is a killer.’

“So rūpaṃ upeti upādiyati adhiṭṭhāti ‘attā me’ti. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ upeti upādiyati adhiṭṭhāti ‘attā me’ti. Tassime pañcupādānakkhandhā upetā upādinnā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti.

He approaches form, grasps it, and resolves upon it, thinking: ‘This is my self.’ He approaches feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, grasps it, and resolves upon it, thinking: ‘This is my self.’ These five aggregates subject to clinging, thus approached and grasped, lead to his harm and suffering for a long time.

“Sutavā [M 2.0094] ca kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī…pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ; na attani rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ. Na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ attānaṃ; na attani viññāṇaṃ, na viññāṇasmiṃ attānaṃ.

But, friend, a learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones… who is well-trained in the Dhamma of the good people, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form. He does not regard feeling… perception… formations… consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness.

“So [P 3.0115] aniccaṃ rūpaṃ ‘aniccaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Aniccaṃ vedanaṃ [V 2.0105]… aniccaṃ saññaṃ… anicce saṅkhāre [T 3.0140]… aniccaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘aniccaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

He knows distinctly, as it really is, impermanent form as ‘form is impermanent.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, impermanent feeling… impermanent perception… impermanent formations… impermanent consciousness as ‘consciousness is impermanent.’

“Dukkhaṃ rūpaṃ ‘dukkhaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ… dukkhaṃ saññaṃ… dukkhe saṅkhāre… dukkhaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘dukkhaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

He knows distinctly, as it really is, suffering form as ‘form is suffering.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, suffering feeling… suffering perception… suffering formations… suffering consciousness as ‘consciousness is suffering.’

“Anattaṃ rūpaṃ ‘anattā rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Anattaṃ vedanaṃ… anattaṃ saññaṃ… anatte saṅkhāre… anattaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘anattā viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

He knows distinctly, as it really is, not-self form as ‘form is not-self.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, not-self feeling… not-self perception… not-self formations… not-self consciousness as ‘consciousness is not-self.’

“Saṅkhataṃ rūpaṃ ‘saṅkhataṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Saṅkhataṃ vedanaṃ… saṅkhataṃ saññaṃ… saṅkhate saṅkhāre… saṅkhataṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘saṅkhataṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

He knows distinctly, as it really is, conditioned form as ‘form is conditioned.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, conditioned feeling… conditioned perception… conditioned formations… conditioned consciousness as ‘consciousness is conditioned.’

“Vadhakaṃ rūpaṃ ‘vadhakaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vadhakaṃ vedanaṃ… vadhakaṃ saññaṃ… vadhake saṅkhāre “vadhakā saṅkhārā”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vadhakaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘vadhakaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.
