He knows distinctly, as it really is, form the killer as ‘form is a killer.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, feeling the killer as ‘feeling is a killer’… perception the killer as ‘perception is a killer’… formations the killers as ‘formations are killers.’ He knows distinctly, as it really is, consciousness the killer as ‘consciousness is a killer.’

“So rūpaṃ na upeti, na upādiyati, nādhiṭṭhāti – ‘attā me’ti. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ na upeti, na upādiyati, nādhiṭṭhāti – ‘attā me’ti. Tassime pañcupādānakkhandhā anupetā anupādinnā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattantī”ti. “Evametaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, hoti yesaṃ āyasmantānaṃ tādisā sabrahmacārino anukampakā atthakāmā ovādakā anusāsakā. Idañca pana me āyasmato [T 3.0141] sāriputtassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti. Tatiyaṃ.

He does not approach form, does not grasp it, and does not resolve upon it as ‘my self.’ He does not approach feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, does not grasp it, and does not resolve upon it as ‘my self.’ For him, these five aggregates subject to clinging, not being approached and not being grasped, conduce to his welfare and happiness for a long time.” “Indeed, friend Sāriputta, this is how it is for those venerable ones who have such fellow practitioners in the holy life who are compassionate, who desire their welfare, who are advisors and instructors. And having heard this Dhamma teaching from the Venerable Sāriputta, my mind has been liberated from the taints through non-clinging.”

4. Anurādhasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse to Anurādha

86. Evaṃ [V 2.0106][P 3.0116] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā anurādho bhagavato avidūre [M 2.0095] araññakuṭikāyaṃ viharati. Atha kho sambahulā aññatitthiyā paribbājakā yena āyasmā anurādho tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā anurādhena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā āyasmantaṃ anurādhaṃ etadavocuṃ – “yo so, āvuso anurādha, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto, taṃ tathāgato imesu catūsu ṭhānesu paññāpayamāno paññāpeti – ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā”ti?

86. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. Now at that time the Venerable Anurādha was dwelling not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut. Then many wanderers of other sects approached the Venerable Anurādha; having approached, they exchanged courteous greetings with the Venerable Anurādha. When they had exchanged courteous and amiable talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to the Venerable Anurādha: “Friend Anurādha, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the most excellent person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—when the Tathāgata makes a declaration, does he declare him in terms of these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā anurādho te aññatitthiye paribbājake etadavoca – “yo so āvuso tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṃ tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti – ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, aññatitthiyā [T 3.0142] paribbājakā āyasmantaṃ anurādhaṃ etadavocuṃ – “so cāyaṃ bhikkhu navo bhavissati acirapabbajito, thero vā pana bālo abyatto”ti. Atha kho aññatitthiyā paribbājakā āyasmantaṃ anurādhaṃ navavādena ca bālavādena ca apasādetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu.

When this was said, the Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: “Friends, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the most excellent person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—when making a declaration, declares him apart from these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’” When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to the Venerable Anurādha: “This bhikkhu must be new and not long ordained, or if an elder, he is a fool and incompetent.” Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged the Venerable Anurādha with talk of his newness and foolishness, rose from their seats and departed.

Atha [P 3.0117] kho āyasmato anurādhassa acirapakkantesu tesu aññatitthiyesu paribbājakesu etadahosi – “sace kho maṃ te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā uttariṃ pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ. Kathaṃ byākaramāno nu khvāhaṃ tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assaṃ, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyaṃ, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyaṃ, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā”ti?

Then, not long after those wanderers of other sects had departed, this thought occurred to the Venerable Anurādha: ‘If indeed those wanderers of other sects were to question me further, how should I answer so that I would be one who states what was spoken by the Blessed One, not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no legitimate, consequential statement would provide grounds for censure?’”

Atha [V 2.0107] kho āyasmā anurādho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā anurādho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato avidūre araññakuṭikāyaṃ viharāmi. Atha kho, bhante, sambahulā aññatitthiyā paribbājakā yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu [M 2.0096] …pe… maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘yo so, āvuso anurādha, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṃ tathāgato imesu catūsu ṭhānesu paññāpayamāno paññāpeti – hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, na hoti… hoti ca na ca hoti, neva [T 3.0143] hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā’”ti?

Then the Venerable Anurādha approached the Blessed One; having approached... seated to one side, the Venerable Anurādha said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, I am dwelling not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut. Then, venerable sir, many wandering ascetics of other sects approached me... and said to me: “Friend Anurādha, when the Tathāgata—the supreme person, the ultimate person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—makes a declaration, does he declare it in these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”'

Evaṃ vuttāhaṃ, bhante, te aññatitthiye paribbājake etadavocaṃ – “yo so, āvuso, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto, taṃ tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti – ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā…pe… ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vāti. Evaṃ vutte, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘so cāyaṃ bhikkhu na vo bhavissati acirapabbajito thero vā pana bālo abyatto’ti. Atha kho maṃ, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā navavādena bālavādena ca apasādetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu”.

When they said this, venerable sir, I said to those wandering ascetics of other sects: 'Friends, the Tathāgata—the supreme person, the ultimate person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—when making a declaration, declares it apart from these four positions: “The Tathāgata exists after death,” … or “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”' When I had spoken thus, venerable sir, those wandering ascetics of other sects said to me: 'This bhikkhu must be a new one, recently gone forth, or if he is an elder, he is a fool and incompetent.' Then, venerable sir, those wandering ascetics of other sects, having disparaged me with talk of being new and talk of being a fool, rose from their seats and departed.

“Tassa [P 3.0118] mayhaṃ, bhante, acirapakkantesu tesu aññatitthiyesu paribbājakesu etadahosi – ‘sace kho maṃ te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā uttariṃ pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ. Kathaṃ byākaramāno nu khvāhaṃ tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assaṃ, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyaṃ, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyaṃ, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā’”ti?

Then, venerable sir, not long after those wandering ascetics of other sects had departed, this thought occurred to me: 'If those wandering ascetics of other sects were to question me further, how should I answer so that I would be one who speaks in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no reasonable, doctrinal line of argument would become censurable?'

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, anurādha, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ[T 3.0144], bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ bhante”…pe… tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti”.

“What do you think, Anurādha, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it proper to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No indeed, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” … “Therefore… seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is no more for this state of being.’”

“Taṃ [V 2.0108] kiṃ maññasi, anurādha, rūpaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “No indeed, venerable sir.” “Do you regard feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ [M 2.0097] kiṃ maññasi, anurādha, rūpasmiṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Aññatra rūpā tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanāya…pe… aññatra vedanāya…pe… saññāya… aññatra saññāya… saṅkhāresu… aññatra saṅkhārehi… viññāṇasmiṃ… aññatra viññāṇā tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?” “No indeed, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No indeed, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as in feeling… as apart from feeling… as in perception… as apart from perception… as in volitional formations… as apart from volitional formations… as in consciousness… as apart from consciousness?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, anurādha, rūpaṃ… vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness taken together as the Tathāgata?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, anurādha, ayaṃ so arūpī avedano asaññī asaṅkhāro aviññāṇo tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard one who is without form, without feeling, without perception, without volitional formations, and without consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”

“Ettha ca te, anurādha, diṭṭheva dhamme saccato thetato tathāgate anupalabbhiyamāne kallaṃ nu te taṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ – ‘yo so, āvuso, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṃ [T 3.0145] tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi [P 3.0119] ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti – hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā… neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“And so, Anurādha, when the Tathāgata is not apprehended by you as true and real here and now, is it fitting for you to make that declaration: ‘Friends, the Tathāgata—the supreme person, the ultimate person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—when making a declaration, declares it apart from these four positions: “The Tathāgata exists after death,” or… or “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death”’?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, anurādha! Pubbe cāhaṃ, anurādha, etarahi ca dukkhañceva paññapemi, dukkhassa ca nirodha”nti. Catutthaṃ.

“Good, good, Anurādha! Both formerly and now, Anurādha, I proclaim only suffering and the cessation of suffering.”

5. Vakkalisuttaṃ

5. The Vakkali Sutta

87. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena [V 2.0109] āyasmā vakkali kumbhakāranivesane viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho āyasmā vakkali upaṭṭhāke āmantesi – “etha tumhe, āvuso, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha – ‘vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, so bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatī’ti. Evañca vadetha – ‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu; anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā yena [M 2.0098] bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, so bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati; evañca pana vadeti – ‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu; anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

87. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Now at that time the Venerable Vakkali was dwelling in a potter's workshop, afflicted with sickness, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the Venerable Vakkali addressed his attendants: 'Come, friends, approach the Blessed One and, having approached, pay homage with your head at his feet in my name and say: "Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Vakkali is afflicted with sickness, suffering, and gravely ill; he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet." And say this: "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would come to the bhikkhu Vakkali out of compassion."' 'Yes, friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Vakkali, and then they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Vakkali is afflicted with sickness, suffering, and gravely ill; he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet and says this: "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would come to the bhikkhu Vakkali out of compassion."' The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Atha [T 3.0146] kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yenāyasmā vakkali tenupasaṅkami. Addasā [P 3.0120] kho āyasmā vakkali bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna mañcake samadhosi samañcosi (sī.), samañcopi (syā. kaṃ.) saṃ + dhū + ī = samadhosi. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ etadavoca – “alaṃ, vakkali, mā tvaṃ mañcake samadhosi. Santimāni āsanāni paññattāni; tatthāhaṃ nisīdissāmī”ti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ etadavoca – “kacci te, vakkali, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti, no abhikkamanti; paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no abhikkamo”ti? “Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ, na yāpanīyaṃ; bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti; abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no paṭikkamo”ti. “Kacci te, vakkali, na kiñci kukkuccaṃ, na koci vippaṭisāro”ti? “Taggha me, bhante, anappakaṃ kukkuccaṃ, anappako vippaṭisāro”ti. “Kacci pana taṃ, vakkali, attā sīlato na upavadatī”ti? “Na kho maṃ, bhante, attā sīlato upavadatī”ti. “No ce kira taṃ, vakkali, attā sīlato upavadati; atha kiñca te kukkuccaṃ ko ca vippaṭisāro”ti? “Cirapaṭikāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamitukāmo, natthi ca me kāyasmiṃ tāvatikā balamattā, yāvatāhaṃ yāhaṃ (sī.), yāyāhaṃ (pī.) bhagavantaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkameyya”nti.

Then the Blessed One, having adjusted his lower robe and taking his bowl and outer robe, approached the Venerable Vakkali. The Venerable Vakkali saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he stirred on his bed. Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Vakkali: “Enough, Vakkali, do not stir on your bed. These seats are prepared; I will sit there.” The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Vakkali: “Vakkali, are you enduring? Are you managing? Are your painful feelings subsiding and not increasing? Is their subsiding apparent, and not their increase?” “Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not managing. My severe painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding. Their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.” “Vakkali, do you have no worry, no remorse?” “Indeed, venerable sir, I have much worry and much remorse.” “But, Vakkali, does your self not reproach you with regard to virtue?” “No, venerable sir, my self does not reproach me with regard to virtue.” “If, Vakkali, your self does not reproach you with regard to virtue, then what is your worry and what is your remorse?” “For a long time, venerable sir, I have been wanting to approach to see the Blessed One, but I do not have enough strength in my body to approach to see the Blessed One.”

“Alaṃ[V 2.0110], vakkali, kiṃ te iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena? Yo [T 3.0147] kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati so maṃ passati; yo maṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati. Dhammañhi, vakkali, passanto maṃ passati; maṃ passanto dhammaṃ passati.

“Enough, Vakkali. What use is there in seeing this foul body? Indeed, Vakkali, one who sees the Dhamma sees me; one who sees me sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, in seeing the Dhamma, one sees me; in seeing me, one sees the Dhamma.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, vakkali, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ[P 3.0121], bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ [M 2.0099] nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe… eso me attāti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“What do you think, Vakkali, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, is it permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” … “is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘…this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore… seeing thus… one understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ iminā ovādena ovaditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena gijjhakūṭo pabbato tena pakkāmi. Atha kho āyasmā vakkali acirapakkantassa bhagavato upaṭṭhāke āmantesi – “etha maṃ, āvuso, mañcakaṃ āropetvā yena isigilipassaṃ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkamatha. Kathañhi nāma mādiso antaraghare kālaṃ kattabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ mañcakaṃ āropetvā yena isigilipassaṃ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Atha kho bhagavā tañca rattiṃ tañca divāvasesaṃ gijjhakūṭe pabbate vihāsi. Atha [T 3.0148] kho dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu…pe… ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho ekā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu vimokkhāya cetetī”ti. Aparā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [V 2.0111] – “so hi nūna, bhante, suvimutto vimuccissatī”ti. Idamavocuṃ tā devatāyo. Idaṃ vatvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu.

Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Vakkali with this instruction, rose from his seat and went to Vulture Peak Mountain. Soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Vakkali addressed his attendants: “Come, friends, lift me onto a litter and take me to the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili. For how could one like me think of dying inside a house?” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Vakkali. They lifted the Venerable Vakkali onto a litter and carried him to the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili. Then the Blessed One spent that night and the remaining part of the day on Vulture Peak Mountain. When the night had advanced, two deities of surpassing radiance, illuminating the entire Vulture Peak, approached the Blessed One… stood to one side. Standing there, one deity said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Vakkali is intent on liberation.” The other deity said: “Surely, venerable sir, being well-liberated, he will be liberated.” This is what those deities said. Having said this, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and vanished right there.

Atha kho bhagavā tassā rattiyā accayena bhikkhū āmantesi – “etha tumhe, bhikkhave, yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā vakkaliṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadetha –

Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Come, bhikkhus, approach where the bhikkhu Vakkali is; having approached, speak thus to the bhikkhu Vakkali:

“‘Suṇāvuso tvaṃ, vakkali, bhagavato vacanaṃ dvinnañca [P 3.0122] devatānaṃ. Imaṃ, āvuso, rattiṃ dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho, āvuso, ekā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu vimokkhāya cetetīti. Aparā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – so hi nūna, bhante, suvimutto vimuccissatīti. Bhagavā ca taṃ, āvuso vakkali, evamāha – mā bhāyi, vakkali; mā bhāyi, vakkali! Apāpakaṃ te maraṇaṃ bhavissati, apāpikā kālakiriyā’”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te [M 2.0100] bhikkhū [T 3.0149] bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā vakkali tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ etadavocuṃ – “suṇāvuso vakkali, bhagavato vacanaṃ dvinnañca devatāna”nti.

'Listen, friend Vakkali, to the word of the Blessed One and of two deities. This night, friend, when the night was far advanced, two deities of surpassing radiance, having illuminated the entire Gijjhakūṭa mountain, approached where the Blessed One was. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, friend, one deity said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the monk Vakkali is intent on liberation.” The other deity said this to the Blessed One: “Surely, venerable sir, being well-liberated, he will be liberated.” And the Blessed One, friend Vakkali, said this to you: “Do not fear, Vakkali; do not fear, Vakkali! Your death will not be an evil one, your passing away will not be an evil one.”' 'Very well, venerable sir.' Having thus assented to the Blessed One, those monks approached where the Venerable Vakkali was; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Vakkali: 'Listen, friend Vakkali, to the word of the Blessed One and of two deities.'

Atha kho āyasmā vakkali upaṭṭhāke āmantesi – “etha maṃ, āvuso, mañcakā oropetha. Kathañhi nāma mādiso ucce āsane nisīditvā tassa bhagavato sāsanaṃ sotabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti! “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ mañcakā oropesuṃ. “Imaṃ, āvuso, rattiṃ dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā…pe… ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho, āvuso, ekā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu vimokkhāya cetetī’ti. Aparā devatā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘so hi nūna, bhante, suvimutto vimuccissatī’ti. Bhagavā ca taṃ, āvuso vakkali, evamāha – ‘mā bhāyi, vakkali; mā bhāyi, vakkali! Apāpakaṃ te maraṇaṃ bhavissati, apāpikā kālakiriyā’”ti. “Tena hāvuso, mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha – ‘vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. So bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatī’ti. Evañca vadetha – ‘rūpaṃ aniccaṃ. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmi. Vedanā [P 3.0123] aniccā. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi[V 2.0112]. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na [T 3.0150] vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmi. Saññā… saṅkhārā aniccā. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmi. Viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmī’”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā pakkamiṃsu. Atha kho āyasmā vakkali acirapakkantesu tesu bhikkhūsu satthaṃ āharesi.

Then the Venerable Vakkali addressed his attendant monks: “Come, friends, lower me from the bed. For how indeed could one like me think it proper to hear the teaching of the Blessed One while sitting on a high seat?” “So be it, friend.” Having thus assented to the Venerable Vakkali, those monks lowered the Venerable Vakkali from the bed. “Friend, this night, when the night was far advanced, two deities... stood to one side. Standing to one side, friend, one deity said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the monk Vakkali is intent on liberation.’ The other deity said this to the Blessed One: ‘Surely, venerable sir, being well-liberated, he will be liberated.’ And the Blessed One, friend Vakkali, said this to you: ‘Do not fear, Vakkali; do not fear, Vakkali! Your death will not be an evil one; your passing away will not be an evil one.’” “Well then, friends, with my words, pay homage to the Blessed One’s feet with your heads, saying: ‘Venerable sir, the monk Vakkali is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. He pays homage to the Blessed One’s feet with his head.’ And say this also: ‘Venerable sir, form is impermanent; of this I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity. Feeling is impermanent; of this, venerable sir, I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity. Perception… Volitional formations are impermanent; of this, venerable sir, I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity. Consciousness is impermanent; of this, venerable sir, I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity.’” “So be it, friend.” Having thus assented to the Venerable Vakkali, those monks departed. Then, not long after those monks had departed, the Venerable Vakkali brought forth a knife.

Atha kho te bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno; so bhagavato [M 2.0101] pāde sirasā vandati; evañca vadeti – ‘rūpaṃ aniccaṃ. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmi. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā [T 3.0151]… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Tāhaṃ, bhante, na kaṅkhāmi. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti na vicikicchāmi. Yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vāti na vicikicchāmī’”ti.

Then those monks approached the Blessed One; having approached, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the monk Vakkali is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. He pays homage to the Blessed One’s feet with his head and says this: ‘Form is impermanent; of this, venerable sir, I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity. Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is impermanent; of this, venerable sir, I have no doubt. That what is impermanent is suffering; of this I have no perplexity. That what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that I have no desire, lust, or affection for it—of this I have no perplexity.’”

Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “āyāma, bhikkhave, yena isigilipassaṃ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkamissāma; yattha vakkalinā kulaputtena satthamāharita”nti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Atha kho bhagavā sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ yena isigilipassaṃ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ vakkaliṃ dūratova mañcake vivattakkhandhaṃ semānaṃ.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Come, monks, let us go to the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili, where the clansman Vakkali has brought forth a weapon.” “Even so, venerable sir,” those monks assented to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with many monks, went to the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili. From a distance, the Blessed One saw the Venerable Vakkali lying on a cot, his body turned.

Tena [P 3.0124] kho pana samayena dhūmāyitattaṃ timirāyitattaṃ gacchateva purimaṃ disaṃ, gacchati pacchimaṃ disaṃ, gacchati uttaraṃ disaṃ, gacchati dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ, gacchati uddhaṃ disaṃ, gacchati adho [V 2.0113] disaṃ, gacchati anudisaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṃ dhūmāyitattaṃ timirāyitattaṃ gacchateva purimaṃ disaṃ…pe… gacchati anudisa”nti. “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Eso kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā vakkalissa kulaputtassa viññāṇaṃ samanvesati samannesati (ka. sī. pī.) – ‘kattha vakkalissa kulaputtassa viññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhita’nti? Appatiṭṭhitena ca, bhikkhave, viññāṇena vakkali kulaputto parinibbuto”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

At that time, a mass of smoke and darkness was going to the eastern direction, going to the western direction, going to the northern direction, going to the southern direction, going upwards, going downwards, and going to the intermediate directions. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks, do you see this mass of smoke and darkness going to the eastern direction… and going to the intermediate directions?’ ‘Yes, Venerable Sir.’ ‘Monks, that is the evil Māra searching for the consciousness of the clansman Vakkali, thinking: “Where is the consciousness of the clansman Vakkali established?” But, monks, with unestablished consciousness, the clansman Vakkali has attained final Nibbāna.’

6. Assajisuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Assaji

88. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā assaji kassapakārāme viharati [T 3.0152] ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho āyasmā assaji upaṭṭhāke āmantesi – “etha tumhe, āvuso, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha – ‘assaji, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. So bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatī’ti. Evañca vadetha – ‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā [M 2.0102] yena assaji bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato assajissa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “assaji, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko…pe… sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena assaji bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

88. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. At that time, the Venerable Assaji was dwelling in Kassapa's monastery, sick, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the Venerable Assaji addressed his attendant monks: ‘Come, friends, approach the Blessed One. Having approached, in my name venerate the Blessed One's feet with your head and say: “Venerable Sir, the monk Assaji is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. He venerates the Blessed One's feet with his head.” And also say this: “It would be good indeed, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One would approach the monk Assaji out of compassion.”’ ‘Yes, friend,’ those monks replied in assent to the Venerable Assaji, and they approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, the monk Assaji is sick… It would be good indeed, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One would approach the monk Assaji out of compassion.’ The Blessed One consented by means of silence.

Atha [P 3.0125] kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā assaji tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho āyasmā assaji bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna mañcake samadhosi. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ assajiṃ āyasmato assajissa (pī. ka.) etadavoca – “alaṃ, assaji, mā tvaṃ mañcake samadhosi. Santimāni āsanāni paññattāni, tatthāhaṃ nisīdissāmī”ti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ assajiṃ etadavoca – “kacci te, assaji, khamanīyaṃ, kacci [T 3.0153] yāpanīyaṃ…pe… paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no abhikkamo”ti?

Then in the evening, the Blessed One, having arisen from seclusion, approached the Venerable Assaji. The Venerable Assaji saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he stirred on his couch. Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Assaji: ‘Enough, Assaji, do not stir on your couch. These seats are prepared; I will sit there.’ The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Assaji: ‘Are you enduring, Assaji? Are you managing? … Is their decline apparent, and not their increase?’

“Na [V 2.0114] me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ…pe… abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo”ti. “Kacci te, assaji, na kiñci kukkuccaṃ na koci vippaṭisāro”ti? “Taggha me, bhante, anappakaṃ kukkuccaṃ anappako vippaṭisāro”ti. “Kacci pana taṃ, assaji, attā sīlato na upavadatī”ti? “Na kho maṃ, bhante, attā sīlato upavadatī”ti. “No ce kira taṃ, assaji, attā sīlato upavadati, atha kiñca te kukkuccaṃ ko ca vippaṭisāro”ti? “Pubbe khvāhaṃ, bhante, gelaññe passambhetvā passambhetvā kāyasaṅkhāre viharāmi, sohaṃ samādhiṃ nappaṭilabhāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, taṃ samādhiṃ appaṭilabhato evaṃ hoti – ‘no cassāhaṃ parihāyāmī’”ti. “Ye te, assaji, samaṇabrāhmaṇā samādhisārakā samādhisāmaññā tesaṃ taṃ samādhiṃ appaṭilabhataṃ evaṃ hoti – ‘no cassu mayaṃ parihāyāmā’”ti.

‘Venerable Sir, I am not enduring… their increase is apparent, not their decline.’ ‘Assaji, do you have no anxiety, no remorse?’ ‘Indeed, Venerable Sir, I have no small amount of anxiety and no small amount of remorse.’ ‘But Assaji, does your own self not reproach you regarding virtue?’ ‘No, Venerable Sir, my own self does not reproach me regarding virtue.’ ‘If your own self does not reproach you regarding virtue, Assaji, then what is your anxiety and what is your remorse?’ ‘Formerly, Venerable Sir, I used to dwell repeatedly tranquilizing the bodily formations during sickness, but now I do not attain concentration. For me, Venerable Sir, not attaining that concentration, it occurs to me thus: “Might I not be falling away?”’ ‘Those ascetics and brahmins, Assaji, who have concentration as their essence, who have concentration as their asceticism, for them, upon not attaining that concentration, it occurs thus: “Might we not be falling away?”’

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assaji, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe… viññāṇaṃ [P 3.0126] …pe… tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti. So sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati vediyati (sī. pī.), sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anajjhositā’ti [M 2.0103] pajānāti. ‘Anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti. Dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anajjhositā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti…pe… ‘anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti. So sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati[T 3.0154], visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati; dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati; adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati. So kāyapariyantikaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānāti.

‘What do you think, Assaji, is form permanent or impermanent?’ ‘Impermanent, Venerable Sir.’ … consciousness … Therefore … Seeing thus … he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘It is not clung to.’ He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘It is not clung to.’ He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ … He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detachedly; if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detachedly; if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detachedly. When feeling a feeling with the body as its limit, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling with the body as its limit.’ When feeling a feeling with life as its limit, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling with life as its limit.’ He understands: ‘After the breakup of the body, with the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’

“Seyyathāpi[V 2.0115], assaji, telañca paṭicca, vaṭṭiñca paṭicca, telappadīpo jhāyeyya; tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya. Evameva kho, assaji, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Just as, Assaji, an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick; with the exhaustion of that oil and wick, and being without fuel, it would be extinguished. In the same way, Assaji, a monk, when feeling a feeling with the body as its limit, understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling with the body as its limit.’ When feeling a feeling with life as its limit, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling with life as its limit.’ He understands: ‘After the breakup of the body, with the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’” Sixth.

7. Khemakasuttaṃ

7. The Khemaka Sutta

89. Ekaṃ samayaṃ sambahulā therā bhikkhū kosambiyaṃ viharanti ghositārāme. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā khemako badarikārāme viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha [P 3.0127] kho therā bhikkhū sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitā āyasmantaṃ dāsakaṃ āmantesuṃ – “ehi tvaṃ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā [T 3.0155] khemakaṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadehi – ‘therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – kacci te, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti no abhikkamanti, paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no abhikkamo’”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ khemakaṃ etadavoca – “therā taṃ, āvuso [M 2.0104] khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – ‘kacci te, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ…pe… no abhikkamo’”ti? “Na me, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ na yāpanīyaṃ…pe… abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo”ti.

89. At one time many elder monks were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Now at that time Venerable Khemaka was dwelling in the Badarikā Park, afflicted, suffering, gravely ill. Then in the late afternoon, the elder monks arose from their seclusion and addressed Venerable Dāsaka: “Come, friend Dāsaka, go to the monk Khemaka and say to him: ‘The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: “Is it tolerable for you, friend? Are you getting by? Are your painful feelings subsiding and not increasing? Is their subsidence evident, and not their increase?”’” “Yes, friends,” replied Venerable Dāsaka, assenting to the elder monks. He went to Venerable Khemaka; having approached, he said to Venerable Khemaka: “The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: ‘Is it tolerable for you, friend…pe… and not their increase?’” “It is not tolerable for me, friend, I am not getting by…pe… their increase is evident, and not their subsidence.”

Atha kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca – “khemako, āvuso, bhikkhu evamāha – ‘na me, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ…pe… abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo’”ti. “Ehi tvaṃ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadehi – ‘therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho[V 2.0116]. Imesu āyasmā [T 3.0156] khemako pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassatī’”ti?

Then Venerable Dāsaka approached the elder monks; having approached, he said to the elder monks: “Friends, the monk Khemaka says: ‘It is not tolerable for me, friend…pe… their increase is evident, and not their subsidence.’” “Come, friend Dāsaka, go to the monk Khemaka; having approached, say to him: ‘The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: “Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Does Venerable Khemaka regard anything among these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to self?”’”

“Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – “pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Imesu āyasmā khemako pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassatī”ti? “Pañcime[P 3.0128], āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Imesu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassāmī”ti.

“Yes, friends,” replied Venerable Dāsaka, assenting to the elder monks. He then approached Venerable Khemaka; having approached…pe… he said to him: “The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: ‘Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Does Venerable Khemaka regard anything among these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to self?’” “Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Indeed, friend, among these five aggregates subject to clinging, I do not regard anything as self or as belonging to self.”

Atha kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca – “khemako, āvuso, bhikkhu evamāha – ‘pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Imesu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassāmī’”ti. “Ehi tvaṃ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadehi – ‘therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. No ce kirāyasmā khemako imesu [M 2.0105] pañcasu [T 3.0157] upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassati. Tenahāyasmā khemako arahaṃ khīṇāsavo’”ti.

Then Venerable Dāsaka approached the elder monks; having approached, he said to the elder monks: “Friends, the monk Khemaka says: ‘Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Indeed, friend, among these five aggregates subject to clinging, I do not regard anything as self or as belonging to self.’” “Come, friend Dāsaka, go to the monk Khemaka; having approached, say to him: ‘The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: “Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. If indeed Venerable Khemaka does not regard anything among these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to self, then Venerable Khemaka is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.”’”

“Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako…pe… therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – “pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho; no ce kirāyasmā khemako imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassati, tenahāyasmā khemako arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti. “Pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Imesu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassāmi[V 2.0117], na camhi arahaṃ khīṇāsavo; api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmī”ti.

“Yes, friends,” replied Venerable Dāsaka, assenting to the elder monks. He then went to Venerable Khemaka…pe… and said to him: “The elders say to you, friend Khemaka: ‘Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. If indeed Venerable Khemaka does not regard anything among these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to self, then Venerable Khemaka is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.’” “Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging…pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Indeed, friend, among these five aggregates subject to clinging, I do not regard anything as self or as belonging to self, and I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed. And yet, friend, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, I have acquired the conceit ‘I am,’ but I do not regard ‘This am I.’”

Atha [P 3.0129] kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū…pe… there bhikkhū etadavoca – “khemako, āvuso, bhikkhu evamāha – pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Imesu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṃ vā attaniyaṃ vā samanupassāmi, na camhi arahaṃ khīṇāsavo; api ca me[T 3.0158], āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmī”ti.

Then the Venerable Dāsaka went to the elder monks… and said this to the elder monks: “Friends, the monk Khemaka says this: ‘Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Indeed, friend, among these five aggregates subject to clinging, I do not contemplate anything as self or as belonging to self, and I am not an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. And yet, friend, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, I have acquired ‘I am,’ but I do not contemplate ‘This am I.’”

“Ehi tvaṃ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadehi – ‘therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – yametaṃ, āvuso khemaka, asmīti vadesi, kimetaṃ asmīti vadesi? Rūpaṃ asmīti vadesi, aññatra rūpā asmīti vadesi, vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ asmīti vadesi, aññatra viññāṇā asmīti vadesi. Yametaṃ, āvuso khemaka, asmīti vadesi. Kimetaṃ asmīti vadesī’”ti?

“Come, friend Dāsaka, go to where the monk Khemaka is. Having approached him, say this to the monk Khemaka: ‘The elders, friend Khemaka, say this to you: “When you say, ‘I am,’ friend Khemaka, what is this ‘I am’ that you speak of? Do you say, ‘I am form,’ or do you say, ‘I am’ apart from form? Do you say, ‘I am feeling’… ‘I am perception’… ‘I am formations’… ‘I am consciousness,’ or do you say, ‘I am’ apart from consciousness? When you say, ‘I am,’ friend Khemaka, what is this ‘I am’ that you speak of?”’”

“Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ khemakaṃ etadavoca – therā taṃ, āvuso khemaka, evamāhaṃsu – “yametaṃ, āvuso [M 2.0106] khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Rūpaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Yametaṃ, āvuso khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi”ti? “Alaṃ, āvuso dāsaka, kiṃ imāya sandhāvanikāya! Āharāvuso, daṇḍaṃ; ahameva yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamissāmī”ti.

“Very well, friends,” replied Venerable Dāsaka, assenting to the elder monks, and then he approached Venerable Khemaka. Having approached, he said to Venerable Khemaka: “The elders, friend Khemaka, say this to you: ‘When you say, “I am,” friend Khemaka, what is this “I am” that you speak of? Do you say, “I am form,” or do you say, “I am” apart from form? Do you say, “I am feeling”… “I am perception”… “I am formations”… “I am consciousness,” or do you say, “I am” apart from consciousness? When you say, “I am,” friend Khemaka, what is this “I am” that you speak of?’” “Enough, friend Dāsaka, what need is there for this going back and forth? Bring a staff, friend; I myself will go to where the elder monks are.”

Atha kho āyasmā khemako daṇḍamolubbha yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā therehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ [T 3.0159] kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ [V 2.0118][P 3.0130] nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ khemakaṃ therā bhikkhū etadavocuṃ – “yametaṃ, āvuso khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Rūpaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi, aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesi, aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadesi? Yametaṃ, āvuso khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadesī”ti? “Na khvāhaṃ, āvuso, rūpaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi; napi aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi. Na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi; napi aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi. Api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṃ ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmi”.

Then the Venerable Khemaka, leaning on a staff, approached the elder monks. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the elder monks. After concluding a pleasant and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. To the Venerable Khemaka, who was seated to one side, the elder monks said this: “Friend Khemaka, this that you say, ‘I am,’ what is it that you say ‘I am’? Do you say, ‘I am form,’ or do you say, ‘I am’ apart from form? Do you say, ‘I am feeling’… ‘I am perception’… ‘I am formations’… ‘I am consciousness,’ or do you say, ‘I am’ apart from consciousness? Friend Khemaka, this that you say, ‘I am,’ what is it that you say ‘I am’?” “Indeed, friends, I do not say, ‘I am form’; nor do I say, ‘I am’ apart from form. I do not say, ‘I am feeling’… ‘I am perception’… ‘I am formations’… ‘I am consciousness’; nor do I say, ‘I am’ apart from consciousness. Yet, friends, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, I have acquired ‘I am,’ but I do not contemplate ‘This I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso, uppalassa vā padumassa vā puṇḍarīkassa vā gandho. Yo nu kho evaṃ vadeyya – ‘pattassa gandho’ti vā ‘vaṇṇassa vaṇḍassa (katthaci) gandho’ti vā ‘kiñjakkhassa gandho’ti vā sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Yathā kathaṃ, panāvuso, sammā byākaramāno byākareyyā”ti? “‘Pupphassa gandho’ti kho, āvuso, sammā byākaramāno byākareyyā”ti. “Evameva khvāhaṃ, āvuso, na rūpaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi, napi aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi. Na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na [T 3.0160] viññāṇaṃ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi, napi aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi. Api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṃ ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmi”.

“Just as, friends, with the scent of a blue lotus, or a red lotus, or a white lotus. If someone were to say—‘It is the scent of the petal,’ or ‘It is the scent of the color,’ or ‘It is the scent of the filament’—would that person, in saying so, be speaking rightly?” “That is not so, friend.” “Then how, friends, would one, explaining, explain rightly?” “‘It is the scent of the flower’—thus, friend, would one, explaining, explain rightly.” “In the very same way, friends, I do not say, ‘I am form’; nor do I say, ‘I am’ apart from form. I do not say, ‘I am feeling’… ‘I am perception’… ‘I am formations’… ‘I am consciousness’; nor do I say, ‘I am’ apart from consciousness. Yet, friends, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, I have acquired ‘I am,’ but I do not contemplate ‘This I am.’”

“Kiñcāpi, āvuso, ariyasāvakassa pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni bhavanti, atha khvassa hoti – ‘yo ca pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato [M 2.0107] asmīti māno, asmīti chando, asmīti anusayo asamūhato. So aparena samayena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati – iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa [P 3.0131] atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Tassimesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato yopissa hoti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṃ gacchati.

“Although, friends, for a noble disciple the five lower fetters are abandoned, still, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, there remains a subtle, un-uprooted conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am.’ At a later time, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever subtle, un-uprooted conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am’ there is in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, that too is brought to utter destruction.”

“Seyyathāpi[V 2.0119], āvuso, vatthaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ malaggahitaṃ. Tamenaṃ sāmikā rajakassa anupadajjuṃ. Tamenaṃ rajako ūse vā khāre vā gomaye vā sammadditvā acche udake vikkhāleti. Kiñcāpi taṃ hoti vatthaṃ parisuddhaṃ pariyodātaṃ, atha khvassa hoti yeva anusahagato ūsagandho vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato. Tamenaṃ rajako sāmikānaṃ deti. Tamenaṃ sāmikā gandhaparibhāvite karaṇḍake nikkhipanti. Yopissa hoti anusahagato ūsagandho [T 3.0161] vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṃ gacchati. Evameva kho, āvuso, kiñcāpi ariyasāvakassa pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni bhavanti, atha khvassa hoti yeva pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato. So aparena samayena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati. ‘Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Tassa imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato yopissa hoti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṃ gacchatī”ti.

Just as, friends, a cloth is soiled and stained, and its owners give it to a washerman. The washerman thoroughly scrubs it with ash-lye, lye, or cow dung, and rinses it in clear water. Though the cloth becomes clean and bright, there still remains in it a subtle, unremoved odor of ash-lye, lye, or cow dung. The washerman gives it back to the owners. The owners place it in a scented casket, and whatever subtle, unremoved odor of ash-lye, lye, or cow dung remains, that too is completely eradicated. In the very same way, friends, although a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, there yet remains in him, in regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, a subtle, unremoved conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am.’ At a later time, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are volitional formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in these five aggregates subject to clinging, that subtle, unremoved conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am’ regarding the five aggregates is also completely eradicated.

Evaṃ vutte, therā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ khemakaṃ etadavocuṃ – “na kho na kho pana (ka.) mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ khemakaṃ [P 3.0132] vihesāpekhā pucchimha, api cāyasmā khemako pahosi tassa bhagavato sāsanaṃ vitthārena ācikkhituṃ desetuṃ paññāpetuṃ [M 2.0108] paṭṭhapetuṃ vivarituṃ vibhajituṃ uttānīkātuṃ. Tayidaṃ āyasmatā khemakena tassa bhagavato sāsanaṃ vitthārena ācikkhitaṃ desitaṃ paññāpitaṃ paṭṭhapitaṃ vivaritaṃ vibhajitaṃ uttānīkata”nti.

When this was said, the elder monks said to the Venerable Khemaka: “We did not ask the Venerable Khemaka wishing to trouble him, but the Venerable Khemaka is able to explain, teach, declare, establish, disclose, analyze, and make plain in detail the Blessed One’s teaching. And so the Blessed One’s teaching has been explained, taught, declared, established, disclosed, analyzed, and made plain in detail by the Venerable Khemaka.”

Idamavoca āyasmā khemako. Attamanā therā bhikkhū āyasmato khemakassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanduṃ. Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ [T 3.0162] bhaññamāne saṭṭhimattānaṃ therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu, āyasmato khemakassa cāti. Sattamaṃ.

The Venerable Khemaka said this. The elder monks, delighted, rejoiced in what the Venerable Khemaka had said. And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of some sixty elder monks, and also of the Venerable Khemaka, were liberated from the taints without clinging. The Seventh.

8. Channasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse with Channa

90. Ekaṃ [V 2.0120] samayaṃ sambahulā therā bhikkhū bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā channo sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito avāpuraṇaṃ apāpuraṇaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) ādāya vihārena vihāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca – “ovadantu maṃ āyasmanto therā, anusāsantu maṃ āyasmanto therā, karontu me āyasmanto therā dhammiṃ kathaṃ, yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyya”nti.

90. On one occasion, a number of elder monks were dwelling in Bārāṇasī, at Isipatana in the Deer Park. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Channa, having arisen from seclusion, took a key and went from dwelling to dwelling, saying to the elder monks: “May the venerable elders advise me, may the venerable elders instruct me, may the venerable elders give me a talk on the Dhamma, so that I may see the Dhamma.”

Evaṃ vutte, therā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ channaṃ etadavocuṃ – “rūpaṃ kho, āvuso channa, aniccaṃ; vedanā aniccā; saññā aniccā; saṅkhārā aniccā; viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Rūpaṃ anattā; vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā; sabbe dhammā anattā”ti.

When this was said, the elder monks said to the Venerable Channa: “Friend Channa, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is not-self. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”

Atha kho āyasmato channassa etadahosi – “mayhampi kho etaṃ evaṃ mayhampi kho evaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) hoti – ‘rūpaṃ aniccaṃ, vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; rūpaṃ anattā, vedanā [P 3.0133]… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti. Atha ca pana me sabbasaṅkhārasamathe sabbūpadhipaṭinissagge taṇhākkhaye virāge nirodhe nibbāne cittaṃ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati nādhimuccati. Paritassanā upādānaṃ uppajjati; paccudāvattati mānasaṃ – ‘atha ko carahi me attā’ti[T 3.0163]? Na kho panevaṃ dhammaṃ passato hoti. Ko nu kho me tathā dhammaṃ deseyya yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyya”nti.

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Channa: “For me, too, it is the case that: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is not-self. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’ And yet my mind does not leap toward, gain confidence in, become steady upon, or resolve upon the stilling of all volitional formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Agitation and clinging arise; my mind recoils, thinking, ‘Then who, indeed, is my self?’ But it is not so for one who sees the Dhamma. Who, then, might teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma?”

Atha kho āyasmato channassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ kho āyasmā ānando kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito [M 2.0109] ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti ca me āyasmā ānando tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyyaṃ; atthi ca me āyasmante ānande tāvatikā vissaṭṭhi vissatthi (?). Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkameyya”nti. Atha kho āyasmā channo senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena kosambī ghositārāmo yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ sammodi…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā channo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca –

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Channa: “This Venerable Ānanda is staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. He is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma, and I have sufficient familiarity with the Venerable Ānanda. What if I were to go to where the Venerable Ānanda is?” Then the Venerable Channa set his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and went to Kosambī, to Ghosita’s Park, to where the Venerable Ānanda was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda… Seated to one side, the Venerable Channa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Ekamidāhaṃ[V 2.0121], āvuso ānanda, samayaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ viharāmi isipatane migadāye. Atha khvāhaṃ, āvuso, sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito avāpuraṇaṃ ādāya vihārena vihāraṃ upasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘ovadantu maṃ āyasmanto therā, anusāsantu maṃ āyasmanto therā, karontu me āyasmanto therā dhammiṃ kathaṃ yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyya’nti. Evaṃ vutte maṃ, āvuso, therā bhikkhū etadavocuṃ – ‘rūpaṃ kho, āvuso channa, aniccaṃ; vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; rūpaṃ anattā…pe… viññāṇaṃ [T 3.0164] anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’”ti.

Once, friend Ānanda, I was staying at Isipatana in the Deer Park in Varanasi. Then, friend, in the evening, I emerged from seclusion, took a key, and went from monastery to monastery, approaching the elder monks and saying: ‘May the venerable elders advise me, may the venerable elders instruct me, may the venerable elders give me a Dhamma talk so that I may see the Dhamma.’ When this was said, friend, the elder monks said to me: ‘Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self… consciousness is not-self. All conditioned things are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’”

“Tassa mayhaṃ, āvuso, etadahosi – ‘mayhampi kho etaṃ [P 3.0134] evaṃ hoti – rūpaṃ aniccaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, rūpaṃ anattā, vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti. Atha ca pana me sabbasaṅkhārasamathe sabbūpadhipaṭinissagge taṇhākkhaye virāge nirodhe nibbāne cittaṃ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati nādhimuccati. Paritassanā upādānaṃ uppajjati; paccudāvattati mānasaṃ – ‘atha ko carahi me attā’ti? Na kho panevaṃ dhammaṃ passato hoti. Ko nu kho me tathā dhammaṃ deseyya yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyyanti!

“Then, friend, it occurred to me: ‘This is also true for me—form is impermanent… consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is not-self. All conditioned things are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’ And yet, my mind does not leap forward, become serene, become firm, or get resolved upon the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Agitation and clinging arise; the mind recoils, thinking: ‘Then what, indeed, is my self?’ But this does not happen to one who sees the Dhamma. Who, then, could teach me the Dhamma so that I might see the Dhamma?”

“Tassa mayhaṃ, āvuso, etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā ānando kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositarāme satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti ca me āyasmā ānando tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyyaṃ. Atthi ca me āyasmante ānande [M 2.0110] tāvatikā vissaṭṭhi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkameyya’nti. Ovadatu maṃ, āyasmā ānando; anusāsatu maṃ, āyasmā ānando; karotu me, āyasmā ānando dhammiṃ kathaṃ yathāhaṃ dhammaṃ passeyya”nti.

“Then, friend, this occurred to me: ‘This Venerable Ānanda is staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park, praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow practitioners of the holy life. Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma. And I have such familiarity with Venerable Ānanda. Why don’t I go to him?’ Advise me, Venerable Ānanda; instruct me, Venerable Ānanda; give me a talk on the Dhamma so that I may see the Dhamma.”

“Ettakenapi mayaṃ āyasmato channassa attamanā api nāma taṃ attamanā abhiraddhā, taṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) āyasmā channo āvi akāsi khīlaṃ chindi pabhindi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Odahāvuso, channa[T 3.0165], sotaṃ; bhabbosi bhabbo tvaṃ (ka.) dhammaṃ viññātu”nti. Atha kho āyasmato channassa tāvatakeneva tāvadeva (sī.) uḷāraṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji – “bhabbo kirasmi dhammaṃ viññātu”nti.

“Even with just this, we are heartened by Venerable Channa. He has indeed made it manifest and cut the stake. Give ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.” Then, for Venerable Channa, just with that much, a great joy and gladness arose: “It seems I am capable of understanding the Dhamma!”

“Sammukhā [V 2.0122] metaṃ, āvuso channa, bhagavato sutaṃ, sammukhā ca paṭiggahitaṃ kaccānagottaṃ bhikkhuṃ ovadantassa – dvayanissito khvāyaṃ, kaccāna, loko yebhuyyena [P 3.0135] atthitañceva natthitañca. Lokasamudayaṃ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato yā loke natthitā, sā na hoti. Lokanirodhaṃ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato yā loke atthitā, sā na hoti. Upayupādānābhinivesavinibandho khvāyaṃ, kaccāna, loko yebhuyyena taṃ cāyaṃ upayupādānaṃ cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayaṃ na upeti na upādiyati nādhiṭṭhāti ‘attā me’ti. Dukkhameva uppajjamānaṃ uppajjati, dukkhaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ nirujjhatīti na kaṅkhati na vicikicchati. Aparappaccayā ñāṇamevassa ettha hoti. Ettāvatā kho, kaccāna, sammādiṭṭhi hoti. Sabbamatthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto. Sabbaṃ natthīti ayaṃ dutiyo anto. Ete te, kaccāna, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti – avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti.

“Friend Channa, this was heard by me in the presence of the Blessed One, received in his presence while he was instructing the monk of the Kaccāna clan: ‘This world, Kaccāna, for the most part relies on a duality—on existence and non-existence. But for one who sees the origin of the world with right wisdom as it really is, the notion of non-existence in the world does not arise. For one who sees the cessation of the world with right wisdom as it really is, the notion of existence in the world does not arise. This world, Kaccāna, for the most part is shackled by engagement, clinging, and adherence. But this one does not engage in, cling to, or resolve upon that engagement and clinging—that mental standpoint, adherence, and underlying tendency—with the thought: ‘This is my self.’ One understands: ‘Only suffering, when arising, arises; suffering, when ceasing, ceases.’ Regarding this, one does not doubt or waver. Herein, one's knowledge is independent of others. To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view. “Everything exists”—this is one extreme. “Everything does not exist”—this is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: With ignorance as a condition, formations arise; with formations as a condition, consciousness… Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, formations cease… Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

“Evametaṃ, āvuso ānanda, hoti yesaṃ āyasmantānaṃ tādisā sabrahmacārayo [T 3.0166] anukampakā atthakāmā ovādakā anusāsakā. Idañca pana me āyasmato ānandassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā dhammo abhisamito”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Indeed, friend Ānanda, this is how it is for those venerable ones who have such spiritual companions—compassionate, desiring their welfare, advisors, instructors. And now, having heard this Dhamma teaching from Venerable Ānanda, the Dhamma has been thoroughly understood by me.”

9. Rāhulasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse to Rāhula

91. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0111]. Atha kho āyasmā rāhulo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavantaṃ [P 3.0136] etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti?

91. At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One... and, having approached, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Rāhula said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that in this conscious body and in regard to all external signs, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not arise?”

“Yaṃ kiñci, rāhula, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Yā kāci vedanā [V 2.0123]… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā…pe… sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Evaṃ kho, rāhula, jānato evaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one sees all form as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external… and so on… one sees all consciousness as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ For one who knows thus and sees thus, Rāhula, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not arise in this conscious body and in regard to all external signs.” The ninth.

10. Dutiyarāhulasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse to Rāhula

92. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṃ [T 3.0167] mānasaṃ hoti vidhāsamatikkantaṃ santaṃ suvimutta”nti? “Yaṃ kiñci, rāhula, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti. Yā kāci vedanā… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ [P 3.0137] sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti. Evaṃ kho, rāhula[M 2.0112], jānato evaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṃ mānasaṃ hoti vidhā samatikkantaṃ santaṃ suvimutta”nti. Dasamaṃ.

92. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, the Venerable Rāhula said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that in this conscious body and in regard to all external signs, the mind is devoid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit, has transcended the varieties of conceit, is peaceful, and well liberated?” “Whatever form, Rāhula, whether past, future, or present, internal or external… far or near, having seen all form as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ one is liberated without clinging. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever volitional formations… whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, having seen all consciousness as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ one is liberated without clinging. Thus, Rāhula, for one who knows thus, for one who sees thus, in this conscious body and in regard to all external signs, the mind is devoid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit, has transcended the varieties of conceit, is peaceful, and well liberated.” The tenth.

Theravaggo navamo.

The Chapter of Elders, the Ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of it:

Ānando [V 2.0124] tisso yamako, anurādho ca vakkali;

Assaji khemako channo, rāhulā apare duve.

Ānanda, Tissa, Yamaka, Anurādha, and Vakkali; Assaji, Khemaka, Channa, and two further discourses on Rāhula.

10. Pupphavaggo

10. The Chapter on Flowers

1. Nadīsuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the River

93. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0168]. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, nadī pabbateyyā ohārinī dūraṅgamā sīghasotā. Tassā ubhosu tīresu ubhato tīre (sī.), ubhato tīresu (syā. kaṃ.) kāsā cepi jātā assu, te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ; kusā cepi jātā assu, te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ; pabbajā babbajā (sī. pī.) cepi jātā assu, te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ; bīraṇā cepi jātā assu, te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ; rukkhā cepi jātā assu, te naṃ ajjholambeyyuṃ. Tassā puriso sotena vuyhamāno kāse cepi gaṇheyya, te palujjeyyuṃ. So tatonidānaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyya. Kuse cepi gaṇheyya, pabbaje cepi gaṇheyya, bīraṇe cepi gaṇheyya, rukkhe cepi gaṇheyya, te palujjeyyuṃ[P 3.0138]. So tatonidānaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Tassa taṃ rūpaṃ palujjati. So tatonidānaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajjati. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ[M 2.0113]; attani vā viññāṇaṃ[T 3.0169], viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Tassa taṃ viññāṇaṃ palujjati. So tatonidānaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ bhante”. “Tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… [V 2.0125] nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

93. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose there was a river originating from the mountains, flowing downwards, far-reaching, with a swift current. If on both its banks kāsa grass were to grow, they would overhang it; if kusa grass were to grow, they would overhang it; if pabbaja grass were to grow, they would overhang it; if bīraṇa grass were to grow, they would overhang it; if trees were to grow, they would overhang it. Then a man being carried along by the current, were he to grab hold of the kāsa grass, it would break apart. Because of that, he would meet with ruin and disaster. Were he to grab hold of the kusa grass, the pabbaja grass, the bīraṇa grass, or the trees, they would break apart. Because of that, he would meet with ruin and disaster. “So too, bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has not seen the true persons, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. That form of his perishes. Because of that, he meets with ruin and disaster. He regards feeling… perception… formations… consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That consciousness of his perishes. Because of that, he meets with ruin and disaster. “What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Therefore… Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” First.

2. Pupphasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Flowers

94. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, lokena vivadāmi, lokova mayā vivadati. Na, bhikkhave, dhammavādī kenaci lokasmiṃ vivadati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, natthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ, ahampi taṃ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, atthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ, ahampi taṃ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi”.
