94. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. Bhikkhus, a proponent of the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. What is agreed upon by the wise in the world as non-existent, I too declare to be non-existent. What is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existent, I too declare to be existent.”

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, natthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ, yamahaṃ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi? Rūpaṃ[P 3.0139], bhikkhave, niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ natthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ natthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi. Idaṃ kho, bhikkhave, natthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi”.

“And what, bhikkhus, is agreed upon by the wise in the world as non-existent, which I too declare to be non-existent? Bhikkhus, that form is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as non-existent; I too declare that it is non-existent. That feeling… perception… formations… consciousness are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as non-existent; I too declare that they are non-existent. This, bhikkhus, is what is agreed upon by the wise in the world as non-existent, and I too declare that it is non-existent.”

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, atthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ, yamahaṃ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ atthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi. Vedanā aniccā…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ [T 3.0170] dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ atthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi. Idaṃ kho, bhikkhave, atthisammataṃ loke paṇḍitānaṃ; ahampi taṃ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi”.

“And what, monks, is that which is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existing, which I too declare ‘exists’? Monks, that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existing; I too declare that it ‘exists’. That feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existing; I too declare that it ‘exists’. This, monks, is what is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existing, and I too declare that it ‘exists’.”

“Atthi, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo, taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti; abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā taṃ ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.

“Monks, there is a worldly phenomenon in the world. The Tathāgata fully awakens to and comprehends it. Having fully awakened to and comprehended it, he announces, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes it plain.”

“Kiñca[V 2.0126], bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo, taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti, abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti. Abhisambujjhitvā [M 2.0114] abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.

“And what, monks, is the worldly phenomenon in the world that the Tathāgata fully awakens to and comprehends? Having fully awakened to and comprehended it, he announces, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes it plain. Form, monks, is the worldly phenomenon in the world. The Tathāgata fully awakens to and comprehends it. Having fully awakened to and comprehended it, he announces, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes it plain.”

“Yo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena evaṃ ācikkhiyamāne desiyamāne paññapiyamāne paṭṭhapiyamāne vivariyamāne [P 3.0140] vibhajiyamāne uttānīkariyamāne na jānāti na passati tamahaṃ, bhikkhave, bālaṃ puthujjanaṃ andhaṃ acakkhukaṃ ajānantaṃ apassantaṃ kinti karomi! Vedanā, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo…pe… saññā, bhikkhave… saṅkhārā, bhikkhave… viññāṇaṃ, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti. Abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.

“Monks, when it is being thus announced, taught, proclaimed, established, disclosed, analyzed, and made plain by the Tathāgata, if a certain person does not know and does not see, what, monks, shall I do with that foolish ordinary person who is blind, without eyes, unknowing, and unseeing? Feeling, monks, is a worldly phenomenon in the world… and so on… Perception, monks… and so on… Volitional formations, monks… and so on… Consciousness, monks, is a worldly phenomenon in the world. The Tathāgata fully awakens to and comprehends it. Having fully awakened to and comprehended it, he announces, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes it plain.”

“Yo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena evaṃ ācikkhiyamāne desiyamāne paññapiyamāne paṭṭhapiyamāne vivariyamāne vibhajiyamāne uttānīkariyamāne na [T 3.0171] jānāti na passati tamahaṃ, bhikkhave, bālaṃ puthujjanaṃ andhaṃ acakkhukaṃ ajānantaṃ apassantaṃ kinti karomi!

“Monks, when it is being thus announced, taught, proclaimed, established, disclosed, analyzed, and made plain by the Tathāgata, if a certain person does not know and does not see, what, monks, shall I do with that foolish ordinary person who is blind, without eyes, unknowing, and unseeing?”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uppalaṃ vā padumaṃ vā puṇḍarīkaṃ vā udake jātaṃ udake saṃvaḍḍhaṃ udakā accuggamma ṭhāti tiṭṭhantaṃ (ka.) anupalittaṃ udakena; evameva kho, bhikkhave, tathāgato loke jāto loke saṃvaḍḍho lokaṃ abhibhuyya viharati anupalitto lokenā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“Just as, monks, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water and grown in the water, rises up out of the water and stands unsoiled by the water; in the very same way, monks, the Tathāgata, born in the world and grown in the world, having overcome the world, dwells unsoiled by the world.” The Second.

3. Pheṇapiṇḍūpamasuttaṃ

3. The Simile of the Lump of Foam

95. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā ayujjhāyaṃ ayojjhāyaṃ (sī. pī.) viharati gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi –

95. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjha on the bank of the river Ganges. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ gaṅgā nadī mahantaṃ pheṇapiṇḍaṃ āvaheyya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato [V 2.0127] rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, pheṇapiṇḍe sāro? Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā taṃ bhikkhu [P 3.0141] passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati[M 2.0115], tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, rūpe sāro?

“Suppose, monks, this river Ganges were carrying along a great mass of foam. A man endowed with sight would see it, scrutinize it, and investigate it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it would appear void, hollow, and essenceless. For what essence could there be, monks, in a mass of foam? In the same way, monks, whatever form—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a monk sees, scrutinizes, and investigates it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it appears void, hollow, and essenceless. For what essence could there be, monks, in form?”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, saradasamaye thullaphusitake deve vassante udake udakapubbuḷaṃ udakabubbuḷaṃ (sī. pī.) uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso [T 3.0172] passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, udakapubbuḷe sāro? Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yā kāci vedanā atītānāgatapaccuppannā…pe… yā dūre santike vā taṃ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, vedanāya sāro?

“Just as, monks, in the autumn season, when heavy raindrops are falling, a water bubble arises and ceases on the water. A man endowed with sight would see it, scrutinize it, and investigate it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it would appear void, hollow, and essenceless. For what essence could there be, monks, in a water bubble? In the same way, monks, whatever feeling—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a monk sees, scrutinizes, and investigates it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it appears void, hollow, and essenceless. For what essence could there be, monks, in feeling?”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse ṭhite majjhanhike kāle marīcikā phandati. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya…pe… kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, marīcikāya sāro? Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yā kāci saññā…pe….

“Suppose, monks, in the last month of the hot season, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A man endowed with sight would see it, scrutinize it, and investigate it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it would appear void, hollow, and essenceless. For what essence could there be, monks, in a mirage? In the same way, monks, whatever perception… and so on…”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ kudhāriṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha passeyya mahantaṃ kadalikkhandhaṃ ujuṃ navaṃ akukkukajātaṃ akukkajātaṃ (ka. sī. pī.), akusajātaṃ (ka. sī.), akukkujakajātaṃ (ka.). Tamenaṃ mūle chindeyya; mūle chetvā agge chindeyya, agge chetvā pattavaṭṭiṃ vinibbhujeyya. So tassa pattavaṭṭiṃ vinibbhujanto pheggumpi [T 3.0173] nādhigaccheyya, kuto sāraṃ! Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato [P 3.0142] rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva [V 2.0128] khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, kadalikkhandhe sāro? Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye keci saṅkhārā atītānāgatapaccuppannā…pe… ye [M 2.0116] dūre santike vā taṃ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, saṅkhāresu sāro?

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he might see a large plantain trunk—straight, new, and without a solid core. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut it at the top; having cut it at the top, he would peel off the leaf-sheaths. As he was peeling off the leaf-sheaths, he would not find even softwood, let alone heartwood. A man with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and investigate it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it would appear to be just empty, just hollow, just without substance. For what substance, bhikkhus, could there be in a plantain trunk? In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever formations there are, past, future, or present… far or near, a bhikkhu sees them, scrutinizes them, and investigates them wisely. To him, seeing them, scrutinizing them, and investigating them wisely, they appear to be just empty, just hollow, just without substance. For what substance, bhikkhus, could there be in formations?”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, māyākāro vā māyākārantevāsī vā catumahāpathe cātummahāpathe (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) māyaṃ vidaṃseyya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, māyāya sāro? Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, taṃ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṃ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, viññāṇe sāro?

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a magician or a magician’s apprentice might display a magic trick at a crossroads. A man with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and investigate it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it would appear only empty, only hollow, and only without substance. For what substance, bhikkhus, could there be in a magic trick? In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present... whether far or near—a bhikkhu sees it, scrutinizes it, and investigates it wisely. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, and investigating it wisely, it appears only empty, only hollow, and only without substance. For what substance, bhikkhus, could there be in consciousness?”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi… saññāyapi… saṅkhāresupi [T 3.0174]… viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti”.

“Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with perception, becomes disenchanted with formations, and becomes disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises, ‘I am liberated.’ … He understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

The Blessed One spoke this. Having spoken this, the Well-farer, the Teacher, furthermore spoke this:

“Pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ rūpaṃ, vedanā bubbuḷūpamā bubbulūpamā (sī.), pubbuḷopamā (ka.);

Marīcikūpamā saññā, saṅkhārā kadalūpamā;

Māyūpamañca viññāṇaṃ, desitādiccabandhunā.

“Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a water bubble; perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain trunk; and consciousness is like a magic trick—thus it has been taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.

“Yathā yathā nijjhāyati, yoniso upaparikkhati;

Rittakaṃ tucchakaṃ hoti, yo naṃ passati yoniso.

“In whatever way one scrutinizes and wisely investigates it, it becomes empty and hollow to the one who sees it wisely.

“Imañca [V 2.0129][P 3.0143] kāyaṃ ārabbha, bhūripaññena desitaṃ;

Pahānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ, rūpaṃ passatha passetha (sī.) chaḍḍitaṃ.

“Concerning this very body, it has been taught by the one of vast wisdom; with the abandoning of three things, see form as discarded.

“Āyu [M 2.0117] usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Apaviddho apaviṭṭho (syā. kaṃ.) tadā seti, parabhattaṃ acetanaṃ.

“When the life-faculty, heat, and consciousness abandon this body, then it lies discarded, food for others, without volition.

“Etādisāyaṃ santāno, māyāyaṃ bālalāpinī;

Vadhako esa akkhāto, sāro ettha na vijjati.

“This continuity is of such a nature; this is an illusion that deludes fools. This is declared a slayer; no substance is found herein.

“Evaṃ khandhe avekkheyya, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo;

Divā vā yadi vā rattiṃ, sampajāno paṭissato.

“Thus a bhikkhu with aroused energy should contemplate the aggregates, whether by day or by night, being clearly comprehending and mindful.

“Jaheyya sabbasaṃyogaṃ, kareyya saraṇattano;

Careyyādittasīsova, patthayaṃ accutaṃ pada”nti. tatiyaṃ;

“He should abandon all fetters; he should make a refuge for himself. He should fare as one with head ablaze, longing for the unmoving state.”

4. Gomayapiṇḍasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Lump of Cow Dung

96. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0175]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci rūpaṃ yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kāci vedanā yā vedanā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kāci saññā yā saññā…pe… atthi nu kho, bhante, keci saṅkhārā ye saṅkhārā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassanti? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci viññāṇaṃ, yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ [P 3.0144] dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti? “Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kiñci rūpaṃ, yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kāci vedanā… kāci saññā… keci saṅkhārā… kiñci viññāṇaṃ[V 2.0130], yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti.

96. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, is there any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal? Venerable Sir, is there any feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal? Venerable Sir, is there any perception… Venerable Sir, are there any formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal? Venerable Sir, is there any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal?” “There is no form, bhikkhu, that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal. There is no feeling, bhikkhu… no perception… no formations… no consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain just so, like the eternal.”

Atha kho bhagavā parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍaṃ pāṇinā gahetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “ettakopi kho, bhikkhu, attabhāvapaṭilābho natthi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Ettako cepi, bhikkhu, attabhāvapaṭilābho abhavissa nicco dhuvo sassato [M 2.0118] avipariṇāmadhammo, nayidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhu, ettakopi attabhāvapaṭilābho [T 3.0176] natthi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

Then the Blessed One, taking a small lump of cow dung in his hand, said this to that bhikkhu: “Bhikkhu, there is not even this much of an attainment of individuality that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that would remain just so, like the eternal. If even this much of an attainment of individuality, bhikkhu, were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be apparent. But because, bhikkhu, there is not even this much of an attainment of individuality that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is apparent.”

“Bhūtapubbāhaṃ, bhikkhu, rājā ahosiṃ khattiyo muddhāvasitto. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītinagarasahassāni ahesuṃ kusāvatī rājadhānippamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītipāsādasahassāni ahesuṃ dhammapāsādappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītikūṭāgārasahassāni ahesuṃ mahābyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni mahāviyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni (dī. ni. 2.263). Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītipallaṅkasahassāni ahesuṃ dantamayāni sāramayāni sovaṇṇamayāni goṇakatthatāni paṭikatthatāni paṭalikatthatāni kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni [P 3.0145] kādalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni (sī.) sauttaracchadāni ubhatolohitakūpadhānāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītināgasahassāni ahesuṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇaddhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni uposathanāgarājappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītiassasahassāni ahesuṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇaddhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni [T 3.0177] valāhakaassarājappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītirathasahassāni ahesuṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇaddhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni vejayantarathappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu, rañño sato khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa caturāsītimaṇisahassāni ahesuṃ maṇiratanappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu…pe… caturāsītiitthisahassāni ahesuṃ subhaddādevippamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu…pe… caturāsītikhattiyasahassāni ahesuṃ anuyantāni pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu…pe… caturāsītidhenusahassāni ahesuṃ dukūlasandanāni kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni. Tassa [V 2.0131] mayhaṃ, bhikkhu…pe… caturāsītivatthakoṭisahassāni ahesuṃ khomasukhumāni koseyyasukhumāni kambalasukhumāni [M 2.0119] kappāsikasukhumāni. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhu…pe… caturāsītithālipākasahassāni ahesuṃ; sāyaṃ pātaṃ bhattābhihāro abhihariyittha.

Once, monk, I was a king, a consecrated Kshatriya. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī the royal capital as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, with the Mahābyūha gabled chamber as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand couches—made of ivory, of heartwood, and of gold, covered with long-fleeced rugs, with white woolen rugs, with embroidered rugs, spread with choice antelope hides, with canopies above, and with red cushions at both ends. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand elephants—adorned with gold ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden nets, with Uposatha the royal elephant as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand horses—adorned with gold ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden nets, with Valāhaka the royal steed as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand chariots—adorned with gold ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden nets, with the Vejayanta chariot as the foremost. At that time, monk, as a king, a consecrated Kshatriya, I had eighty-four thousand jewels, with the jewel treasure as the foremost. At that time, monk… I had eighty-four thousand women, with Queen Subhaddā as the foremost. At that time, monk… I had eighty-four thousand Kshatriya vassals, with the counselor treasure as the foremost. At that time, monk… I had eighty-four thousand milch cows, with fine linen tethers and bronze milking pails. At that time, monk… I had eighty-four thousand koṭis of garments—of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton. At that time, monk… I had eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice, and a meal was brought morning and evening.

“Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā nagarasahassānaṃ ekaññeva taṃ nagaraṃ hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena ajjhāvasāmi – kusāvatī rājadhānī. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā pāsādasahassānaṃ [P 3.0146] ekoyeva so pāsādo hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena ajjhāvasāmi – dhammo pāsādo. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā kūṭāgārasahassānaṃ ekaññeva taṃ kūṭāgāraṃ hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena ajjhāvasāmi – mahābyūhaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā pallaṅkasahassānaṃ ekoyeva so pallaṅko hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena paribhuñjāmi – dantamayo vā sāramayo vā sovaṇṇamayo [T 3.0178] vā rūpiyamayo vā. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā nāgasahassānaṃ ekoyeva so nāgo hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena abhiruhāmi – uposatho nāgarājā. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā assasahassānaṃ ekoyeva so asso hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena abhiruhāmi – valāhako assarājā. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā rathasahassānaṃ ekoyeva so ratho hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena abhiruhāmi – vejayanto ratho. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā itthisahassānaṃ ekāyeva sā itthī hoti yā maṃ tena samayena paccupaṭṭhāti – khattiyānī vā velāmikā vā. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā vatthakoṭisahassānaṃ ekaññeva taṃ vatthayugaṃ hoti yamahaṃ tena samayena paridahāmi – khomasukhumaṃ vā koseyyasukhumaṃ vā kambalasukhumaṃ vā kappāsikasukhumaṃ vā. Tesaṃ kho pana, bhikkhu, caturāsītiyā thālipākasahassānaṃ ekoyeva so thālipāko hoti yato nāḷikodanaparamaṃ bhuñjāmi tadupiyañca sūpeyyaṃ sūpabyañjanaṃ (syā. kaṃ.). Iti kho, bhikkhu, sabbe te saṅkhārā atītā niruddhā vipariṇatā. Evaṃ aniccā kho, bhikkhu, saṅkhārā. Evaṃ addhuvā kho, bhikkhu, saṅkhārā. Evaṃ anassāsikā kho, bhikkhu, saṅkhārā. Yāvañcidaṃ[P 3.0147], bhikkhu, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṃ, alaṃ virajjituṃ, alaṃ vimuccitu”nti. Catutthaṃ.

Monk, of those eighty-four thousand cities, I resided at that time in only one city—the royal capital Kusāvatī. Of those eighty-four thousand palaces, I resided at that time in only one palace—the Dhamma Palace. Of those eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, I resided at that time in only one gabled chamber—the Mahābyūha gabled chamber. Of those eighty-four thousand couches, I used at that time only one couch—whether made of ivory, heartwood, gold, or silver. Of those eighty-four thousand elephants, I rode at that time only one elephant—the royal elephant Uposatha. Of those eighty-four thousand horses, I rode at that time only one horse—the royal horse Valāhaka. Of those eighty-four thousand chariots, I rode at that time only one chariot—the chariot Vejayanta. Of those eighty-four thousand women, only one woman attended on me at that time—a khattiya woman or a velāmikā woman. Of those eighty-four thousand koṭis of garments, I wore at that time only one pair of garments—whether of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, or fine cotton. Of those eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice, it was from only one pot that I ate, at most a nāḷika measure of rice and suitable curry. Thus, monk, all those formations have passed, ceased, and changed. So impermanent, monk, are formations. So unstable, monk, are formations. So unreliable, monk, are formations. This much, monk, is enough to become disenchanted with all formations, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated.” The fourth.

5. Nakhasikhāsuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Fingernail Tip

97. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0132][M 2.0120]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu [T 3.0179] bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci rūpaṃ yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kāci vedanā yā vedanā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kāci saññā…pe… keci saṅkhārā, ye saṅkhārā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassanti? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci viññāṇaṃ, yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti? “Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kiñci rūpaṃ, yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kāci vedanā… kāci saññā… keci saṅkhārā…pe… kiñci viññāṇaṃ, yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti.

97. At Sāvatthī. Then that bhikkhu, seated to one side, said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, is there any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal? Venerable sir, is there any feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal? Venerable sir, is there any perception… any formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal? Venerable sir, is there any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal?' 'Bhikkhu, there is no form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. Bhikkhu, there is no feeling… no perception… no formations… no consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal.'

Atha kho bhagavā parittaṃ nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsuṃ āropetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “ettakampi kho, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ natthi niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Ettakaṃ cepi, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ abhavissa niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ, nayidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhu, ettakampi rūpaṃ natthi niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya”.

Then the Blessed One, having placed a tiny bit of dust on the tip of his fingernail, addressed that bhikkhu thus: 'Bhikkhu, there is not even this much form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. If, bhikkhu, even this much form were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, bhikkhu, even this much form is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.'

“Ettakāpi [P 3.0148] kho, bhikkhu, vedanā natthi niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ [T 3.0180] tatheva ṭhassati. Ettakā cepi, bhikkhu, vedanā abhavissa niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā, na yidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhu, ettakāpi vedanā natthi niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

Bhikkhu, there is not even this much feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. If, bhikkhu, even this much feeling were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, bhikkhu, there is not even this much feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.

“Ettakāpi kho, bhikkhu, saññā natthi…pe… ettakāpi kho, bhikkhu, saṅkhārā natthi niccā [V 2.0133] dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassanti. Ettakā cepi, bhikkhu, saṅkhārā abhavissaṃsu niccā dhuvā sassatā [M 2.0121] avipariṇāmadhammā, na yidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhu, ettakāpi saṅkhārā natthi niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

Bhikkhu, there is not even this much perception… Bhikkhu, there are not even this many formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. If, bhikkhu, even this many formations were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, bhikkhu, there are not even this many formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.

“Ettakampi kho, bhikkhu, viññāṇaṃ natthi niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Ettakampi kho, bhikkhu, viññāṇaṃ abhavissa niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ, na yidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhu, ettakampi viññāṇaṃ natthi niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

Bhikkhu, there is not even this much consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. If, bhikkhu, even this much consciousness were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, bhikkhu, there is not even this much consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhikkhu, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ [P 3.0149] bhante”…pe… “tasmātiha…pe… evaṃ [T 3.0181] passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

'What do you think, bhikkhu, is form permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, venerable sir.' 'Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, venerable sir.' … 'Therefore… seeing thus… he understands: “There is nothing further for this state of being.”' Fifth.

6. Suddhikasuttaṃ

6. The Suddhika Sutta

98. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “atthi nu kho, bhante, kiñci rūpaṃ, yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati? Atthi nu kho, bhante, kāci vedanā…pe… kāci saññā… keci saṅkhārā… kiñci viññāṇaṃ, yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti? “Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kiñci rūpaṃ yaṃ rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ [V 2.0134] avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassati. Natthi kho, bhikkhu, kāci vedanā… kāci saññā… keci saṅkhārā… kiñci viññāṇaṃ, yaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhammaṃ sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

98. At Sāvatthī. Then that bhikkhu, seated to one side, said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, is there any form whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal? Venerable sir, is there any feeling… any perception… any formations… any consciousness whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal?' 'Bhikkhu, there is no form whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal. Bhikkhu, there is no feeling… no perception… no formations… no consciousness whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will endure just so, like that which is eternal.' Sixth.

7. Gaddulabaddhasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Leash

99. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro. Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ. Hoti so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṃ mahāsamuddo ussussati visussati na [M 2.0122] bhavati; na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ dukkhassa antakiriyaṃ vadāmi. Hoti so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṃ sineru pabbatarājā ḍayhati vinassati na bhavati; na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ [P 3.0150] sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ [T 3.0182] dukkhassa antakiriyaṃ vadāmi. Hoti so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṃ mahāpathavī ḍayhati vinassati na bhavati; na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ dukkhassa antakiriyaṃ vadāmi”.

99. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, veiled by ignorance and fettered by craving. There is a time, bhikkhus, when the great ocean dries up, is completely drained, and is no more; yet I do not say that for beings roaming and wandering on, veiled by ignorance and fettered by craving, there is an end-making of suffering. There is a time, bhikkhus, when Sineru, the king of mountains, burns up, is destroyed, and is no more; yet I do not say that for beings roaming and wandering on, veiled by ignorance and fettered by craving, there is an end-making of suffering. There is a time, bhikkhus, when the great earth burns up, is destroyed, and is no more; yet I do not say that for beings roaming and wandering on, veiled by ignorance and fettered by craving, there is an end-making of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, sā gaddulabaddho gaddūlabandho (syā. kaṃ.) daḷhe khīle vā thambhe vā upanibaddho tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā anuparidhāvati anuparivattati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… vedanaṃ attato samanupassati… saññaṃ attato samanupassati… saṅkhāre attato samanupassati… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. So rūpaññeva anuparidhāvati anuparivattati, vedanaññeva…pe… saññaññeva… saṅkhāreyeva… viññāṇaññeva anuparidhāvati anuparivattati. So rūpaṃ anuparidhāvaṃ anuparivattaṃ, vedanaṃ…pe… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ anuparidhāvaṃ anuparivattaṃ, na parimuccati rūpamhā, na parimuccati vedanāya, na parimuccati saññāya, na parimuccati saṅkhārehi, na parimuccati viññāṇamhā, na parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇena sokehi [V 2.0135] paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a dog tied by a leash to a strong post or pillar runs around and circles that very post or pillar; even so, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones… who is not trained in the Dhamma of true men, regards form as self… regards feeling as self… regards perception as self… regards formations as self… regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. He runs around and circles form itself… feeling itself… perception itself… formations themselves… consciousness itself. Running around and circling form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, he is not freed from form, not freed from feeling, not freed from perception, not freed from formations, not freed from consciousness; he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. He is not freed from suffering, I say.”

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī…pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto, na rūpaṃ attato [T 3.0183] samanupassati…pe… na vedanaṃ… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā viññāṇaṃ, na viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. So rūpaṃ nānuparidhāvati nānuparivattati, vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ nānuparidhāvati nānuparivattati. So rūpaṃ ananuparidhāvaṃ ananuparivattaṃ, vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ ananuparidhāvaṃ ananuparivattaṃ; parimuccati rūpamhā, parimuccati vedanāya, parimuccati saññāya, parimuccati saṅkhārehi, parimuccati viññāṇamhā, parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“But, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones… who is well-trained in the Dhamma of true men—does not regard form as self… nor feeling… nor perception… nor formations… nor consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness. He does not run around or circle form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness. Not running around or circling form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, he is freed from form, freed from feeling, freed from perception, freed from formations, freed from consciousness; he is freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. ‘He is freed from suffering,’ I say.” Seventh.

8. Dutiyagaddulabaddhasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on One Tied by a Leash

100. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0123][P 3.0151]. “Anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro. Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, sā gaddulabaddho daḷhe khīle vā thambhe vā upanibaddho. So gacchati cepi tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā upagacchati; tiṭṭhati cepi tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā upatiṭṭhati; nisīdati cepi tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā upanisīdati; nipajjati cepi tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā upanipajjati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me [T 3.0184] attā’ti samanupassati. So gacchati cepi ime pañcupādānakkhandhe upagacchati; tiṭṭhati cepi ime pañcupādānakkhandhe upatiṭṭhati; nisīdati cepi ime pañcupādānakkhandhe upanisīdati; nipajjati cepi ime pañcupādānakkhandhe upanipajjati. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, abhikkhaṇaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – ‘dīgharattamidaṃ [V 2.0136] cittaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ rāgena dosena mohenā’ti. Cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti; cittavodānā sattā visujjhanti.

100. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, veiled by ignorance and fettered by craving. Just as, bhikkhus, a dog tied by a leash to a strong stake or pillar: if it goes, it approaches that very stake or pillar; if it stands, it stands near that very stake or pillar; if it sits, it sits near that very stake or pillar; if it lies down, it lies down near that very stake or pillar. In the very same way, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person regards form thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards feeling… perception… formations… consciousness thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ If he goes, he approaches these five aggregates subject to clinging; if he stands, he stands near these five aggregates subject to clinging; if he sits, he sits near these five aggregates subject to clinging; if he lies down, he lies down near these five aggregates subject to clinging. Therefore, bhikkhus, one’s own mind should be frequently reflected upon thus: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.’ Through the defilement of the mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.”

“Diṭṭhaṃ vo, bhikkhave, caraṇaṃ nāma citta”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Tampi kho, bhikkhave, caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ citteneva cittitaṃ. Tenapi kho, bhikkhave, caraṇena cittena cittaññeva cittataraṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, abhikkhaṇaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – ‘dīgharattamidaṃ cittaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ rāgena dosena mohenā’ti. Cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti; cittavodānā sattā visujjhanti.

“Bhikkhus, have you seen the variegated painting called a ‘show-piece’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, even that variegated painting called a ‘show-piece’ is designed by the mind. But, bhikkhus, the mind itself is even more variegated than that variegated painting. Therefore, bhikkhus, one’s own mind should be frequently reflected upon thus: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.’ Through the defilement of the mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.”

“Nāhaṃ[P 3.0152], bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ. Yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā, tepi kho, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā citteneva cittitā, tehipi kho, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatehi pāṇehi cittaññeva cittataraṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, abhikkhaṇaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – ‘dīgharattamidaṃ cittaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ rāgena dosena mohenā’ti. Cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti; cittavodānā sattā visujjhanti.

“Monks, I do not see any other single group so variegated as these animals. Indeed, monks, those animals are made variegated by the mind. And, monks, the mind is even more variegated than those animals. Therefore, monks, one's own mind should be frequently reflected upon thus: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.’ Through the defilement of the mind, monks, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.”

“Seyyathāpi[T 3.0185][M 2.0124], bhikkhave, rajako vā cittakārako vā rajanāya vā lākhāya vā haliddiyā vā nīliyā vā mañjiṭṭhāya mañjeṭṭhāya (sī. syā. kaṃ.), mañjeṭṭhiyā (pī.) vā suparimaṭṭhe phalake vā bhittiyā vā dussapaṭṭe vā itthirūpaṃ vā purisarūpaṃ vā abhinimmineyya sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ; evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano rūpaññeva abhinibbattento abhinibbatteti, vedanaññeva…pe… saññaññeva… saṅkhāre yeva… viññāṇaññeva abhinibbattento abhinibbatteti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ…pe… “tasmātiha, bhikkhave, evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, a dyer or a painter, using dye or lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder, would create the figure of a woman or a man, complete in all its major and minor limbs, on a well-polished board, a wall, or a piece of cloth; just so, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, in generating form, generates it; in generating feeling… in generating perception… in generating volitional formations… in generating consciousness, generates it. What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness… Therefore, monks, seeing thus… one understands: ‘…there is no more for this state of being.’”

9. Vāsijaṭasuttaṃ

9. The Adze Handle

101. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0137]. “Jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. Kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato kiṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti? ‘Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa [P 3.0153] atthaṅgamo’ti – evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti”.

101. At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And for one knowing what, monks, for one seeing what, does the destruction of the taints occur? ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are volitional formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.’ It is for one knowing thus and seeing thus, monks, that the destruction of the taints occurs.”

“Bhāvanānuyogaṃ ananuyuttassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno viharato kiñcāpi evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti, atha khvassa neva anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ [T 3.0186] vimuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Abhāvitattā’ tissa vacanīyaṃ. Kissa abhāvitattā? Abhāvitattā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ, abhāvitattā catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ, abhāvitattā catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ, abhāvitattā pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ, abhāvitattā pañcannaṃ balānaṃ, abhāvitattā sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ, abhāvitattā ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa.

“Monks, when a bhikkhu dwells without being devoted to development, even if this wish should arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!’—still his mind is not liberated from the taints without clinging. For what reason? It should be said: ‘Because of not having been developed.’ Not developed in what? Because of not having developed the four establishments of mindfulness, because of not having developed the four right strivings, because of not having developed the four bases for spiritual power, because of not having developed the five faculties, because of not having developed the five powers, because of not having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, because of not having developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā. Tānassu kukkuṭiyā na sammā adhisayitāni, na sammā pariseditāni, na sammā paribhāvitāni. Kiñcāpi tassā kukkuṭiyā evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho, vata me [M 2.0125] kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjeyyu’nti, atha kho abhabbāva te kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjituṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi pana, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā; tāni kukkuṭiyā na sammā adhisayitāni, na sammā pariseditāni, na sammā paribhāvitāni. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhāvanānuyogaṃ ananuyuttassa bhikkhuno viharato kiñcāpi evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho, vata me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti, atha khvassa neva anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Abhāvitattā’tissa [V 2.0138] vacanīyaṃ. Kissa abhāvitattā? Abhāvitattā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ…pe… [T 3.0187] aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa.

“Just as, monks, a hen might have eight, ten, or twelve eggs, but they have not been well sat upon by the hen, not well warmed, not well brooded over. Even if this wish should arise in that hen: ‘Oh, that my chicks might break through the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and hatch safely!’—still those chicks are incapable of breaking through the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and hatching safely. For what reason? Because, monks, the hen’s eight, ten, or twelve eggs have not been well sat upon, not well warmed, not well brooded over. In the same way, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells without being devoted to development, even if this wish should arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!’—still his mind is not liberated from the taints without clinging. For what reason? It should be said: ‘Because of not having been developed.’ Not developed in what? Because of not having developed the four establishments of mindfulness… the Noble Eightfold Path.”

“Bhāvanānuyogaṃ anuyuttassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno viharato [P 3.0154] kiñcāpi na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti, atha khvassa anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Bhāvitattā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Kissa bhāvitattā? Bhāvitattā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ, bhāvitattā catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ, bhāvitattā catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ, bhāvitattā pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ, bhāvitattā pañcannaṃ balānaṃ, bhāvitattā sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ, bhāvitattā ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa.

“Monks, when a bhikkhu dwells applying himself to development, even if this wish should not arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!’—still his mind is liberated from the taints without clinging. For what reason? It should be said: ‘Because of having been developed.’ Because of having developed what? Because of having developed the four establishments of mindfulness, because of having developed the four right strivings, because of having developed the four bases of spiritual power, because of having developed the five faculties, because of having developed the five powers, because of having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, because of having developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā. Tānassu kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitāni, sammā pariseditāni, sammā paribhāvitāni[T 3.0188]. Kiñcāpi tassā kukkuṭiyā na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata me kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjeyyu’nti, atha kho bhabbāva te kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjituṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi pana, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā; tānassu kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitāni, sammā pariseditāni, sammā paribhāvitāni. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhāvanānuyogaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno viharato kiñcāpi na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti, atha khvassa anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Bhāvitattā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Kissa [M 2.0126] bhāvitattā? Bhāvitattā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ…pe… bhāvitattā ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs. They are properly sat upon, properly warmed, and properly brooded over by the hen. Even if this wish should not arise in that hen: ‘Oh, that my chicks might break through the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and hatch safely!’—still those chicks are capable of breaking through the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and hatching safely. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the hen’s eight, ten, or twelve eggs have been properly sat upon, properly warmed, and properly brooded over. In the same way, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells applying himself to development, even if this wish should not arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!’—still his mind is liberated from the taints without clinging. For what reason? It should be said: ‘Because of having been developed.’ Because of having developed what? Because of having developed the four establishments of mindfulness… because of having developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, palagaṇḍassa vā palagaṇḍantevāsissa vā vāsijaṭe dissanteva aṅgulipadāni dissati aṅguṭṭhapadaṃ. No ca khvassa evaṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti – ‘ettakaṃ vata me ajja vāsijaṭassa khīṇaṃ, ettakaṃ hiyyo, ettakaṃ pare’ti. Atha khvassa khīṇe khīṇantveva ñāṇaṃ hoti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhāvanānuyogaṃ anuyuttassa [P 3.0155] bhikkhuno viharato kiñcāpi [V 2.0139] na evaṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti – ‘ettakaṃ vata me ajja āsavānaṃ khīṇaṃ, ettakaṃ hiyyo, ettakaṃ pare’ti, atha khvassa khīṇe khīṇantveva ñāṇaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, sāmuddikāya nāvāya vettabandhanabaddhāya vassamāsāni udake pariyādāya hemantikena thalaṃ ukkhittāya vātātapaparetāni vettabandhanāni. Tāni pāvusakena meghena abhippavuṭṭhāni appakasireneva paṭippassambhanti [T 3.0189] pūtikāni bhavanti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhāvanānuyogaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno viharato appakasireneva saṃyojanāni paṭippassambhanti pūtikāni bhavantī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, just as for a master carpenter or a master carpenter’s apprentice, the marks of his fingers and the mark of his thumb are seen on his adze handle. Yet he does not have the knowledge: ‘This much of my adze handle has been worn away today, this much yesterday, this much the day before.’ Rather, when it is worn away, he has the knowledge that it is worn away. In the same way, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu dwelling devoted to the practice of meditation, although he does not have the knowledge: ‘This many of my taints have been worn away today, this many yesterday, this many the day before,’ yet when they are worn away, he has the knowledge that they are worn away. Bhikkhus, just as a seagoing ship, bound with rattan bindings, after spending the rainy season months in the water, is hauled up on land for the winter, its rattan bindings are afflicted by wind and sun. When they are thoroughly drenched by a rain cloud of the rainy season, they easily become slack and rotten. In the same way, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu dwelling devoted to the practice of meditation, the fetters easily become slack and rotten.”

10. Aniccasaññāsuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Perception of Impermanence

102. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Aniccasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ rūparāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ bhavarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ avijjaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati”.

102. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated, it consumes all sensual lust, it consumes all lust for form, it consumes all lust for existence, it consumes all ignorance, and it uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, saradasamaye kassako mahānaṅgalena kasanto sabbāni mūlasantānakāni sampadālento kasati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ rūparāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ bhavarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ avijjaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, in the autumn season a farmer, plowing with a great plow, plows while thoroughly breaking up all the root-networks; in the same way, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, consumes all sensual lust, it consumes all lust for form, it consumes all lust for existence, it consumes all ignorance, and it uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pabbajalāyako pabbajaṃ lāyitvā agge gahetvā odhunāti niddhunāti nicchoṭeti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a man who reaps rushes, having reaped the rushes, takes hold of them at the tip and shakes them, shakes them off, and shakes them out; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, consumes all sensual lust… and uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi[M 2.0127], bhikkhave, ambapiṇḍiyā vaṇṭacchinnāya yāni [P 3.0156] tattha ambāni vaṇṭapaṭibandhāni sabbāni tāni tadanvayāni bhavanti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā bhāvitā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, when the stalk of a mango cluster is cut, all the mangoes that are attached to the stalk follow along with it; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kūṭāgārassa yā kāci gopānasiyo sabbā tā kūṭaṅgamā kūṭaninnā [V 2.0140] kūṭasamosaraṇā, kūṭaṃ tāsaṃ aggamakkhāyati[T 3.0190]; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā bhāvitā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, in a gabled house, whatever rafters there are, they all go to the peak, incline towards the peak, and converge at the peak, and the peak is said to be the foremost of them; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci mūlagandhā kāḷānusārigandho tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, among whatever root fragrances there are, the fragrance of black aloe-wood is said to be the foremost; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci sāragandhā, lohitacandanaṃ tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, among whatever heartwood fragrances there are, red sandalwood is said to be the foremost; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci pupphagandhā, vassikaṃ tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, among whatever flower fragrances there are, jasmine is said to be the foremost; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci kuṭṭarājāno kuḍḍarājāno (sī.), sabbete rañño cakkavattissa anuyantā bhavanti, rājā tesaṃ cakkavatti aggamakkhāyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, whatever petty kings there are, they are all vassals of the wheel-turning king, and the wheel-turning king is said to be the chief among them; even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yā kāci tārakarūpānaṃ pabhā, sabbā tā candimappabhāya kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ, candappabhā tāsaṃ aggamakkhāyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, whatever light there is from the host of stars, all of it is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon’s light; the moon’s light is said to be the foremost of them. Even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence… uproots all conceit ‘I am.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, saradasamaye viddhe vigatavalāhake deve ādicco nataṃ abbhussakkamāno, sabbaṃ ākāsagataṃ tamagataṃ abhivihacca bhāsate ca tapate ca virocate ca; evameva kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ rūparāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ bhavarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ avijjaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati.

Just as, Bhikkhus, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, ascending into the sky, having dispelled all darkness in space, shines, blazes, and is resplendent; even so, Bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, consumes all sensual lust, consumes all lust for form, consumes all lust for existence, consumes all ignorance, and uproots all conceit 'I am'.

“Kathaṃ [T 3.0191] bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā [P 3.0157] sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati…pe… sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanati? ‘Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa [M 2.0128] samudayo, iti [V 2.0141] rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti – evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aniccasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ rūparāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ bhavarāgaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ avijjaṃ pariyādiyati, sabbaṃ asmimānaṃ samūhanatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

And how, Bhikkhus, is the perception of impermanence developed, how is it cultivated, that it consumes all sensual lust... uproots all conceit 'I am'? 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling... such is perception... such are formations... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.' It is in this way, Bhikkhus, that the perception of impermanence, when so developed and so cultivated, consumes all sensual lust, consumes all lust for form, consumes all lust for existence, consumes all ignorance, and uproots all conceit 'I am'. Tenth.

Pupphavaggo dasamo.

The Flower Chapter, the tenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Nadī pupphañca pheṇañca, gomayañca nakhāsikhaṃ;

Suddhikaṃ dve ca gaddulā, vāsījaṭaṃ aniccatāti.

Nadī, Puppha, and Pheṇa, Gomaya and Nakhasikha; Suddhika, the two Gaddulas, Vāsijaṭa and Aniccatā.

Majjhimapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Middle Fifty is finished.

Tassa majjhimapaṇṇāsakassa vagguddānaṃ –

The chapter summary of that Middle Fifty:

Upayo arahanto ca, khajjanī therasavhayaṃ;

Pupphavaggena paṇṇāsa, dutiyo tena vuccatīti.

Upāya and Arahanta, Khajjanī, the one called Thera; with the Flower Chapter, the second fifty is thus called.

11. Antavaggo

11. The Chapter on Portions

1. Antasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Portions

103. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0192]. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, antā. Katame cattāro? Sakkāyanto[P 3.0158], sakkāyasamudayanto, sakkāyanirodhanto, sakkāyanirodhagāminippaṭipadanto. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyanto? Pañcupādānakkhandhātissa vacanīyaṃ. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyanto”.

103. At Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, there are these four portions. What four? The portion of the existing body, the portion of the origin of the existing body, the portion of the cessation of the existing body, and the portion of the practice leading to the cessation of the existing body. And what, Bhikkhus, is the portion of the existing body? It should be said: the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, Bhikkhus, is called the portion of the existing body.'

“Katamo [V 2.0142] ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyasamudayanto? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā nandirāgasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinī, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā. Ayaṃ [M 2.0129] vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyasamudayanto.

And what, Bhikkhus, is the portion of the origin of the existing body? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, Bhikkhus, is called the portion of the origin of the existing body.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhanto? Yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhanto.

And what, Bhikkhus, is the portion of the cessation of the existing body? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up, the relinquishing, the release, and the non-attachment. This, Bhikkhus, is called the portion of the cessation of the existing body.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhagāminippaṭipadanto? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhagāminippaṭipadanto[T 3.0193]. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro antā”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

And what, Bhikkhus, is the portion of the practice leading to the cessation of the existing body? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, Bhikkhus, is called the portion of the practice leading to the cessation of the existing body. These, Bhikkhus, are indeed the four portions.' First.

2. Dukkhasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Suffering

104. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Dukkhañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi dukkhasamudayañca dukkhanirodhañca dukkhanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamañca, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ? Pañcupādānakkhandhātissa vacanīyaṃ. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayo? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā…pe… kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayo. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodho? Yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodho. Katamā [P 3.0159] ca, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

104. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Listen to that. And what, Bhikkhus, is suffering? It should be said: the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is, the form aggregate subject to clinging… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, Bhikkhus, is called suffering. And what, Bhikkhus, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence… namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, Bhikkhus, is called the origin of suffering. And what, Bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its giving up, relinquishment, liberation, and non-attachment. This, Bhikkhus, is called the cessation of suffering. And what, Bhikkhus, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path. That is, right view… right concentration. This, Bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” Second.

3. Sakkāyasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Identity

105. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Sakkāyañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi sakkāyasamudayañca sakkāyanirodhañca [V 2.0143] sakkāyanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyo? Pañcupādānakkhandhātissa vacanīyaṃ[T 3.0194]. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyo. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyasamudayo? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā…pe… kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyasamudayo. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodho? Yo tassāyeva taṇhāya…pe… ayaṃ vuccati[M 2.0130], bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodho. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

105. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you identity, the origin of identity, the cessation of identity, and the way leading to the cessation of identity. Listen to that. And what, Bhikkhus, is identity? It should be said: the five aggregates subject to clinging. Which five? That is, the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, Bhikkhus, is called identity. And what, Bhikkhus, is the origin of identity? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence… that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, Bhikkhus, is called the origin of identity. And what, Bhikkhus, is the cessation of identity? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving… This, Bhikkhus, is called the cessation of identity. And what, Bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of identity? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view… right concentration. This, Bhikkhus, is called the way leading to the cessation of identity.” Third.

4. Pariññeyyasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on What Is to Be Fully Understood

106. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Pariññeyye ca, bhikkhave, dhamme desessāmi pariññañca pariññātāviñca puggalaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, pariññeyyā dhammā? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, pariññeyyo dhammo. Vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ pariññeyyo dhammo. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pariññeyyā dhammā. Katamā [P 3.0160] ca, bhikkhave, pariññā? Rāgakkhayo, dosakkhayo, mohakkhayo – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, pariññā. Katamo [T 3.0195] ca, bhikkhave, pariññātāvī puggalo? Arahātissa vacanīyaṃ. Yvāyaṃ āyasmā evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, pariññātāvī puggalo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

106. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the phenomena to be fully understood, full understanding, and the person who has fully understood. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be fully understood? Form, bhikkhus, is a phenomenon to be fully understood. Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness is a phenomenon to be fully understood. These, bhikkhus, are called the phenomena to be fully understood. And what, bhikkhus, is full understanding? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called full understanding. And who, bhikkhus, is the person who has fully understood? It should be said: the Arahant. That venerable one of such a name and such a clan—this, bhikkhus, is called the person who has fully understood.” The fourth.

5. Samaṇasuttaṃ

5. The Recluse

107. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, upādānakkhandhā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… pajānanti, sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

107. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is: the aggregate of form subject to clinging… the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging… [but those who] do understand, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter upon and dwell therein.” The fifth.

6. Dutiyasamaṇasuttaṃ

6. The Second Discourse on Recluses

108. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0144]. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, upādānakkhandhā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ [T 3.0196] – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… pajānanti, sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

108. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is: the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of formations subject to clinging, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand as it actually is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging… [but those who] do understand, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter upon and dwell therein.” The sixth.

7. Sotāpannasuttaṃ

7. The Stream-Enterer

109. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0131]. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, upādānakkhandhā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca [P 3.0161] ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sotāpanno avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyano”ti. Sattamaṃ.

109. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is: the aggregate of form subject to clinging… the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands as it actually is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging, this one is called, bhikkhus, a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, not subject to perdition, assured, and bound for enlightenment.” The seventh.

8. Arahantasuttaṃ

8. The Arahant

110. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, upādānakkhandhā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto hoti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññāvimutto”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

110. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? That is: the form aggregate subject to clinging... the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having known as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging, is liberated through non-clinging. This one, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, has destroyed the fetters of being, and is liberated by right knowledge.” The eighth.

9. Chandappahānasuttaṃ

9. Abandonment of Desire

111. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0145]. “Rūpe, bhikkhave, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā, taṃ pajahatha. Evaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati ucchinnamūlaṃ [T 3.0197] tālāvatthukataṃ anabhāvaṃkataṃ āyatiṃ anuppādadhammaṃ. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā, taṃ pajahatha. Evaṃ taṃ viññāṇaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati ucchinnamūlaṃ tālāvatthukataṃ anabhāvaṃkataṃ āyatiṃ anuppādadhamma”nti. Navamaṃ.

111. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for form, abandon it. Thus that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and not subject to future arising. For feeling… for perception… for formations… whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for consciousness, abandon it. Thus that consciousness will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and not subject to future arising.” The ninth.

10. Dutiyachandappahānasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on Abandonment of Desire

112. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Rūpe, bhikkhave, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā ye upayupādānā cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā, te pajahatha[P 3.0162]. Evaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati ucchinnamūlaṃ…pe… vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu yo chando…pe… evaṃ te saṅkhārā pahīnā bhavissanti ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ [M 2.0132] anuppādadhammā. Viññāṇe yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā ye upayupādānā cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā, te pajahatha. Evaṃ taṃ viññāṇaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati ucchinnamūlaṃ tālāvatthukataṃ anabhāvaṃkataṃ āyatiṃ anuppādadhamma”nti. Dasamaṃ.

112. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever approaches and clingings, whatever mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding form, abandon them. Thus that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root… For feeling… for perception… regarding formations, abandon them. Thus those formations will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and not subject to future arising. Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever approaches and clingings, whatever mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding consciousness, abandon them. Thus that consciousness will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and not subject to future arising.” The tenth.

Antavaggo ekādasamo.

The Chapter on the End, the eleventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Anto dukkhañca sakkāyo, pariññeyyā samaṇā duve;

Sotāpanno arahā ca, duve ca chandappahānāti.

The End, Suffering, and Identity, To Be Fully Understood, two on Recluses; The Stream-Enterer and the Arahant, and two on the Abandonment of Desire.

12. Dhammakathikavaggo

12. The Chapter on Dhamma Speakers

1. Avijjāsuttaṃ

1. Ignorance

113. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0198][V 2.0146]. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘avijjā avijjā’ti, bhante, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, bhante, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti? “Idha, bhikkhu, assutavā puthujjano rūpaṃ nappajānāti, rūpasamudayaṃ nappajānāti, rūpanirodhaṃ nappajānāti, rūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānāti; vedanaṃ nappajānāti… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre nappajānāti…pe… viññāṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ [P 3.0163] vuccati, bhikkhu, avijjā. Ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

113. At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance, and to what extent is one overcome by ignorance?” “Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed ordinary person does not understand form, does not understand the origin of form, does not understand the cessation of form, does not understand the path leading to the cessation of form; he does not understand feeling... perception... formations... and does not understand the path leading to the cessation of consciousness. This, bhikkhu, is called ignorance. And to this extent, one is overcome by ignorance.” The first.
