2. Vijjāsuttaṃ

2. Knowledge

114. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā vijjā’ti, bhante, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, bhante, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti? “Idha, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpaṃ pajānāti, rūpasamudayaṃ pajānāti, rūpanirodhaṃ pajānāti, rūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre pajānāti…pe… viññāṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, vijjā. Ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

114. At Sāvatthī. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “‘Knowledge, knowledge,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is knowledge, and to what extent is one possessed of knowledge?” “Here, bhikkhu, a well-instructed noble disciple understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, and understands the path leading to the cessation of form. He understands feeling... perception... formations... and understands the path leading to the cessation of consciousness. This, bhikkhu, is called knowledge. And to this extent, one is possessed of knowledge.”

3. Dhammakathikasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Speaker of the Dhamma

115. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0133]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘dhammakathiko dhammakathiko’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu [T 3.0199] kho, bhante, dhammakathiko hotī”ti[V 2.0147]? “Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Vedanāya ce, bhikkhu…pe… saññāya ce, bhikkhu… saṅkhārānaṃ ce, bhikkhu… viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā [P 3.0164] nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

115. At Sāvatthī. That bhikkhu, having sat down to one side, said this to the Blessed One: “‘A speaker of the Dhamma, a speaker of the Dhamma,’ it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is one a speaker of the Dhamma?” “If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with form, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a Dhamma-speaking bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with form, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with form, through dispassion towards it, and through its cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’ So too for feeling… for perception… for volitional formations… If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a Dhamma-speaking bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with consciousness, through dispassion towards it, and through its cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’”

4. Dutiyadhammakathikasuttaṃ

4. The Second Discourse on the Speaker of the Dhamma

116. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘dhammakathiko dhammakathiko’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, dhammakathiko hoti, kittāvatā dhammānudhammappaṭipanno hoti, kittāvatā diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotī”ti? “Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno [T 3.0200] hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Rūpassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Vedanāya ce, bhikkhu…pe… saññāya ce, bhikkhu… saṅkhārānaṃ ce, bhikkhu… viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāya. Viññāṇassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā [M 2.0134] nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā”ti. Catutthaṃ.

116. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “‘A speaker of the Dhamma, a speaker of the Dhamma,’ it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is one a speaker of the Dhamma? To what extent is one practicing in accordance with the Dhamma? To what extent has one attained Nibbāna in this very life?” “If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with form, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a Dhamma-speaking bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with form, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with form, through dispassion towards it, and through its cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’ So too for feeling… for perception… for volitional formations… If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a Dhamma-speaking bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion towards it, and for its cessation, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with consciousness, through dispassion towards it, and through its cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to call him ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’”

5. Bandhanasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Bondage

117. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0148]. “Idha bhikkhave assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano rūpabandhanabaddho santarabāhirabandhanabaddho atīradassī apāradassī, baddho jīyati baddho jāyati (sī. pī.) baddho jāyati baddho jīyati (sī. aṭṭha. syā. aṭṭha.) baddho mīyati baddho asmā lokā [T 3.0201] paraṃ lokaṃ gacchati. Vedanaṃ [P 3.0165] attato samanupassati…pe… vedanāya vā attānaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano vedanābandhanabaddho santarabāhirabandhanabaddho atīradassī apāradassī, baddho jīyati baddho mīyati baddho asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gacchati. Saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano viññāṇabandhanabaddho santarabāhirabandhanabaddho atīradassī apāradassī, baddho jīyati baddho mīyati baddho asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gacchati”.

117. At Sāvatthī. “Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones... untrained in the Dhamma of the good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. This, bhikkhus, is called an uninstructed ordinary person, bound by the bond of form, bound by internal and external bonds, not seeing this shore, not seeing the far shore. Bound, he ages; bound, he dies; bound, he goes from this world to the next. He regards feeling as self... or self in feeling. This, bhikkhus, is called an uninstructed ordinary person, bound by the bond of feeling, bound by internal and external bonds, not seeing this shore, not seeing the far shore. Bound, he ages; bound, he dies; bound, he goes from this world to the next. He regards perception… volitional formations… consciousness as self… This, bhikkhus, is called an uninstructed ordinary person, bound by the bond of consciousness, bound by internal and external bonds, not seeing this shore, not seeing the far shore. Bound, he ages; bound, he dies; bound, he goes from this world to the next.”

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī…pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ; na attani vā rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako na rūpabandhanabaddho, na santarabāhirabandhanabaddho, tīradassī, pāradassī; ‘parimutto so dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi. Na vedanaṃ attato…pe… na saññaṃ attato…pe… na saṅkhāre attato…pe… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako na viññāṇabandhanabaddho, na santarabāhirabandhanabaddho, tīradassī, pāradassī, ‘parimutto so dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones... and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the good persons, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form in self, nor self in form. This, bhikkhus, is called an instructed noble disciple, not bound by the bond of form, not bound by internal and external bonds, one who sees this shore, one who sees the far shore. ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I declare. He does not regard feeling as self… nor perception as self… nor volitional formations as self… nor consciousness as self… This, bhikkhus, is called an instructed noble disciple, not bound by the bond of consciousness, not bound by internal and external bonds, one who sees this shore, one who sees the far shore. ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I declare.”

6. Paripucchitasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Questioning

118. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso [V 2.0149] me attā’ti samanupassathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu, bhikkhave! Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ [M 2.0135] yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ [P 3.0166] ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu, bhikkhave! Viññāṇaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi[T 3.0202], na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… evaṃ passaṃ…pe… kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

118. At Sāvatthī. “What do you think, monks? Do you regard form thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Good, monks! Form, monks, should be seen with perfect wisdom as it truly is, thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Do you regard feeling… perception… formations… consciousness thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Good, monks! Consciousness, monks, should be seen with perfect wisdom as it truly is, thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’… Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

7. Dutiyaparipucchitasuttaṃ

7. The Second Sutta on Questioning

119. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassathā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu bhikkhave! Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassathā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu bhikkhave! Viññāṇaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… evaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

119. At Sāvatthī. “What do you think, monks? Do you regard form thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Good, monks! Form, monks, should be seen with perfect wisdom as it truly is, thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Do you regard feeling… perception… formations… consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Good, monks! Consciousness, monks, should be seen with perfect wisdom as it truly is, thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’… Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

8. Saṃyojaniyasuttaṃ

8. The Sutta on Things Conducive to Fetters

120. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0150]. “Saṃyojaniye ca, bhikkhave, dhamme desessāmī saṃyojanañca. Taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyā dhammā, katamaṃ saṃyojanaṃ? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyo dhammo; yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ [P 3.0167] saṃyojaniyo dhammo; yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyā dhammā, idaṃ saṃyojana”nti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

120. At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I shall teach you the phenomena that are objects of fetters and the fetter itself. Listen to that. And what, monks, are the phenomena that are objects of fetters, and what is the fetter? Form, monks, is a phenomenon that is an object of a fetter; whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is the fetter there. Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is a phenomenon that is an object of a fetter; whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is the fetter there. These, monks, are called the phenomena that are objects of fetters, and this is called the fetter.”

9. Upādāniyasuttaṃ

9. The Sutta on Things that are Objects of Clinging

121. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Upādāniye ca, bhikkhave, dhamme desessāmi upādānañca[T 3.0203]. Taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, upādāniyā dhammā, katamaṃ upādānaṃ? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, upādāniyo dhammo, yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha upādānaṃ. Vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ upādāniyo dhammo; yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha upādānaṃ. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, upādāniyā dhammā, idaṃ upādāna”nti. Navamaṃ.

121. At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I shall teach you the phenomena that are objects of clinging and clinging itself. Listen to that. And what, monks, are the phenomena that are objects of clinging, and what is clinging? Form, monks, is a phenomenon that is an object of clinging; whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is clinging there. Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is a phenomenon that is an object of clinging; whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is clinging there. These, monks, are called the phenomena that are objects of clinging, and this is called clinging.”

10. Sīlavantasuttaṃ

10. The Sutta on the Virtuous One

122. Ekaṃ [M 2.0136] samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko mahākoṭṭhito (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami…pe… etadavoca – “sīlavatāvuso, sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasikātabbā”ti? “Sīlavatāvuso, koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Sīlavatāvuso, koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato [V 2.0151] dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho [T 3.0204] panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ sīlavā bhikkhu [P 3.0168] ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi karonto sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikareyyā”ti.

122. On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita rose from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta… and said to him: “Friend Sāriputta, what things should a virtuous bhikkhu wisely attend to?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, a virtuous bhikkhu should wisely attend to the five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as an affliction, as an ailment, as other, as perishable, as empty, and as not-self. Which five? They are: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Friend Koṭṭhika, a virtuous bhikkhu should wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as an affliction, as an ailment, as other, as perishable, as empty, and as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a virtuous bhikkhu, by wisely attending to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, may realize the fruit of stream-entry.”

“Sotāpannena panāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Sotāpannenapi kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ sotāpanno bhikkhu ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi karonto sakadāgāmiphalaṃ sacchikareyyā”ti.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer wisely attend to?” “A bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer, friend Koṭṭhika, should also wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer, by wisely attending to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, may realize the fruit of once-returning.”

“Sakadāgāminā panāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Sakadāgāmināpi kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ sakadāgāmī bhikkhu ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi karonto anāgāmiphalaṃ sacchikareyyā”ti.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a once-returner wisely attend to?” “A bhikkhu who is a once-returner, friend Koṭṭhika, should also wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a once-returner bhikkhu, by wisely attending to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, may realize the fruit of non-returning.”

“Anāgāminā [M 2.0137] panāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Anāgāmināpi kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ anāgāmī bhikkhu ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato [T 3.0205] yoniso manasi karonto arahattaṃ sacchikareyyā”ti.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a non-returner attend to wisely?” “Even a bhikkhu who is a non-returner, friend Koṭṭhika, should attend wisely to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a non-returner bhikkhu, by attending wisely to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, may realize arahantship.”

“Arahatā panāvuso sāriputta, katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Arahatāpi kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Natthi, khvāvuso, arahato uttari karaṇīyaṃ katassa vā paticayo[P 3.0169]; api ca ime [V 2.0152] dhammā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ceva saṃvattanti satisampajaññā cā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should an arahant attend to wisely?” “Even an arahant, friend Koṭṭhika, should attend wisely to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as pain, as an affliction, as alien, as perishable, as empty, as not-self. For an arahant, friend, there is nothing further to do, nor any adding to what has been done; yet these things, when developed and cultivated, conduce both to a pleasant abiding in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.” The Tenth.

11. Sutavantasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on the Learned

123. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… etadavoca –

123. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika rose from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached… he said this:

“Sutavatāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Sutavatāvuso koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Katame pañca? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho…pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Sutavatāvuso koṭṭhika, bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati – yaṃ sutavā bhikkhu ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi karonto sotāpattiphalaṃ [T 3.0206] sacchikareyyā”ti.

“Friend Sāriputta, what things should a learned bhikkhu wisely attend to?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, a learned bhikkhu should wisely attend to the five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. Which five? They are: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Friend Koṭṭhika, a learned bhikkhu should wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a learned bhikkhu, by wisely attending to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, might realize the fruit of stream-entry.”

“Sotāpannena panāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Sotāpannenapi kho āvuso koṭṭhika[M 2.0138], bhikkhunā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati – yaṃ sotāpanno bhikkhu ime pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccato…pe… anattato yoniso manasi karonto sakadāgāmiphalaṃ…pe… anāgāmiphalaṃ…pe… arahattaphalaṃ sacchikareyyā”ti.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer wisely attend to?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer should also wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self. It is possible, friend, that a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer, by wisely attending to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent… as not-self, might realize the fruit of once-returning… the fruit of non-returning… the fruit of arahantship.”

“Arahatā panāvuso sāriputta, katame dhammā yoniso manasi kātabbā”ti? “Arahatāpi khvāvuso, koṭṭhika, ime pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato yoniso manasi kātabbā. Natthi, khvāvuso, arahato uttari karaṇīyaṃ, katassa vā paticayo; api ca kho ime dhammā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya ceva saṃvattanti satisampajaññā cā”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should an arahant wisely attend to?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, an arahant should also wisely attend to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as pain, as an affliction, as alien, as perishable, as empty, and as not-self. For an arahant, friend, there is nothing further to be done, nor any accumulation of what has been done. However, these things, when developed and cultivated, conduce both to a pleasant abiding in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.” Eleventh.

12. Kappasuttaṃ

12. The Discourse with Kappa

124. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0153]. Atha kho āyasmā kappo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā kappo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti?

124. At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kappa approached the Blessed One… Seated to one side, the Venerable Kappa said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, for one who knows how, and for one who sees how, do the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit not occur in regard to this body with consciousness and all external signs?”

“Yaṃ kiñci, kappa, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ [T 3.0207] ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Evaṃ kho, kappa, jānato evaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

“Kappa, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one sees all form as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one sees all consciousness as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ It is for one who knows and sees in this way, Kappa, that the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not occur in regard to this body with consciousness and all external signs.” Twelfth.

13. Dutiyakappasuttaṃ

13. The Second Discourse with Kappa

125. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0139][P 3.0170]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā kappo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṃ mānasaṃ hoti vidhā samatikkantaṃ santaṃ suvimutta”nti?

125. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, the Venerable Kappa said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, for one who knows how, and for one who sees how, in regard to this body with consciousness and all external signs, does the mind become free from I-making, mine-making, and conceit, transcending discrimination, peaceful, and well liberated?”

“Yaṃ kiñci, kappa, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā anupādāvimutto hoti. Yā [V 2.0154] kāci vedanā… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā [T 3.0208] oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā anupādāvimutto hoti. Evaṃ kho, kappa, jānato evaṃ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṃ mānasaṃ hoti vidhā samatikkantaṃ santaṃ suvimutta”nti. Terasamaṃ.

“Whatever form, Kappa, whether past, future, or present… and so forth… all form, ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus having seen it as it actually is with right wisdom, one is liberated without clinging. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness, ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus having seen it as it actually is with right wisdom, one is liberated without clinging. Thus, Kappa, for one who knows thus and sees thus, in this body with consciousness and in all external signs, the mind is devoid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit, has transcended the threefold conceit, is peaceful, and is well liberated.” The thirteenth.

Dhammakathikavaggo dvādasamo.

The Chapter on Dhamma-Speakers, the twelfth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that is:

Avijjā vijjā dve kathikā, bandhanā paripucchitā duve;

Saṃyojanaṃ upādānaṃ, sīlaṃ sutavā dve ca kappenāti.

Ignorance and Knowledge, two on the Speakers; Bondage and the Questioned are two; The Fetter, Clinging; Virtue, the Learned One, and two with Kappa.

13. Avijjāvaggo

13. The Chapter on Ignorance

1. Samudayadhammasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Nature of Arising

126. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0209]. Atha [P 3.0171] kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘avijjā avijjā’ti, bhante, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, bhante, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

126. At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, and having approached… he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, it is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance? And to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?”

“Idha[M 2.0140], bhikkhu, assutavā puthujjano samudayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti[V 2.0155]; vayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘vayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘samudayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; vayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘vayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; samudayavayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ saññaṃ…pe… samudayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; vayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘vayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; samudayavayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayavayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; vayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘vayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti.

“Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed ordinary person does not know distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to arise as ‘form is of the nature to arise’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to perish as ‘form is of the nature to perish’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘form is of the nature to arise and perish’. He does not know distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to arise as ‘feeling is of the nature to arise’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to perish as ‘feeling is of the nature to perish’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘feeling is of the nature to arise and perish’. He does not know distinctly perception… and so forth… He does not know distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to arise as ‘formations are of the nature to arise’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to perish as ‘formations are of the nature to perish’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to arise and perish as ‘formations are of the nature to arise and perish’. He does not know distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to arise as ‘consciousness is of the nature to arise’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to perish as ‘consciousness is of the nature to perish’; he does not know distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘consciousness is of the nature to arise and perish’. This, bhikkhu, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance.”

Evaṃ vutte, so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā vijjā’ti, bhante, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, bhante, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “‘Knowledge, knowledge,’ venerable sir, it is said. What, venerable sir, is knowledge? And to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?”

“Idha, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako samudayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; vayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘vayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti[P 3.0172]; samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘samudayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; vayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘vayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; samudayavayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ saññaṃ… samudayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; vayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘vayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; samudayavayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayavayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; vayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘vayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Here, bhikkhu, a learned noble disciple knows distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to arise as ‘form is of the nature to arise’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to perish as ‘form is of the nature to perish’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: form which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘form is of the nature to arise and perish’. He knows distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to arise as ‘feeling is of the nature to arise’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to perish as ‘feeling is of the nature to perish’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: feeling which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘feeling is of the nature to arise and perish’. He knows distinctly perception… He knows distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to arise as ‘formations are of the nature to arise’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to perish as ‘formations are of the nature to perish’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: formations which are of the nature to arise and perish as ‘formations are of the nature to arise and perish’. He knows distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to arise as ‘consciousness is of the nature to arise’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to perish as ‘consciousness is of the nature to perish’; he knows distinctly, as it really is: consciousness which is of the nature to arise and perish as ‘consciousness is of the nature to arise and perish’. This, bhikkhu, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge.” The first.

2. Dutiyasamudayadhammasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on the Nature of Arising

127. Ekaṃ [V 2.0156][M 2.0141] samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito…pe… ekamantaṃ [T 3.0211] nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

127. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika arose from seclusion... Sitting to one side, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “'Ignorance, ignorance,' it is said, friend Sāriputta. What, friend, is ignorance, and to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?”

“Idhāvuso assutavā puthujjano samudayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti; vayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… vayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… ‘samudayavayadhammā vedanā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ saññaṃ…pe… samudayadhamme saṅkhāre…pe… vayadhamme saṅkhāre…pe… samudayavayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayavayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ…pe… samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, āvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

Here, friend, an uninstructed ordinary person does not distinctly know as it really is form that is subject to arising, thus: ‘Form is subject to arising’; he does not distinctly know as it really is form that is subject to perishing… he does not distinctly know as it really is form that is subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Form is subject to arising and perishing.’ He does not distinctly know as it really is feeling that is subject to arising… feeling that is subject to perishing… he does not distinctly know as it really is feeling that is subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Feeling is subject to arising and perishing.’ He does not distinctly know as it really is perception that is subject to arising… formations that are subject to arising… formations that are subject to perishing… formations that are subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Formations are subject to arising and perishing.’ He does not distinctly know as it really is consciousness that is subject to arising… he does not distinctly know as it really is consciousness that is subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Consciousness is subject to arising and perishing.’ This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance. Second.

3. Tatiyasamudayadhammasuttaṃ

3. The Third Discourse on the Nature of Arising

128. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko bārāṇasiyaṃ [P 3.0173] viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā, vijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

128. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana… Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “‘Knowledge, knowledge,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. What, friend, is knowledge, and to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?”

“Idhāvuso, sutavā ariyasāvako samudayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; vayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ [T 3.0212] pajānāti; samudayadhammaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… samudayavayadhammā vedanā [V 2.0157]… samudayadhammaṃ saññaṃ…pe… samudayadhamme saṅkhāre… vayadhamme saṅkhāre… samudayavayadhamme saṅkhāre ‘samudayavayadhammā saṅkhārā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Samudayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ… vayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ… samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘samudayavayadhammaṃ viññāṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

Here, friend, a learned noble disciple distinctly knows as it really is form that is subject to arising, thus: ‘Form is subject to arising’; he distinctly knows as it really is form that is subject to perishing… he distinctly knows as it really is form that is subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Form is subject to arising and perishing.’ He distinctly knows as it really is feeling that is subject to arising… feeling that is subject to arising and perishing… perception that is subject to arising… formations that are subject to arising… formations that are subject to perishing… formations that are subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Formations are subject to arising and perishing.’ He distinctly knows as it really is consciousness that is subject to arising… consciousness that is subject to perishing… consciousness that is subject to arising and perishing, thus: ‘Consciousness is subject to arising and perishing.’ This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge. Third.

4. Assādasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Gratification

129. Bārāṇasiyaṃ [M 2.0142] viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

129. They were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana... Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. Now what, friend, is ignorance, and to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?”

“Idhāvuso assutavā puthujjano rūpassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Here, friend, an uninstructed ordinary person does not distinctly know as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of form. He does not distinctly know as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance.” Fourth.

5. Dutiyaassādasuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse on Gratification

130. Bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… “‘vijjā, [P 3.0174] vijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

130. They were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana... “‘Knowledge, knowledge,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. Now what, friend, is knowledge, and to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?”

“Idhāvuso, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa [T 3.0213] assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Here, friend, a learned noble disciple distinctly knows as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of form. He distinctly knows as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge.” Fifth.

6. Samudayasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Origination

131. Bārāṇasiyaṃ [V 2.0158] viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

131. They were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana… “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. What, friend, is ignorance? And to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?”

“Idhāvuso, assutavā puthujjano rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Here, friend, an uninstructed ordinary person does not distinctly know as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of form. He does not distinctly know as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance.” Sixth.

7. Dutiyasamudayasuttaṃ

7. The Second Discourse on Origination

132. Bārāṇasiyaṃ [M 2.0143] viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā, vijjā’ti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

132. They were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana… Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “‘Knowledge, knowledge,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. What, friend, is knowledge? And to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?”

“Idhāvuso, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Here, friend, a learned noble disciple distinctly knows as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of form. He distinctly knows as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge.” Seventh.

8. Koṭṭhikasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse with Koṭṭhika

133. Bārāṇasiyaṃ [T 3.0214][P 3.0175] viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṃ…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ mahākoṭṭhikaṃ etadavoca [V 2.0159] – “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

133. They were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta... seated to one side, said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: “Friend Koṭṭhika, ‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ it is said. What, friend, is ignorance, and to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?”

“Idhāvuso, assutavā puthujjano rūpassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti.

Here, friend, an uninstructed worldling does not understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form. They do not understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance.

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ mahākoṭṭhikaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā, vijjā’ti, āvuso koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, it is said, "Knowledge, knowledge." What, friend, is knowledge, and to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?'

“Idhāvuso sutavā ariyasāvako rūpassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Here, friend, a learned noble disciple understands as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form. They understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent has one arrived at knowledge. The eighth.

9. Dutiyakoṭṭhikasuttaṃ

9. Second Koṭṭhika Sutta

134. Bārāṇasiyaṃ [M 2.0144] viharanti isipatane migadāye…pe… “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso [T 3.0215] koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

134. Dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana... 'Friend Koṭṭhika, it is said, "Ignorance, ignorance." What, friend, is ignorance, and to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?'

“Idhāvuso, assutavā puthujjano rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ [P 3.0176] vuccatāvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti.

Here, friend, an uninstructed worldling does not understand as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form. They do not understand as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent has one arrived at ignorance.

Evaṃ [V 2.0160] vutte, āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ mahākoṭṭhikaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā, vijjā’ti, āvuso koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti?

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, it is said, "Knowledge, knowledge." What, friend, is knowledge, and to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?'

“Idhāvuso, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhārānaṃ… viññāṇassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Navamaṃ.

Here, friend, a learned noble disciple understands as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form. They understand as it really is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to feeling... perception... formations... consciousness. This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge. The ninth.

10. Tatiyakoṭṭhikasuttaṃ

10. Third Koṭṭhika Sutta

135. Taññeva nidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ mahākoṭṭhikaṃ etadavoca – “‘avijjā, avijjā’ti, āvuso koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, avijjā, kittāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti?

135. The setting is the same. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, it is said, "Ignorance, ignorance." What, friend, is ignorance, and to what extent has one arrived at ignorance?'

“Idhāvuso, assutavā puthujjano rūpaṃ nappajānāti, rūpasamudayaṃ nappajānāti, rūpanirodhaṃ nappajānāti, rūpanirodhagāminiṃ [T 3.0216] paṭipadaṃ nappajānāti. Vedanaṃ nappajānāti…pe… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ nappajānāti, viññāṇasamudayaṃ nappajānāti, viññāṇanirodhaṃ nappajānāti, viññāṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, avijjā; ettāvatā ca avijjāgato hotī”ti.

Here, friend, an uninstructed worldling does not understand form, does not understand the origin of form, does not understand the cessation of form, and does not understand the path of practice leading to the cessation of form. They do not understand feeling… perception… formations… consciousness; they do not understand the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the path of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness. This, friend, is called ignorance; and to this extent one has arrived at ignorance.

Evaṃ [M 2.0145] vutte, āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ mahākoṭṭhikaṃ etadavoca – “‘vijjā, vijjā’ti, āvuso koṭṭhika, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, āvuso, vijjā, kittāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti? “Idhāvuso, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpaṃ pajānāti, rūpasamudayaṃ [P 3.0177] pajānāti, rūpanirodhaṃ pajānāti, rūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ pajānāti, viññāṇasamudayaṃ pajānāti, viññāṇanirodhaṃ pajānāti[V 2.0161], viññāṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, vijjā; ettāvatā ca vijjāgato hotī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, it is said, "Knowledge, knowledge." What, friend, is knowledge, and to what extent has one arrived at knowledge?' 'Here, friend, a learned noble disciple understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, and understands the path of practice leading to the cessation of form. They understand feeling… perception… formations… consciousness; they understand the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the path of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness. This, friend, is called knowledge; and to this extent one has arrived at knowledge.' The tenth.

Avijjāvaggo terasamo.

The Chapter on Ignorance, the Thirteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this is:

Samudayadhamme tīṇi, assādo apare duve;

Samudaye ca dve vuttā, koṭṭhike apare tayoti.

Three were taught on things subject to origination, and two others on gratification; two were taught on origination, and three others on Koṭṭhika.

14. Kukkuḷavaggo

14. The Chapter on Hot Embers

1. Kukkuḷasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Hot Embers

136. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0217]. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, kukkuḷaṃ, vedanā kukkuḷā, saññā kukkuḷā, saṅkhārā kukkuḷā, viññāṇaṃ kukkuḷaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati, saññāyapi nibbindati, saṅkhāresupi nibbindati, viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

136. At Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, form is hot embers, feeling is hot embers, perception is hot embers, formations are hot embers, consciousness is hot embers. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are liberated. In one who is liberated, the knowledge arises: “I am liberated.” They understand: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.”' The first.

2. Aniccasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Impermanence

137. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Rūpaṃ[P 3.0178], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Vedanā aniccā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

137. At Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon desire for it. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? Form, bhikkhus, is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it. Feeling is impermanent… perception… formations… consciousness is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it. Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon desire for it.' The second.

3. Dutiyaaniccasuttaṃ

3. The Second Discourse on Impermanence

138. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0162][M 2.0146]. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Vedanā aniccā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

138. At Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon lust for it. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? Form, bhikkhus, is impermanent; you should abandon lust for it. Feeling is impermanent… perception… formations… consciousness is impermanent; you should abandon lust for it. Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon lust for it.' The third.

4. Tatiyaaniccasuttaṃ

4. The Third Discourse on Impermanence

139. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo[T 3.0218]. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Vedanā aniccā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

139. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, in that you should abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? Form, bhikkhus, is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire and lust. Feeling is impermanent… perception… formations… consciousness is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is impermanent, in that you should abandon desire and lust.” The Fourth.

5. Dukkhasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Suffering

140. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo…pe… yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

140. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, in that you should abandon desire… Whatever, bhikkhus, is suffering, in that you should abandon desire.” The Fifth.

6. Dutiyadukkhasuttaṃ

6. The Second Discourse on Suffering

141. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo…pe… yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

141. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, in that you should abandon lust… Whatever, bhikkhus, is suffering, in that you should abandon lust.” The Sixth.

7. Tatiyadukkhasuttaṃ

7. The Third Discourse on Suffering

142. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

142. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, in that you should abandon desire and lust… Whatever, bhikkhus, is suffering, in that you should abandon desire and lust.” The Seventh.

8. Anattasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Not-Self

143. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0163]. “Yo, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Ko ca, bhikkhave, anattā? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Vedanā anattā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Yo, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

143. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, in that you should abandon desire. And what, bhikkhus, is not-self? Form, bhikkhus, is not-self; in that you should abandon desire. Feeling is not-self… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, in that you should abandon desire.” The Eighth.

9. Dutiyaanattasuttaṃ

9. The Second Discourse on Not-Self

144. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0147]. “Yo, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo[P 3.0179]. Ko ca, bhikkhave, anattā? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Vedanā anattā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Yo, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo”ti. Navamaṃ.

144. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, in that you should abandon lust. And what, bhikkhus, is not-self? Form, bhikkhus, is not-self; in that you should abandon lust. Feeling is not-self… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self; in that you should abandon lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, in that you should abandon lust.” The Ninth.

10. Tatiyaanattasuttaṃ

10. The Third Discourse on Not-Self

145. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Yo, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Ko ca, bhikkhave, anattā? Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Vedanā anattā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yo[T 3.0219], bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti. Dasamaṃ.

145. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, in that you should abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is not-self? Form, bhikkhus, is not-self; in that you should abandon desire and lust. Feeling is not-self… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self; in that you should abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, in that you should abandon desire and lust.” The Tenth.

11. Nibbidābahulasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on Being Full of Disenchantment

146. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Saddhāpabbajitassa, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa ayamanudhammo hoti – yaṃ rūpe nibbidābahulo nibbidābahulaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) vihareyya. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe nibbidābahulo vihareyya. Yo rūpe nibbidābahulo viharanto, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe nibbidābahulo viharanto rūpaṃ parijānāti, vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ parijānāti; so rūpaṃ parijānaṃ [V 2.0164] vedanaṃ parijānaṃ saññaṃ parijānaṃ saṅkhāre parijānaṃ viññāṇaṃ parijānaṃ parimuccati rūpamhā, parimuccati vedanāya, parimuccati saññāya, parimuccati saṅkhārehi, parimuccati viññāṇamhā, parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi; ‘parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

146. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for a clansman who has gone forth in faith, this is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma: that he should dwell being full of disenchantment towards form… towards feeling… towards perception… towards formations… that he should dwell being full of disenchantment towards consciousness. One who, while dwelling being full of disenchantment towards form… feeling… perception… formations… and consciousness, fully understands form… feeling… perception… formations… and consciousness. He, by fully understanding form… feeling… perception… formations… and consciousness, is liberated from form, is liberated from feeling, is liberated from perception, is liberated from formations, is liberated from consciousness; he is liberated from birth, aging and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I say.” The Eleventh.

12. Aniccānupassīsuttaṃ

12. The Discourse on Contemplating Impermanence

147. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Saddhāpabbajitassa, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa ayamanudhammo hoti – yaṃ rūpe aniccānupassī vihareyya. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe aniccānupassī vihareyya…pe… ‘parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

147. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: that he should dwell contemplating impermanence in form. In feeling… in perception… in formations… in consciousness, he should dwell contemplating impermanence… ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I say.” The Twelfth.

13. Dukkhānupassīsuttaṃ

13. The Discourse on Contemplating Suffering

148. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0148]. “Saddhāpabbajitassa, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa ayamanudhammo hoti – yaṃ rūpe dukkhānupassī vihareyya. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe dukkhānupassī vihareyya…pe… ‘parimuccati [P 3.0180] dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Terasamaṃ.

148. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: that he should dwell contemplating suffering in form. In feeling… in perception… in formations… in consciousness, he should dwell contemplating suffering… ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I say.” The Thirteenth.

14. Anattānupassīsuttaṃ

14. The Discourse on Contemplating Not-Self

149. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0220]. “Saddhāpabbajitassa, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa ayamanudhammo hoti – yaṃ rūpe anattānupassī vihareyya. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe anattānupassī vihareyya. (So rūpe) anattānupassī viharanto, vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe anattānupassī viharanto rūpaṃ parijānāti, vedanaṃ…pe… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ parijānāti. So rūpaṃ parijānaṃ vedanaṃ parijānaṃ saññaṃ parijānaṃ saṅkhāre parijānaṃ viññāṇaṃ parijānaṃ parimuccati rūpamhā, parimuccati vedanāya, parimuccati saññāya, parimuccati saṅkhārehi, parimuccati viññāṇamhā[V 2.0165], parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi; ‘parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Cuddasamaṃ.

149. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: that he should dwell contemplating not-self in form. In feeling… in perception… in formations… in consciousness, he should dwell contemplating not-self. Dwelling thus contemplating not-self in form, in feeling… in perception… in formations… in consciousness, he fully understands form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Fully understanding form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, he is liberated from form, liberated from feeling, liberated from perception, liberated from formations, liberated from consciousness; he is liberated from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. ‘He is liberated from suffering,’ I say.” The Fourteenth.

Kukkuḷavaggo cuddasamo.

The Chapter on Embers, the Fourteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for this chapter:

Kukkuḷā tayo aniccena, dukkhena apare tayo;

Anattena tayo vuttā, kulaputtena dve dukāti.

The Embers, three with impermanence, another three with suffering; three are spoken on not-self, with the clansman, and two concerning suffering.

15. Diṭṭhivaggo

15. The Chapter on Views

1. Ajjhattasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Internal

150. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 3.0221]. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkha”nti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā [P 3.0181] no, bhante, dhammā…pe… “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati rūpaṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Vedanāya sati…pe… saññāya [M 2.0149] sati… saṅkhāresu sati… viññāṇe sati viññāṇaṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya uppajjeyya ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkha”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya uppajjeyya [V 2.0166] ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkha”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

150. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, clinging to what, does internal pleasure and pain arise?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…pe….” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, clinging to form, internal pleasure and pain arise. When feeling exists…pe… when perception exists… when formations exist… when consciousness exists, clinging to consciousness, internal pleasure and pain arise. What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would internal pleasure and pain arise without clinging to it?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is feeling…pe… perception… formations… is consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would internal pleasure and pain arise without clinging to it?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus…pe… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The first.

2. Etaṃmamasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on ‘This Is Mine’

151. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassatī”ti[T 3.0222]? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe… “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati, rūpaṃ upādāya, rūpaṃ abhinivissa [P 3.0182] …pe… viññāṇe sati, viññāṇaṃ upādāya, viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe… vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attāti samanupasseyyāti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ bhante”…pe… vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attāti samanupasseyyāti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ passaṃ..pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

151. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does one regard thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…pe….” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, by clinging to form, by adhering to form…pe… when consciousness exists, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, one regards thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” …pe… “Regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would one, without clinging to it, regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” …pe… “Regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would one, without clinging to it, regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus…pe… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Second.

3. Soattāsuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on 'That Self'

152. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0167]. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘so attā, so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’”ti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe…. “Rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati, rūpaṃ upādāya, rūpaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘so attā, so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhāresu [M 2.0150] …pe… [T 3.0223] viññāṇe sati, viññāṇaṃ upādāya, viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati [P 3.0183] – ‘so attā, so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’”ti.

152. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does such a view as this arise: ‘That which is the self is the world; that I shall be after death—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change’?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…pe….” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, such a view as this arises: ‘That which is the self is the world; that I shall be after death—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ When there is feeling…pe… perception… formations…pe… when there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view as this arises: ‘That which is the self is the world; that I shall be after death—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjeyya – ‘so attā, so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjeyya – ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti. Tatiyaṃ.

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, without clinging to it, would such a wrong view arise: ‘That is the self, that is the world; that I shall be after death—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change’?” “Surely not, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, without clinging to it, would such a wrong view arise: ‘That is the self, that is the world; that I shall be after death—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change’?” “Surely not, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus…pe… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The third.

4. Nocamesiyāsuttaṃ

4. It Would Not Be Mine

153. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0168]. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, nābhavissa, na me bhavissatī’”ti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe… “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati, rūpaṃ upādāya, rūpaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi [T 3.0224] uppajjati – ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, nābhavissa, na me bhavissatī’ti. Vedanāya sati… saññāya sati… saṅkhāresu sati… viññāṇe [P 3.0184] sati, viññāṇaṃ upādāya, viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa, evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati – ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, nābhavissa, na me bhavissatī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjeyya – ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, nābhavissa, na me bhavissatī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjeyya – ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, nābhavissa, na me bhavissatī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

153. At Savatthi. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does such a view arise: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine’?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, such a view arises: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine.’ When feeling exists… When perception exists… When volitional formations exist… When consciousness exists, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view arises: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine.’ What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Without clinging to that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would such a view arise: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Without clinging to that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would such a view arise: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine’?” “No, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus… He understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The fourth.

5. Micchādiṭṭhisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Wrong View

154. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0169][M 2.0151]. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa micchādiṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe… “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati, rūpaṃ upādāya, rūpaṃ abhinivissa micchādiṭṭhi uppajjati. Vedanāya sati… micchādiṭṭhi uppajjati. Saññāya sati… saṅkhāresu [T 3.0225] sati… viññāṇe sati, viññāṇaṃ upādāya, viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa micchādiṭṭhi uppajjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ[P 3.0185], bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ…pe… api nu taṃ anupādāya micchādiṭṭhi uppajjeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya micchādiṭṭhi uppajjeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.‘Pañcamaṃ.

154. At Savatthi. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does wrong view arise?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, wrong view arises. When feeling exists… wrong view arises. When perception exists… When volitional formations exist… When consciousness exists, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, wrong view arises. What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And as for that which is impermanent… without clinging to it, would wrong view arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Without clinging to that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would wrong view arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The fifth.

6. Sakkāyadiṭṭhisuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Self-Identity View

155. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa sakkāyadiṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe… “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati, rūpaṃ upādāya, rūpaṃ abhinivissa sakkāyadiṭṭhi uppajjati. Vedanāya sati… saññāya sati… saṅkhāresu sati… viññāṇe sati, viññāṇaṃ upādāya, viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa sakkāyadiṭṭhi uppajjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”[V 2.0170]. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ…pe… api nu taṃ anupādāya sakkāyadiṭṭhi uppajjeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ[T 3.0226], bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ…pe… api nu taṃ anupādāya sakkāyadiṭṭhi uppajjeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

155. At Savatthi. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does self-identity view arise?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…” “Bhikkhus, when form exists, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, self-identity view arises. When feeling exists… when perception exists… when volitional formations exist… when consciousness exists, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, self-identity view arises. What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And as for that which is impermanent… without clinging to it, would self-identity view arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Is feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And as for that which is impermanent… without clinging to it, would self-identity view arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Seeing thus… he understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The sixth.

7. Attānudiṭṭhisuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Self-View

156. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati, kiṃ upādāya, kiṃ abhinivissa attānudiṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti?
